## F198: COMPLETE POSITIONAL GRAMMAR: PS=64-69% PARA TIER; A PS HIERARCHY p(12.41×)>f(9.50×)>k(4.32×)>t(2.72×); B REVERSAL k(9.91×)>f(7.62×)>p(3.71×)>t(2.05×); sh PERFECTLY EXCLUDED FROM B PS; PF-LL: p/f 0.00× EXCLUDED, A=o(1.81×)/ok(1.58×), B=ok(2.71×)/sh(2.66×); NO f1-f16 vs f17+ FOLIO BOUNDARY
**Experiment:** exp_198_grammar_summary
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H194 SUPPORTED — Complete positional grammar table: A-dialect: PS=64.4% PARA, 1.8% LINE_OPEN, 13.5% MID; WP-LF=12.5% PARA, 24.7% LINE_OPEN, 17.6% MID; PF-LL=2.6% PARA, 25.2% MID, 66.9% OTHER. B-dialect: PS=69.3% PARA, 3.0% LINE_OPEN, 4.0% MID; WP-LF=20.0% PARA, 24.0% LINE_OPEN, 12.3% MID. A PS onset enrichment: p(12.41×) > f(9.50×) > k(4.32×) > t(2.72×); y(0.25×), d(0.21×) strongly depleted at PS. B PS onset enrichment: k(9.91×) > f(7.62×) > p(3.71×) > t(2.05×) — k jumps to first rank in B; sh perfectly excluded from B PS (0.00×). Para-final LL: p=0.00×, f=0.00× (both dialects); A: o(1.81×)/ok(1.58×)/ch(1.27×) enriched; B: ok(2.71×)/sh(2.66×)/ch(1.81×) enriched; d neutral in A (1.01×) but strongly depleted in B (0.11×). Grammar strictness by section: A: herbal=74.7%, pharma=63.8%, astro=30.8%; B: pharma=80.0%, herbal=77.3%, stars=78.3%, cosmo=62.5%. (2) H131 NOT SUPPORTED (computational) — No folio boundary at f16/f17 in word statistics: f1-f16 avg daiin=5.56%, f17+ avg daiin=6.14% (0.90× — f17+ is slightly HIGHER). All metrics within ±10% across folio groups. The highest-daiin herbal A folios (f25v=22.73%, f32v=18.52%, f37v=18.18%) are all in f17+ range. The aiin-dom/y-dom split does NOT correspond to the f1-f16 folio boundary.
**Limitation:** H194 PF-LL counts are slightly less than paragraph counts (some single-line paragraphs contribute their only line as both PS and PF; here PS and PF are counted separately, so single-line paras may be counted as PF-LL = 0). The v2 classifier has known imprecision for p/t onset words that serve content rather than grammatical roles (stars section has more p/t content words). H131 test is folio-level, not paragraph-level or quire-level; if the aiin-dom split exists at a finer grain, this test may miss it.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Key new findings: (a) B para-start hierarchy puts k first (9.91× enrichment vs A's p-first at 12.41×) — the k/p hierarchy inversion between dialects is newly quantified in the unified table; (b) sh is perfectly excluded from B para-starts (0.00× vs A=0.76×); (c) d-onset is strongly depleted at B para-final (0.11×) while neutral in A (1.01×) — B's para-final grammar is strictly ok/sh-dominant, not d-neutral like A's.
**Magnitude context:** The complete grammar table (finding a) establishes the final quantitative model. The single most striking feature is that PARA tier is 5.2× more common at PS than WP-LF in A (64.4% vs 12.5%) and 3.5× more common in B (69.3% vs 20.0%). This means the Voynichese grammar is strongly para-initial biased — the "PARA" tier words are primarily paragraph-boundary markers, not uniform content words.

## F197: ch-STEM NB CLASSIFIER ACHIEVES 88.7% 4-SECTION ACCURACY (vs 25% CHANCE); SECTION-DISTINCTIVE: cth-FORMS (HERBAL), cthe-FORMS (PHARMA), ched-FORMS (STARS), sh+CLUSTER (COSMO); 39.7% SHARED VOCAB HERBAL-A vs STARS-B; B-EXCLUSIVE = -edy SUFFIX; A-EXCLUSIVE = cth-FORMS; ZIPF α=1.021 AT RANKS 1-1000; 69.2% HAPAX RATE
**Experiment:** exp_197_ch_classifier_zipf
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H195 STRONGLY SUPPORTED — Naive Bayes ch-stem classifier: 88.7% accuracy (n=212 classified, leave-one-paragraph-out CV) vs 25% baseline. Per-section: herbal=89.0%, pharma=84.6%, stars=87.0%, cosmo=96.4%. Section-distinctive ch-stem words by PMI: herbal=cthy(1.39×), cthor(1.33×); pharma=cheom(2.73×), ctheol(2.41×), ctheey(2.10×); stars=cheeo(1.66×), shedain(1.52×), chedal(1.37×), chedar(1.34×); cosmo=shckhedy(2.37×), shecthy(1.99×), sheety(1.96×). The confusion pattern (7 herbal→stars, 3 stars→cosmo) follows section adjacency. (2) H196 SUPPORTED — Herbal A vs Stars B vocabulary overlap (at ≥2 count threshold): 39.7% shared (81/204). Stars B exclusive ch-words (not in herbal A): shedy(107), sheedy(25), cheedy(24), shckhy(21) — ALL use B-dialect -edy/-eedy suffixes. Herbal A exclusive: cthy(81), cthor(34), choiin(10), cthar(10) — ALL are cth-initial. 53 ch-words appear in all 4 groups (herbal A, stars B, herbal B, pharma A): chol, chor, shol, chey, shey are universal grammar words. (3) H199 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — Corpus: 28,300 words, 6,402 types. Zipf α: ranks 1-100=0.660, 1-500=0.926, 1-1000=1.021. Hapax rate: 69.2% (very high vs natural language ~40-50%). Top 100 words cover 43.6% of corpus. Section top words: herbal=daiin(362)/chol(183)/chor(123); stars=chedy(179)/qokeey(156)/qokeedy(132); cosmo=shedy(209)/chedy(174)/qokain(160). Heaps' prediction (α≈1.35-1.52 from β≈0.66-0.74) is not confirmed — actual α=1.021.
**Limitation:** H195 classifier accuracy is leave-one-paragraph-out within a section that contains similar paragraphs (train contamination risk for small sections: cosmo n=32, stars n=23). Production accuracy would be somewhat lower. The Zipf fitting uses log-log regression; alternative fitting methods (MLE power law) may give different α. The 69.2% hapax rate is strongly corpus-size-dependent — with 28K words the hapax rate is expected to be high for any natural language corpus.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Key new finding: ch-stem vocabulary alone is an extremely powerful section discriminator (88.7% accuracy). The section-distinctive words (cth- for herbal, ched-/shed- for stars, sh+cluster for cosmo, cthe- for pharma) provide a vocabulary-level fingerprint for each section. The hapax rate (69.2%) is newly established.
**Magnitude context:** 88.7% accuracy from ch-stems alone is remarkable — it means a classifier using only 24-34% of the words in a paragraph (the ch-stem fraction) correctly identifies the section in 9 of 10 cases. This validates the section-specific ch-vocabulary findings (F109) and establishes that the Voynich text sections are not merely characterized by different positional grammar but by genuinely different vocabularies at the ch-stem class level.

## F196: BARE GALLOWS (p/f/t/k) NEVER AT PARA-STARTS IN ANY SECTION/DIALECT; GALLOWS+ch HIERARCHY IS p+ch>t+ch>k+ch>f+ch; y+ch AND d+ch ARE FUNCTIONALLY DISTINCT WITHIN-PARA OPENERS (y+ch→o/ok SUCCESSOR; d+ch→sh SUCCESSOR); B k-ONSET MORE PS-CONCENTRATED (9.91× vs A 4.32×); B f+ch IS MID-ONLY -edy VOCABULARY; GRAMMAR STRICTNESS IS SECTION-DRIVEN NOT LENGTH-DRIVEN
**Experiment:** exp_196_grammar_structure
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H161 SUPPORTED — y+ch and d+ch are BOTH excluded from para-starts (0/163 each in A). Within-para, they have opposite successor profiles: after y+ch lines, next line favors o-onset (2.52×) and ok-onset (2.04×); after d+ch lines, next line favors sh-onset (1.77×) and avoids ok (0.22×) and d (0.36×). They co-occur in 17.8% of A paragraphs (not strictly complementary). (2) H171 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — Bare gallows (p, f, t, k as exact words) are NEVER at para-starts in any section or dialect (0/163 A, 0/101 B). The gallows hierarchy applies only to gallows+ch compounds. Hierarchy: p+ch(A=11.66%, B=21.78%) > t+ch(A=7.36%, B=10.89%) > k+ch(A=3.07%, B=4.95%) > f+ch(A=2.45%, B=0.99%). f+ch is the weakest para-starter, NOT second (hypothesis was wrong: f is not second to p). B strongly amplifies p+ch (21.78%) and suppresses f+ch (0.99%). (3) H176 SUPPORTED — A k-onset: PS-enriched 4.32× (PS=12.27%, within-para=2.84%). B k-onset: PS-enriched 9.91× (PS=12.87%, within-para=1.30%). B's within-para k@LF is half A's — B k-onset is more strictly confined to PS positions. Both dialects have similar absolute PS rates (12-13%); the difference is that B's k-onset words almost never appear at non-PS line-firsts. (4) H179 SUPPORTED — A f+ch: 18 words, LF=44.4%, MID=55.6%, PS=2.45%, herbal-section dominant (83%). B f+ch: 37 words, LF=13.5%, MID=75.7%, PS=0.99%, stars-section dominant (57%). B f+ch words use B-edy suffix (fchedy=9 tokens = most common B f+ch word) — B f+ch is normal B-dialect vocabulary (not a para-tier marker). (5) H193 SUPPORTED — Grammar strictness is primarily section-driven: herbal A = 74.7% PARA-tier at PS; pharma A = 63.8%; astro = 30.8%. Within herbal A, length has minimal effect (medium 80.77% vs very_long 62.50% — 18-point range vs 44-point cross-section range). Pharma shows reversed length effect (longer pharma paras are MORE strict, not less).
**Limitation:** H161 successor analysis: the "next-line opener" is the first word of the next line within the same paragraph — cross-paragraph transitions are not included. H171 bare gallows result is definitive (total 0 across all sections) but the gallows+ch hierarchy is based on relatively small n for some cells (f+ch at PS = n=4 in A). H179 B f+ch: stars-section concentration (21/37) may reflect that the stars section has many total B paragraphs (23/101), not specifically f+ch enrichment in stars.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Key new findings: (a) bare gallows never appear at para-starts — the positional grammar involves only gallows+ch compounds, not bare gallows; (b) y+ch and d+ch have opposite successor profiles (y+ch→o/ok; d+ch→sh); (c) f+ch is the weakest gallows para-starter, not second (corrects prior assumption); (d) B f+ch has been absorbed into the MID-position vocabulary with -edy suffix.
**Magnitude context:** The bare gallows 0% at PS finding establishes that the gallows letters p/k/t/f are not directly structural — they function at para-starts only when combined with +ch or +sh. This means the PARA-tier marker in Voynichese is the gallows+ch compound, not the gallows letter alone. The y+ch vs d+ch functional distinction (opposite successor profiles) is the first evidence of systematic functional differentiation within the LINE_OPEN tier.

## F195: STARS B PARA-TIER MARKERS ARE OPEN VOCAB (202 UNIQUE IN 246 TOKENS, MEAN SPACING 3.6 LINES); p/f-ONSET PERFECTLY EXCLUDED FROM PARA-FINAL (0.00× BOTH DIALECTS); k/t NOT EXCLUDED (k=0.88-0.93×, t=0.50-1.52×); d-CHAINS MOSTLY DIVERSE (69%); dam EXCLUSIVELY LL/MID IN BOTH DIALECTS (NEVER LF); she-SUCCESSORS: qo(3.33×)/t(2.51×)/qok(2.18×) ENRICHED; ch(0.49×)/d(0.57×) DEPLETED
**Experiment:** exp_195_stars_dam_she
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H356 SUPPORTED WITH CAVEAT — Stars B: 23 paragraphs, 246 non-PS PARA-tier words (mean 10.7 per para). 202 unique marker words — extremely open vocabulary; top-10 = 16.7%. Only `tchedy` appears in 5+ distinct paragraphs (8 tokens, 6/23 paras). Onset: p=52%, t=34.6%, k=9.8%, f=3.7%. Spacing between consecutive PARA-tier markers: mean=3.6, median=3.0 lines; range 1-18, no regular cycle. First PARA-tier marker appears most commonly at line 4 (7/23 paragraphs), range lines 3-33. The open vocabulary and irregular spacing confirm stars PARA-tier words are entry-opening markers, not a closed formulaic label set. (2) H357 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — ONLY p-onset and f-onset are perfectly excluded from para-final in both dialects (A: p=0.00×, f=0.00×; B: p=0.00×, f=0.00×). k-onset is near-neutral (A=0.88×, B=0.93×). t-onset is depleted in A (0.50×) but ENRICHED in B (1.52×, n=2). The pan-gallows exclusion hypothesis is false — exclusion is specific to p and f, not k/t. This refines F194's "p perfectly excluded" claim: it is p AND f that are excluded, but NOT k and t. (3) H358 SUPPORTED — A-dialect d-chain runs (3+): 29 runs. Vocabulary diversity: 20/29 (69%) have 3+ distinct d-final words (diverse). Only 2/29 are identical (both `daiin, daiin, daiin`). Most common d-final word in runs: `daiin` (31). d-chains are grammatical, not formulaic. This supports the F194 d-chain continuity finding (1.47×) as a genuine grammatical regularity, not a repetition artifact. (4) H127 SUPPORTED — dam is exclusively LL or MID in BOTH dialects: A=LF0%, LL64.1%, MID35.9% (n=39); B=LF0%, LL79.2%, MID20.8% (n=24). This contrasts with general d-onset: A is LL-biased (LL=28.7% > LF=19.6%) while B is LF-biased (LF=28.6% > LL=17.5%) — a dialect reversal in d-onset positional preference. dam specifically resists this reversal — it stays LL-dominant in both dialects. dam is a cross-dialectally stable line-final (LL) function word. (5) H147 SUPPORTED — A-dialect she-prefix words (n=279 successor bigrams). Successor onset enrichment: qo=3.33×, t=2.51×, qok=2.18×, qot=1.67×, k=1.58× (all enriched). ch=0.49× and d=0.57× (depleted). Top specific successors: qodar(17.1×), qokor(9.5×), qockhy(6.1×), qokol(5.0×). she-words at para-starts: 1.84% vs within-para 0.77% → 2.38× enriched at PS. she- words selectively license qo-complex and gallows successors while avoiding ch/d words.
**Limitation:** H357 t-onset enrichment in B (1.52×) is based on n=2 para-final t-onset words — direction established but unstable. dam cross-dialect finding (H127) is also based on moderate n (A=39, B=24) — reliable for the LF=0 claim but LL% estimates have uncertainty ±10%. H147 she-word sample (n=279 successors) is from A-dialect only; B-dialect she-word profile is untested. Stars PARA-tier spacing (H356) treats first word only as the potential marker — words later in the line are not tested for PARA-tier. h358 d-chain detection is within-paragraph only; cross-paragraph d-runs not measured.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Key new finding: dam is cross-dialectally LL-specific (never LF) while other d-onset words show dialect reversal. This establishes dam as the clearest known cross-dialect positional anchor. The p+f exclusion from para-final (0.00×) is confirmed; the k/t non-exclusion refines prior claims. The she-qo-complex affinity is newly established.
**Magnitude context:** dam's LF=0 in both dialects is one of the cleanest positional constraints in the corpus. Combined with dam's LL dominance (64-79%), dam appears to function as a line-terminal marker rather than a content word. The H357 refinement (only p/f, not k/t, excluded from para-final) is important: it means the grammatical polarity is para-STARTS: any gallows word; para-ENDS: no p-onset or f-onset words. k/t can appear at both ends; p/f appear only at starts. The she-qo affinity (3.33×) is the first strong within-line co-occurrence regularity involving qo-onset words.

## F194: BIO MULTI-PARA FOLIOS HAVE SHORTER PARAGRAPHS (15.1 vs 38.7 LINES) AND NEAR-INDEPENDENT VOCABULARY (JACCARD 0.004–0.156); A PARA-FINAL LAST WORD IS ok/o/ot-ENRICHED (1.31-1.66×); d-ONSET IS NEUTRAL AT PARA-FINAL; p-ONSET PERFECTLY EXCLUDED FROM PARA-FINAL IN BOTH DIALECTS; STARS PARAGRAPHS HAVE PARA-TIER WORDS THROUGHOUT (13-43% at LINES 3+); d-CHAIN CONTINUITY IS REAL (1.47×)
**Experiment:** exp_194_para_structure_tests
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H078 SUPPORTED — Bio folios: 13 single-para (mean 38.7 lines/para) vs 7 multi-para (mean 15.1 lines/para, 19 total paragraphs). Multi-para bio folios include f75r(2), f75v(3), f82r(2), f83r(4), f83v(2), f84r(2), f84v(4). Pairwise Jaccard between paragraphs on same bio folio: 0.004-0.156 (mean ~0.08), near-zero overlap — each paragraph describes an independent scene. Multi-para folios have shorter paragraphs (2.6× shorter) AND near-independent vocabulary between paragraphs. (2) H101 SUPPORTED — A para-final last word: o-onset (1.66×), ok (1.47×), ot (1.31×), ch (1.29×) enriched. d-onset is NEUTRAL (0.98× — para-final ≠ para-signal for d despite d being enriched at line-finals generally vs corpus average). p-onset perfectly excluded (0.00×). B para-final last word: ok (2.51×), sh (2.69×), ch (1.70×) enriched; d-onset depleted (0.42×); l depleted (0.21×); p perfectly excluded (0.00×). p-onset exclusion from para-final is CROSS-DIALECT (A=0.00×, B=0.00×). (3) H126 NOT SUPPORTED — Tripartite B model: PS PARA-tier opener = 70.4% (strong); within-para -am = 13.9% (moderate); para-final last word o-onset (bare) = 5.1% (weak). (4) H165 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — After d-final line: d+ch opener next line = 6.6% (1.47× enriched); y+ch suppressed (0.67×). After o-final line: d+ch = 0.28× (strongly avoided). Multi-line d-closer runs: 52 runs of length 3, 19 of length 4, 4 of length 5. No strong o-chain. (5) H186 SUPPORTED — Stars B: 23 paragraphs, mean 47.1 lines (range 37-54). ALL 23 paragraphs have multiple PARA-tier openers at non-PS positions (lines 3+). PARA-tier rate at lines 3+ = 13-43% (vs ~0% in herbal A). No regular N-line cycle; mean ~2.5 lines between PARA-tier words in stars. Lengths do not correspond to astronomical numbers (47/12=3.9; 45/36=1.25 — no clean multiples). (6) H187 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — PARA PS → LINE_OPEN at line 2: A=33%, B=24%. ok-onset OTHER PS → LINE_OPEN = 33% (same as PARA tier!). d-onset OTHER PS → LINE_OPEN = 0%. Stars PARA-tier analysis uses v2 classifier which has lower precision for PARA tier in content-rich sections; stars vocabulary may include more p/t-initial content words, inflating PARA rate by 5-10 percentage points. d-chain run detection uses consecutive d-final lines within paragraphs only; cross-paragraph chains are not measured.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Key new findings: (a) p-onset is cross-dialectally excluded from para-final positions (extending para-start exclusivity to para-end exclusivity), (b) stars paragraphs have a fundamentally different grammatical register with PARA-tier words throughout, (c) d-onset is line-final enriched generally but NOT para-final enriched specifically.
**Magnitude context:** The stars paragraph PARA-tier-throughout finding is the most structurally surprising result. Herbal A drops to 0% PARA-tier from line 3+; stars B maintains 13-43% continuously. This suggests each zodiac entry within a stars paragraph uses a p/k/t-onset marker, creating a catalog structure where individual items are marked within a larger paragraph frame. The p-onset para-final exclusion (0.00× both dialects) paired with the 70% PARA-tier para-start rate establishes a perfect grammatical polarity: p-onset words appear ONLY at para-starts (never at para-ends).

## F193: 'r' IS A MID-CONFINED ch-FRAME PARTICLE; BARE 'r' NEVER AT LF (0/26); ch→r=2.04×, r→ch=1.82×; r IS 3.1× MORE COMMON IN B; cth MAXIMUM CHAIN = 3 (2 LINES IN A)
**Experiment:** exp_193_r_word_cth_chains
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) 'r' word profile (A-dialect, n=53 r-onset words, 49% bare 'r'): Bare 'r' is strictly mid-line — 0/26 occurrences at LF, MID-enriched (1.36×), LL-depleted (0.48×). This bilateral ch↔r association is confirmed from both directions. Multiple [ch][r][ch] sequences identified in full lines (f20.8: cheo r cheody; f24.5: cho r chey; f8.5: do r cheeey). qot also enriched before r (2.05×, n=3). Folio distribution: r-onset words appear in ~27 distinct folios but concentrated in f8 (6), f49 (5), f101 (6). (2) B-dialect r-words: n=334 (1.63% rate) — 3.1× more common than A (0.52%). B has an extensive r-vocabulary: raiin (47), bare 'r' (37), rain (16), rol (15), rar (14), ral (13), ror (11), rchedy (10), ram (10) — r-onset is a B-dominant onset class. (3) cth chain length: A-dialect maximum = 3; only 2 lines have 3-chain runs: f6.16 (`cthar cth[a:o]r cthy`) and f7.2 (`cthol cthy cthd`). Length-2 chains: 19. B-dialect maximum = 2 (1 case: f113: ctheey ctharad). No cth-chains of length 4+ in the corpus. (4) [oty][l@LL]: 3/14 oty@penultimate → l@LL (2.30× enrichment) — same signal as general [oty][l] (2.37× from F185); not a distinct sub-construction.
**Limitation:** A r-onset sample is small (n=53). Artifact tokens in r-words (r,shor; r,aiin; ro,dar) — ~5 artifact cases. cth chain analysis excludes artifact-containing cth-words (some chains may be longer if artifacts were resolved). [oty][l@LL] n=3 — directional only.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Extends F187 (ch_e↔r bidirectionality). No committed claim contradicted. The bare 'r' LF=0 finding is new — it establishes 'r' as a strict mid-line form in A.
**Magnitude context:** Bare 'r' being strictly MID-confined (0/26 at LF) is one of the strongest positional constraints observed in A-dialect. The ch→r (2.04×) and r→ch (1.82×) enrichments together with the LF=0 constraint identify 'r' as a grammatical function word in a ch-frame construction, not a regular content word that happens to be rare. B's 3.1× higher r-rate suggests 'r' is primarily a B grammatical feature that appears in A at much lower frequency.

## F192: [oty][l@LL] IS SAME SIGNAL AS [oty][l] (2.30≈2.37×); cthey LINE CONTEXTS DIVERSE; NO cthey→ch→cthey CYCLE; B cthey APPEARS IN 10 LINES ACROSS 10 FOLIOS

The [oty][l@LL] sub-construction is not distinct — it is the same signal as [oty][l], with half the cases having l-word at LL and half mid-line. (2) B-stars (f103+) oty@penultimate: 7 lines; 2/7 close with l@LL (28.6%). (3) cthey in B: 10 lines, folios 26/33/43/46/48/83/104/106/108/113 — diverse sections (bio, stars, scattered). cthey appears in varied line contexts, no formulaic pattern. cthey→ch bigrams: 3 cases (chol, chey, chedain — all different). [cthey][ch][cthey] trigrams: 0. No cyclic cthey→ch→cthey construction.

**Commitment status:** Not committed. No committed claim contradicted.

Combined with cthey@LF→ch_e (2/2 in F191), the [cthey][ch] pattern suggests cthey is a line-initial marker that introduces ch-onset vocabulary, but the ch-word does not "return" to cthey.

## F191: B-cthedy/cthey LF-ENRICHED (20%, 1.68× B-BASELINE) ≠ chedy/shedy; cthdy LL-ENRICHED (33%, 2.77×); cthey@LF→ch_e BOTH CASES; cthedy/cthey HAVE DISTINCT SUCCESSOR ONSET CLASSES; cthdy IS B-LINE-TERMINAL
**Experiment:** exp_192_cth_chain_structure
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** B-dialect cth-words occupy grammatical positions distinct from other B-edy words: (1) cthedy (n=10): LF=20%, second=20%, MID=50%, LL=10% — LF enriched at 1.68× vs B-baseline (11.9%). (2) cthey (n=10): identical to cthedy — LF=20%, second=20%, MID=50%, LL=10%. (3) cthdy (n=6): LF=0%, MID=67%, LL=33% — LL enriched at 2.77×. Compare to chedy (LF=3.1%, MID=80.2%, LL=5.5%) and shedy (LF=6.1%, MID=73.9%, LL=2.5%) — both are MID-dominant with depleted LL. cthedy and cthey are LF-enriched (line-openers) unlike chedy/shedy. cthdy is LL-enriched (line-closer), parallel to A-dialect cthy (LL=1.81× from F161). (4) Successor onset classes: cthedy→l (5.79×) and ot (5.07×) [F183]; cthey→ch (2.17× general); cthey@LF→ch_e specifically (2/2 cases: chey, chedain). cthedy and cthey have different successor onset preferences despite identical positional profiles. (5) cthdy@LL: all LL cases confirmed (f78.31, f108.9).
**Limitation:** Small n (cthedy=10, cthey=10, cthdy=6). cthey@LF→ch_e based on n=2. Positional enrichments are real but unstable at n=6-10.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Extends F189 (B cth-vocabulary) and F173 (B-cth positional profile). F173's "cthedy LF=1.53×/cthey LF=1.69×" finding is confirmed and expanded. No committed claim contradicted.
**Magnitude context:** cthdy LL=33% (2.77×) makes it a B-dialect line-terminal analogue of A-dialect cthy (LL=1.81×). The parallel is striking: A uses cthy@LL; B uses cthdy@LL. The cth onset class has dialect-specific terminal forms. cthedy/cthey as line-openers suggests they function as B-dialect topic markers or determiner-like elements.

## F190: qok SYSTEMATICALLY AVOIDS cth IN BOTH DIALECTS (A:0.54×, B:0.17×); [ch][daiin][cth] HAS DIVERSE ch-WORDS; DAIIN IS UNIVERSAL ch→cth BRIDGE; cthol IS DOMINANT cth IN [d][cth][d]; 3-CONSECUTIVE cth CONFIRMED
**Experiment:** exp_192_cth_chain_structure
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) H339: qok→cth depletion in A = 0.54× (10 observed, 18.5 expected); B = 0.17× (1 observed). qok has 529 words in A (ample sample). qok prefers ok (1.77×), qok-self (1.62×), ch (1.21×) — morphologically parallel successors. cth is incompatible with qok. This extends the cth-introduction grammar to a negative constraint: qok-onset does NOT introduce cth. (2) H346: [d][cth][d] = 16 trigrams. cthol is the dominant cth-word (5/16). daiin left: 8/16 (50%); daiin right: 5/16 (31%). [daiin][cth][daiin] bilateral bracket: only 2/16 (12.5%). After cth, d-words diversify to dam (2×), dol (3×) — the right d-word favors line-closing forms. (3) H348: [ch][daiin][cth] = 12/20 of all [ch][d][cth] trigrams. daiin is the universal bridge (60% of d-words between ch and cth). ch-words are diverse: chol(3×), chor(2×), 7 others(1×). cth-result: cthy dominant (4/12). (4) H340: cth self-succession (23 cases): cthy dominant cth2 (7/23=30%); [cthol][cthy]=1 case only; 3-CONSECUTIVE cth-WORDS confirmed in f6.16 (4-word line: `cthar cth[a:o]r cthy...`) and f7.2 (`...daiin cthol cthy cthd`). cth-chains of length ≥3 exist. (5) H344: [daiin][cthol][cthy]=1 case (f7.2). H349: daiin symmetric around cthol — no asymmetry (54% left vs 43% right). (6) H343: qok→l = 7 cases (2.44×), 1/folio — same class-level pattern as qot→l.
**Limitation:** Artifact tokens inflate counts in H346 (~2/16 with artifacts), H348 (~2/20). cth-consecutive-3 lines have artifact tokens in cth-word names (f6.16: `cth[a:o]r`; f7.2: `ch{cphh}y`). Small n throughout.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Extends F165 (5-construction cth grammar) with new negative constraint (qok depletes). No committed claim contradicted.
**Magnitude context:** The 3-consecutive-cth finding (f6.16, f7.2) is the most structurally significant result: cth-words can form long adjacency chains, suggesting a cth-phrase grammar rather than simple bigram enrichment. The universal daiin bridge ([ch][daiin][cth]) and the cthol dominance in [d][cth][d] together suggest that the core cth-chain grammar is: [ch-word] → (daiin) → [cthol] → [cthy] — a chain where cthol is the medial cth-word and cthy is the terminal.

## F189: B-DIALECT ch→cth=1.96× (14 CASES/8 CLEAN) IS B-SUFFIX CO-SELECTION; cthedy/cthey/cthdy ARE GENUINE B-VOCABULARY; A cth-EXCLUSIVE CLAIM NARROWED
**Experiment:** exp_191_bigram_specifics
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) B-dialect ch→cth: 14 total bigrams (8 clean, 6 with artifact tokens), enrichment 1.96×. B-ch words driving the construction: chedy (2×), chody (2×) — B-typical -edy/-ody suffixes. B-cth words following ch: cthdy (4×), cthey (3×), cthedy (2×) — B-typical -dy/-ey/-edy suffixes. This is a B-dialect suffix co-selection pattern: [ch+B-suffix] → [cth+B-suffix]. Concentrated in f46/f48 (B-bio) and f113 (B-stars). A-dialect ch→cth = 88 cases (1.33×) — B enrichment (1.96×) stronger despite far fewer B cth-words overall. (2) B-dialect cth vocabulary: 52 tokens total (46 clean), 21 unique. Top items: cthedy (10), cthey (10), cthdy (6), cthy (4), cthar (3). All three dominant B-cth forms (cthedy/cthey/cthdy) appear across multiple folios in B-bio AND B-stars sections; none concentrated in pharma. A-dialect has only 1 cthedy occurrence vs B's 10. (3) F047 "cth=A-exclusive" is narrowed: cth-onset appears in B with B-suffixes at 0.25% rate (52/20,490) — low frequency but genuine B-vocabulary, not scribal error or transcription artifact.
**Limitation:** Artifact token inflation (6/14 B ch→cth cases contain ZL3b artifacts). Clean enrichment estimate: ~8 clean cases → enrichment ≈ 1.5× (still positive). B cth-word counts (n=10, n=6) are small for fine-grained folio distribution analysis.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Narrows F047 ("cth=A-exclusive"): cth appears in B at 0.25%, with B-dialect suffixes; the A-exclusive label applies to the A cth rate (3.77%) not its absolute absence in B.
**Magnitude context:** B ch→cth enrichment (1.96×) is stronger than A ch→cth enrichment (1.33×), suggesting that the ch→cth transition is relatively more important in B despite B's lower absolute cth rate. The B-suffix co-selection pattern implies that B-dialect constructs ch and cth onset words using the same suffix grammar.

## F188: t→ot=1.81× (n=16, A-DIALECT); k→cth=1.57× (n=18); kchor DOMINANT k-WORD; cthy DOMINANT cth RESULT AFTER k; tchy DOMINANT t-WORD; ALL CLASS-LEVEL
**Experiment:** exp_191_bigram_specifics

Several cases contain artifact tokens (~3/16). (2) A-dialect k→cth: 18 bigrams (enrichment 1.57×). kchor is the dominant k-word (3/18 cases → cthol, cthaiin, cthy). cthy is the dominant cth-word result (4/18). ky appears 2× as k-word. All 18 pairs are distinct — class-level enrichment. k-words include compounds with ch- (kchor, kchol-variants), suggesting k-ch compounds specifically target cth successors. ~5/18 cases contain artifact tokens.
**Limitation:** Artifact inflation in both findings (t→ot ~3/16 cases, k→cth ~5/18 cases). Clean estimates: t→ot ~13 cases (~1.5×), k→cth ~13 cases (~1.2×). Small n for reliable word-level analysis.

## F187: ch_e↔r BIDIRECTIONAL 2.55× (n=6 EACH); 'r' IS PREDOMINANTLY BARE SINGLE-CHAR WORD; ch→r=15 CLEAN CASES; cho DOMINANT ch-WORD
**Experiment:** exp_191_bigram_specifics
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** (1) A-dialect [ch_e→r]: 6 cases, enrichment 2.55× (base ch_e=5.3%, r=0.52%; expected 2.35 cases). ch_e words: cheo (2×), cheol (2×), chey (1×, artifact token case), chey (1×). r-words: bare 'r' (2 cases), ro (1), raiin (1), rar (1), ram (1, artifact case). (2) [r→ch_e]: 6 cases, enrichment 2.55×. r-words: predominantly bare 'r' (3/6). ch_e words: cheey (2×), chey (1×), cheeey (1×), chear,een (1×, artifact), cheody (1×, artifact). (3) The bare single-character word 'r' (n=26 in A-dialect, 53 total A+B) is specifically attracted to ch_e words in both directions — [r][ch_e] and [ch_e][r]. (4) Broader ch→r pattern: 21 total bigrams (15 clean), enrichment 1.64× (clean estimate). cho is the dominant ch-word (4/21). ch_e words contribute 6/21 (the H333 subset). **Magnitude context:** 'r' being a single-character word that bidirectionally attracts ch_e words suggests it may be a grammatical function word (particle, preposition, or article fragment) in a grammatical frame with the ch_e word class. The bidirectionality (both [ch_e][r] and [r][ch_e] enriched at 2.55×) implies grammatical adjacency — 'r' and ch_e words appear as adjacent pairs regardless of ordering, consistent with a fixed grammatical construction.

## F186: [dchor][cthor] IS 15.54× ENRICHED (n=1 CLEAN); [dchor@LF][cth@second] BOTH LINES CONFIRM ONSET REDUPLICATION; dchor@LF → cth@second AT 4.42×
**Experiment:** exp_191_bigram_specifics
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Both [dchor@LF][cth@second] lines (identified in F169/exp_162) are confirmed and characterized: (1) f25.2: `dchor cthor chor daiin s okeeaiin daiin ckhey daiin` — [dchor] → [cthor] at second position. Clean case: the cth-word is specifically cthor (same r-suffix as dchor). This is an onset reduplication from d+ch+r compound to cth+r compound. (2) f32.10: `dchor ctho,daiin` — [dchor] → [ctho,daiin] where ctho,daiin is a ZL3b artifact (comma joins what appears to be ctho + daiin). The "cth-word" at second is a ctho stem with artifact suffix. (3) [dchor][cthor] enrichment (across all A bigrams, not just LF): 1/20 dchor bigrams = 5.0% vs base cthor rate 0.32% → **15.54× enrichment**. However, n=1 clean case — directional finding only. (4) dchor@LF → second-position onset profile: cth at 4.42× (2/12 = 16.7%), ch at 1.27× (not enriched). dchor@LF specifically selects cth-onset at second position, consistent with F169's 3.98× enrichment reported from exp_162. The same d+ch compound → cth mechanism documented in F185 (4.42×) applies to the dchor-specific variant. **Magnitude context:** The 15.54× enrichment for [dchor][cthor] is consistent with the 4.42× observed for all d+ch@LF→cth@second in F185 — when both the LF word and cth-word share the same -r suffix, the enrichment is even stronger (15.54× vs 4.42×). This supports a suffix-matching dimension to the d+ch → cth construction.

## F185: daiin DRIVES 38% OF d@LF→cth@second; [oty][l-onset]=2.37× IN B-DIALECT (CORRECTED FROM 15.78×); cthor→ot IS 1-PER-FOLIO; ok→ok HAS 15% EXACT SELF-REPETITION
**Experiment:** exp_190_bigram_inventory (results); exp_191_bigram_specifics (baseline correction)

**Finding:** (1) H324: d@LF→cth@second (n=21, 7.9%, enrichment 2.08×) is driven by daiin@LF (8/21=38%, enrichment 2.99×) and d+ch compound openers (dchor/dchol/dchey/dshor: each 16.7%, 4.42×). Pure d-stem words (dar, dor, dair, dol) → 0 cth@second cases. The d@LF→cth@second enrichment requires the d-opener to be a "complex" d-word (daiin or d+ch), not a simple d-stem. (2) H325: cthor→ot = 7 cases (A-dialect), each in a different folio (f9,f10,f14,f19,f24,f42,f52) — 1-per-folio spread confirms structural grammar rule, not formulaic copy. ot-words after cthor are varied (otol×2, oty×2, otal, otam, otydy). [oty][l-onset] in B-dialect: 6/44 B-oty bigrams = 13.6%, B-base l = 5.8% → enrichment **2.37×** [CORRECTED: exp_190 reported 15.78× using A-dialect l-base rate (0.6%) instead of B-dialect l-base rate (5.8%) — wrong baseline for a B-specific finding]. The 6 cases span f80 (B-bio) and f103-f116 (B-stars); 3/6 have l-word at LL position. l-words: lol, lky, lkchy, lchdy, loldy, lchedy. (4) H327: ot→ot enriched 1.84× (26 cases, expected 14.1). Class-level, pairs diverse. (5) H329: [daiin][dam@LL] = 3 immediate bigrams; dam@LL lines are longer than average (mean 7.4 vs A-mean 6.1). Double-daiin before dam ([daiin][daiin][dam]) in f89.17. (6) H330: qot→qot(15), qot→l(4); class-level enrichment, no word-pair formula. (7) H331: ok→ok = 54 cases; 15% are exact same-word self-repetitions. (8) H332: l→l = 3 cases (10.21×, expected 0.29) but all 3 involve tokenization artifacts — uncertain enrichment.
**Limitation:** Several findings involve ZL3b artifact tokens (commas, `<->`, `<$>` in word tokens). H332 results likely partially artifactual. Small n throughout (H325 n=7, H327 n=26, H329 n=3). [oty][l] 15.78× was a baseline error; corrected to 2.37× in exp_191.

**Magnitude context:** The corrected [oty][l] enrichment (2.37×) is real but modest. The categorical absence of [oty][cth] (n=0 across 65 oty bigrams) remains a hard constraint. The d+ch compound enrichment (4.42×) for cth@second is stronger than the overall d@LF→cth@second enrichment (2.08×), confirming that compound d-openers are more predictive of cth than simple d-stems.

## F183: [chol/chor][daiin] AMPLIFIES cth SUCCESSION 5.30× (vs 2.30× WITHOUT daiin); cthedy SELECTS l/ot ONSET CLASS (5.2×/4.5×) NOT SPECIFIC WORDS; cthol→cthy NOT SPECIFICALLY ENRICHED
**Experiment:** exp_188_cth_chain_analysis

**Finding:** (1) H351: In A-dialect (10,258 tokens), [chol/chor][daiin]→cth-word: 5/25 = 20%, enrichment 5.30×; [chol/chor]→cth-word (direct, no daiin): 32/369 = 8.7%, enrichment 2.30×. daiin acts as a bridge amplifier — inserting daiin between chol and the next word increases the probability of the next word being cth-class by 2.3-fold. cthy is the dominant cth-word in the [ch][daiin]→cth chain (4/12 = 33% of cases). (2) H352: B-dialect cthedy (n=10) successors: all 10 are DIFFERENT WORDS, but onset-class enrichment is strong: l-onset 3/10=30% (base 5.8%, enrichment 5.2×) and ot-onset 3/10=30% (base 6.6%, enrichment 4.5×) — confirming F176's 5.79× and 5.07×. cthedy selects successor ONSET CLASS (l or ot) but not a specific word. [cthol][daiin][cthy] absent; the 2 [cthol][daiin][cth*] cases use ctholdar and cthom. cthol's dominant successors are daiin (6×, baseline rate) and chol (3×, depleted for ch-class). cthol and chol have mutual attraction.

## F182: ITALIAN SOURCE (DANTE) PRODUCES am_ll=3.46–3.76× (51–55% VMS) — FAR BELOW LATIN (94–97%); am_ll METRIC DISCRIMINATES BETWEEN LATIN AND ITALIAN MORPHOLOGICAL TYPES
**Experiment:** exp_187_italian_source
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** The position-aware hybrid architecture (cp=0.76, mp=0.9, p_detect=0.90) applied to Dante's Divina Commedia (medieval Italian) produces am_ll=3.46× (narrow CF, CF_rate=5.5%) and 3.77× (broad CF, CF_rate=6.8%) — 51–55% of VMS 6.811×. This is nearly half of what Cicero Latin achieves (6.42×, 94.3% VMS) at the same parameters. Italian is an analytic language: linguistically motivated clause-final morpheme patterns (accented verb endings -à/-ò/-ì, verbal suffixes -ono/-ano/-endo) cover only 5.5–6.8% of tokens in Dante (vs Latin 34–37%). With CF_rate 5.5%, LL am rate ≈ 0.068 → enrichment only 3.46×. An extreme broad-vowel pattern (any vowel-final word, CF_rate=78.5%) gives am_ll=7.35× (107.9% VMS) — technically exceeds VMS but is linguistically unmotivated (maps all Italian nouns/verbs/adjectives indiscriminately). y_lf is also lower in Italian (1.91–2.10) than Latin (2.47–2.65) — Italian clause-initial patterns (qu-/et/ma-/so-) fire less frequently than Latin conjunctions. ss_mean (1.44–1.47) and adj_rate (0.004) are source-independent (copy component drives both). **The am_ll metric discriminates between Latin and Italian source languages**: VMS am_ll (6.811×) is consistent with Latin synthetic morphology (CF_rate 34-37%) and inconsistent with Italian analytic morphology (CF_rate 5-7%). If VMS is a position-sensitive cipher, the source language requires Latin-like morphological boundary density.
**Limitation:** Only Dante's Commedia tested (medieval verse); other Italian texts (prose, different periods) untested. Italian CI detection regex (qu-/et/ma-/so-) not optimized for Italian — may underestimate y_lf. Broad-vowel result (107.9% VMS) is flagged as extreme target-aware; not a plausible mechanism. Medieval Latin formulaic text (ecclesiastical, notarial) also untested.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Directly answers H351. No committed claim contradicted.
**Magnitude context:** Italian narrow am_ll=3.46× is the lowest am_ll produced by any position-aware hybrid variant in this program (vs Latin exp_186: 6.42–6.61×). The gap between Italian and Latin (Δ≈2.96×) is larger than any parameter variation effect explored in exp_182–186.

## F181: POSITION-AWARE HYBRID HAS HARD am_ll CEILING AT 6.61× (97.1% VMS) AT MAXIMUM p_detect=1.00; 3% GAP IS STRUCTURAL TO THE ARCHITECTURE
**Experiment:** exp_186_pdetect_sweep
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Sweeping detection probability p_ll ∈ {0.90, 0.95, 1.00} × p_lf ∈ {0.90, 1.00} at fixed cp=0.76, mp=0.9 (best joint approximation from exp_185) shows: p_ll increase from 0.90 → 1.00 yields am_ll gain of only +0.159× (0.90→0.95: +0.130×; 0.95→1.00: +0.029× — strongly diminishing returns). At p_ll=1.00, p_lf=1.00: am_ll=6.608 (97.0% of VMS 6.811), ss_mean=1.449 (98.9% VMS), adj_rate=0.00426. The remaining gap at p_detect=1.00 is 0.203× (3.0% of VMS) — structural to the architecture. Algebraic explanation: at p_ll=1.00, LL am rate = CF_rate × 1.00 + (1−CF_rate) × 0.02 ≈ 0.342 + 0.658 × 0.020 ≈ 0.355; the 65.8% of LL words lacking clause-final morphemes always receive base-rate -am (≈2%), permanently limiting the enrichment ceiling. Closing the 3% gap would require CF_rate ≈ 41%; no tested classical Latin source reaches this (Caesar: 36.5%, Cicero: 34.2%, Virgil: 34.1%). ss_mean is stable at 1.443–1.468 across all 6 p_detect combinations (within 1.5% of VMS 1.465) — confirming the copy component drives ss_mean independent of cipher calibration. y_lf ceiling at p_lf=1.00: 2.620–2.651 (74.7–75.6% of VMS 3.506) — the LF y-onset gap (~25%) is a separate structural limitation, not addressed by p_detect tuning. The architecture is fully characterized after exp_180–186.
**Limitation:** Only Cicero tested at p_detect=1.00; Caesar (CF_rate=36.5%) would push am_ll to ~6.67 at p_detect=1.00, narrowing the gap from 3.0% to ~2.1%. CF_rate detection regex is broad (includes verb endings at/it/unt appearing mid-sentence). y_lf gap (~25%) is unexplained by cipher architecture. p_ll=1.00 is maximally target-aware (ALL clause-final words → -am deterministically); result is conditional on this calibration — a non-calibrated cipher would produce am_ll ≈ 1.0×.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. F181 supersedes F180 as the final characterization of the hybrid architecture's limits. No committed claim is contradicted.
**Magnitude context:** am_ll=6.608 (97.0% of VMS) at p_detect=1.00 is the closest the architecture can get — any further gain requires architectural change, not parameter tuning. The architecture is "not ruled out" at 3/3 constraints at optimal settings (ss_mean ≈ VMS, adj_rate < VMS, am_ll = 97.1% VMS), but is not positively confirmed (3% am_ll gap remains unexplained).

## F180: TIMM CHAR MODIFICATION CROSSOVER LOCALIZED AT cp≈0.745–0.750: BEST JOINT APPROXIMATION cp=0.76 mp=0.9 → ss_mean=1.454 (99.2% VMS), am_ll=6.460 (94.8% VMS), adj=0.00425; RESIDUAL GAP IS SOLELY am_ll (5–7%)
**Experiment:** exp_185_timm_char_cp_fine_grid
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Fine-grained grid (cp ∈ {0.70, 0.72, 0.74, 0.76, 0.78, 0.80} × mp ∈ {0.7, 0.8, 0.9}, 50 sims each) localizes the VMS ss_mean crossover: at mp=0.8, ss_mean crosses from underproducing (cp=0.74: 1.450, 99.0%) to overproducing (cp=0.76: 1.490, 101.7%). The exact crossover is cp≈0.745–0.750, consistent with the interpolated prediction from exp_183 (predicted 0.745). Best joint approximation of all three VMS metrics: cp=0.76, mp=0.9 yields ss_mean=1.454 (99.2% of VMS 1.465), am_ll=6.460 (94.8% of VMS 6.811), adj_rate=0.00425 (below VMS 0.009). At cp=0.74, mp=0.8: ss_mean=1.450 (99.0%), am_ll=6.331 (92.9%), adj=0.00707. The mechanism does not reach all three VMS targets simultaneously at any parameter combination: ss_mean and adj_rate are satisfied but am_ll remains 5–7% below VMS in the crossover region. am_ll increases with cp (91.9% at cp=0.70 → 95.1% at cp=0.80, mp=0.8), partly driven by denominator effect (higher cp → more buffer tokens → lower corpus am rate → higher enrichment ratio). Pre-registration confirmed: crossover at cp≈0.745 was predicted and observed.
**Limitation:** am_ll gap (5–7%) persists at optimal cp; closing it would require CF_rate ≈ 60% (exp_184 established Latin ceiling at ~86% VMS). LL table is target-aware (am_ll conditional on calibration). A-dialect not tested. Fine-grid boundary (cp=0.745) not directly measured — bracketed by 0.74 and 0.76.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Advances the project beyond F177/F178 — F180 supersedes F177 as the primary discrimination finding for the hybrid architecture. No committed claim is contradicted.
**Magnitude context:** ss_mean=1.454 (99.2% of VMS) at VMS-level adj_rate is the closest any mechanism has come to reproducing VMS ss_mean under all three joint constraints in this experimental program. am_ll=6.460 (94.8% of VMS) at the same parameter setting is likewise the closest to VMS am_ll under joint constraint satisfaction. Prior best (exp_182): ss=1.368 (93.4%), am_ll=6.308 (92.6%), adj=0.0069.

## F179: POSITION-SENSITIVE CIPHER am_ll IS SOURCE-TEXT INDEPENDENT: ALL TESTED LATIN SOURCES (CICERO/VIRGIL/CAESAR) PRODUCE am_ll=5.76–5.86× (84–86% VMS); CLOSING THE GAP WOULD REQUIRE CLAUSE-FINAL RATE ≈ 60% (UNREALISTIC)
**Experiment:** exp_184_latin_source_comparison
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Three Latin sources tested in the strong-calibration (p=0.90) position-sensitive cipher architecture (exp_177 baseline): Cicero De Officiis (am_ll=5.761), Virgil Aeneid (am_ll=5.756), Caesar Gallic Wars (am_ll=5.856). All three produce 84.5–86.0% of VMS am_ll (6.811×). Clause-final morpheme rates (CF_rate): Cicero 34.2%, Virgil 34.1%, Caesar 36.5%. Caesar's slightly higher CF rate produces marginally higher am_ll (+0.094× vs Cicero). Closing the full residual gap (5.76→6.81, Δ=1.05×) would require CF_rate ≈ 60% — unrealistic for any Latin genre (quantitative argument: Δam_ll / Δcf_rate ≈ 4.1×). Virgil poetry produces LOWER y_lf (1.862×) than Cicero prose (2.355×) due to fewer clause-initial conjunctions — the LF table calibration is source-sensitive for y_lf. All sources produce ss_mean ≈ 1.00 and adj_rate ≈ 0.00281 (both identical, independent of source). Replication of exp_177 Cicero baseline: am_ll=5.761 vs 5.756 (Δ=0.005, 0.09% — confirms architecture correct).
**Limitation:** Medieval Latin, institutional/formulaic Latin, and Italian not tested (vulgate.txt on disk is English Douay-Rheims, not Latin). CF_rate detection regex broad (includes at, it which appear mid-sentence); actual syntactic clause-final rate may differ. Detection probability fixed at 90%.
**Commitment status:** Consistent with C002 (ss_mean ≈ 1.00 across all sources). Not separately committed.
**Magnitude context:** am_ll 5.76–5.86× is comparable to exp_177's 5.756× (same architecture, baseline). The source effect (+0.094× Caesar vs Cicero) is far smaller than the VMS–cipher gap (1.05×). No published prior comparison of am_ll across Latin source texts in position-sensitive cipher simulations.

## F178: EXTENDED TIMM CHAR GRID: CROSSOVER AT cp=0.7–0.8; cp=0.8 mp=0.8 FIRST COMBINATION WITH ss_mean ABOVE VMS TARGET AT VMS-LEVEL adj_rate (ss=1.570, adj=0.00798, am_ll=6.501); OPTIMAL cp ≈ 0.745 FOR VMS ss_mean REPRODUCTION
**Experiment:** exp_183_timm_char_extended_grid

## F177: POSITION-AWARE HYBRID + TIMM CHAR MODIFICATION: 8/36 VIABLE (LENIENT); 3/36 AT VMS-LEVEL adj_rate — FIRST MECHANISM TO CROSS VMS adj_rate THRESHOLD; ss_mean IN VMS RANGE [1.2, 1.7] AT VMS-LEVEL adj_rate
**Experiment:** exp_182_timm_char_modification
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** The position-aware hybrid (MID-only copy buffer, separate LF/MID/LL cipher tables from exp_177) with Timm single-character replace/insert/delete modification (exp_182) produces 8/36 viable combinations under lenient thresholds (am_ll ≥ 5.0×, ss_mean ∈ [1.2, 1.7], adj_rate ≤ 0.015). Three combinations achieve adj_rate ≤ VMS level (0.009) while simultaneously satisfying ss_mean ≥ 1.2 and am_ll ≥ 5.0 — the first such result in the experimental program. Best at VMS-level adj_rate: cp=0.7, mp=0.8 yields am_ll=6.308 (92.6% of VMS 6.811), ss_mean=1.368 (93.4% of VMS 1.465), adj_rate=0.0069 (below VMS 0.009). Best overall lenient-viable: cp=0.7, mp=0.6 yields am_ll=6.190, ss_mean=1.424 (97.2% of VMS), adj_rate=0.0140. The three VMS-adj_rate-viable combinations: (1) cp=0.6, mp=0.7: adj=0.0085, ss=1.279, am_ll=6.093; (2) cp=0.6, mp=0.8: adj=0.0060, ss=1.266, am_ll=6.099; (3) cp=0.7, mp=0.8: adj=0.0069, ss=1.368, am_ll=6.308. Mechanistic explanation: Timm modification has ~2% collision rate (1/3 × 1/16 ≈ 2% per modification operation) vs ~17% for suffix-replacing modification (exp_181). The lower collision rate allows adj_rate to decrease faster with MODIFY_PROB without sacrificing ss_mean. Timm modification achieves moderate onset preservation (~79%, vs 0% in exp_180 and 100% in exp_181), placing its ss_mean intermediate between the two prior architectures (f≈0.71 interpolation). Within-MID self-succession (ss_mid) reaches or exceeds VMS target at cp=0.6, mp=0.8 (ss_mid=1.465, equal to VMS ss_mean); full-corpus dilution by LF/LL positions reduces it to 1.266. This result narrows C004: the "0/36 viable at VMS adj_rate" claim applied to the suffix-replacing exp_181 architecture; character-level modification crosses the threshold.
**Limitation:** Three VMS-viable combinations fall short of VMS am_ll (89.5–92.6%) and ss_mean (86.4–93.4%) — the mechanism is "not ruled out" by VMS adj_rate constraint but does not fully reproduce VMS measured values. The LL cipher table is explicitly target-aware (all Latin clause-final morphemes → EVA -am, calibrated in exp_177); am_ll results are conditional on this calibration. EVA character pool for Timm modification is uniform 16-char distribution, not the actual VMS frequency distribution. A-dialect not tested. No external control corpus (comparison is to exp_180 and exp_181 architectures). The three VMS-viable combinations were discovered exploratorily; the experiment was pre-registered only to test whether 0-4 viable combinations would appear.
**Commitment status:** Narrows C004 (C004 "Narrowed by" annotation already applied per human resolution 2026-04-11). Not separately committed.
**Magnitude context:** 3/36 at VMS-level adj_rate is larger than exp_181's 0/36 at same threshold (the previous best). ss_mean=1.368 at VMS-level adj_rate is larger than any prior mechanism at that constraint. adj_rate=0.0069 (below VMS 0.009) is the first time any tested mechanism passes below the VMS adj_rate threshold in the experimental program. No published prior value for Timm char-modification in a position-aware hybrid is available.

## F176: [ch][daiin]→cth=5.89× (COMPOUND PRECURSOR: [ch-nominal][daiin][cth-nominal] GRAMMATICAL CHAIN); cthol SUCCESSOR ENRICHED FOR cth (2.41×) AND d (2.15×); cthedy→l=5.79×, ot=5.07× IN B-DIALECT (DIVERGENT cth-WORD SUCCESSOR PROFILES)
**Experiment:** exp_169_ch_daiin_cth_compound_cthol_asymmetry
**Date:** 2026-04-10
**Finding:** H348 CONFIRMED STRONGLY: [ch][daiin] bigram → cth at 5.89× enrichment (12 observed vs 2.0 expected). [daiin] alone → cth=3.30×. The [ch][daiin] sequence is a compound predictor — when ch is followed by daiin, cth follows at nearly 6× baseline. Dominant pattern: [chol/chor][daiin][cthy] — medial ch-nominals (chol, chor) specifically introduce the [daiin][cth-word] terminal construction. This represents a [ch-nominal][particle][cth-nominal] three-word grammatical chain. H349 NOT CONFIRMED: no daiin-left asymmetry around cthol (daiin=54.5% before vs 42.9% after — roughly symmetric). NEW H349 FINDING: cthol SUCCESSOR is enriched for cth (2.41×) and d (2.15×) — cthol introduces further cth and d-words. [cthol][daiin]=6 (most common cthol successor), [cthol][chol]=3. Predecessor enrichments: qot=2.23×, cth=1.66×. H350 PARTIAL: cthey@LF→ch_e (2/2) is positionally specific (not general). cthey@MID introduces ok-onset (3.35×). MAJOR BONUS: B-cth words have DIVERGENT SUCCESSOR PROFILES: cthedy→l (5.79×) and ot (5.07×); cthey→ok (3.35×) and ch_e (2.47×); cthdy→qok (4.14×) and s (8.83×, n=1). Each B-cth word selects a different successor class.
**Limitation:** [ch][daiin][cth] n=12 cases — 5.89× enrichment is robust but ch-words are diverse (chol/chor dominant but not exclusive). [chol][daiin][cthy] = 3-5 specific cases — directional pattern but small absolute n. cthol d-asymmetry: [d][cthol]=11 and [cthol][d]=14 (adequate for comparing proportions). cthedy successor enrichments (l=5.79×, ot=5.07×) are from n=9 with-successor — strong signal but small n. cthey→ch_e@LF is n=2 (marginal). cthdy bonus successor n=4 (very small, 8.83× for s is n=1).

## F174: [daiin cthol cthy] TRIGRAM = 1 OCCURRENCE (f7); [d][cth][d]=16 IS 2ND MOST COMMON cth ONSET-TRIGRAM; B-DIALECT cth-WORDS HAVE INTERNAL POSITIONAL PARADIGM (cthedy/cthey=LF-ENRICHED 1.53-1.69×; cthdy=LL-ENRICHED 2.41×); qok→l=7 UNIQUE PAIRS IN LATE A-HERBAL/PHARMA
**Experiment:** exp_167_trigram_analysis
**Date:** 2026-04-10
**Finding:** H344 CONFIRMED: [daiin cthol cthy] trigram = 1 occurrence (f7 herbal): `chochy cthy daiin qoky ch{cphh}y daiin cthol cthy cthd`. The f7 line has double-daiin structure; [daiin cthol cthy cthd] terminates the line. After [daiin cthol], next word is diverse (cthy=only 1/6 cases). [daiin][cthor][chol]=2 occurrences (f15, f19) is more recurrent. H342 CONFIRMED WITH MAJOR SURPRISE: B-dialect cthedy (1.53×) and cthey (1.69×) are LF-ENRICHED — they OPEN lines. This is opposite to standard B-edy words (chedy=LF 0.26×, shedy=LF 0.52×, qokedy=LF 0.86×). B-cthdy is LL-ENRICHED (2.41×) — it CLOSES lines. This explains the F173 "near-baseline" finding: it was the AVERAGE of LF-enriched and LL-enriched sub-words. NEW TRIGRAM FINDING: [d][cth][d]=16 is 2nd highest cth onset-trigram (after [ch][d][cth]=17) — cth-words are frequently surrounded by d-words (daiin) on both sides.
**Limitation:** [daiin cthol cthy] n=1 (single occurrence — cannot confirm as formula vs coincidence). [d][cth][d]=16 onset-level trigram aggregates diverse specific d-words (daiin and others). B cthedy n=11, cthey n=10, cthdy n=7: enrichments directional but small absolute n. The F173 "near-baseline" B cth positional profile was a misleading average of internally-split forms — the subform breakdown is more informative.

**Experiment:** exp_166_b_cth_vocabulary_analysis

## F168: [cthor][ot-word]=5.57× BIGRAM ENRICHMENT; oty NEVER PRECEDES cth (0.00×); ot-cth RELATIONSHIP IS BIGRAM-LEVEL NOT LINE-LEVEL (CO-OCCURRENCE=0.98×); cthom→ot=8.22× (n=3)
**Experiment:** exp_161_ot_cth_grammatical_parallelism
**Date:** 2026-04-10
**Finding:** H319 CONFIRMED WITH SURPRISE. cthor→ot-word: 7/31=22.6%, enrichment=5.57× (strongest cth→onset bigram enrichment found). Top ot-successors of cthor: otol (2), oty (2), otydy (1), otam (1), otal (1). 5 bigrams from cthor@MID, 2 from cthor@second. cthom→ot: 1/3=33.3%, 8.22× (tiny-n). cthy→ot: 5/62=8.1%, 1.99× (moderate). cthol→ot: 2/44=4.5%, 1.12× (baseline). SURPRISE: oty NEVER precedes cth (0/21=0.00×). oty is a categorical LL-terminal word (2.08× from F165) that does not introduce cth-words. The asymmetry is directional: [cthor→oty] is allowed (2 cases); [oty→cth] is forbidden. Reverse (ot→cth): LF-enriched ot-words (otchol=2.30×, otaiin=2.52×, otchor=2.21×) show moderate cth-introduction enrichment. otol→cth: ~1.20× (baseline). Line-level co-occurrence of cth and ot in same line = 20.6% vs 21.0% expected (0.98× — near-baseline). The ot-cth structural relationship operates at IMMEDIATE BIGRAM level, not line level. Both ot and cth have 4-way internal positional paradigms (F165, F161), and the [cthor→ot-word] construction integrates them: cthor (second-enriched) hands off to ot-words filling MID or LL slots.
**Limitation:** cthor→ot n=7 (small absolute, but 5.57× enrichment is large). cthom→ot n=1 bigram (8.22× from n=3 is unreliable). oty→cth=0/21 is categorical but 21 observations. The line-level co-occurrence n=adequate (A-dialect full corpus). Structural interpretation (cth-ot grammatical integration) is inference from bigram patterns, not directly observed grammatical categories.

**Experiment:** exp_145_daiin_transition_matrix

**Finding:** H281 CONFIRMED (corrects F148): exp_141's per-word "LF%" combined LF+second positions. These are the positional equivalents in their respective dialects. lk-words: LF=3.9% (0.33×), MID=74.5% (1.15×), LL=10.2% (0.87×) — MORE MEDIAL than cth-words and more LF-depleted than lch-words; lk is the "most purely medial" B l-subgroup. ALL l-B combined: MID=63.3% (0.98×), LL=19.5% (1.65×) — heavily LL-enriched overall due to small l-words (standalone l, lor) acting as line-final particles. BIGRAM CONTEXT: completely different between cth and lch. Before cth: d(20.2%), ch(18.4%), cth(6.1%). Before lch: qok(16.6%), l(12.1%), ch_e(11.8%). After cth: d(19.1%), ch(16.1%), cth(7.7%). After lch: qok(20.4%), l(14.5%), ch_e(6.9%). Both word types are embedded in their respective dialect's grammatical environment — structural parallel does NOT extend to lexical context. CTHOR ANOMALY: cthor has LF=39.4% (vs cthol=20.4%) — anomalously LF-present for a cth-word. This positional distinctness may explain cthor's disproportionate decline in late A-herbal (F147): cthor marks line-opening constructions, a different grammatical role from medial cthol; if late A-herbal has fewer such line-opening constructions, cthor's specific decline reflects a grammatical/content shift.
**Limitation:** The "lchedy↔cthol equivalence" is based on positional counts from all A-dialect (all sections) for cthol and all B-dialect for lchedy; the comparison doesn't control for section or content type differences. The bigram context analysis uses raw onset frequencies without normalization to baseline dialect onset rates — the d/ch dominance before cth reflects A-herbal's d/ch-heavy vocabulary, not necessarily a grammatical preference for d/ch before cth. Sample sizes: cth_A=386 and lch_B=374 are moderate; individual word counts (cthy=84, cthol=49, cthor=33, lchedy=102) are sufficient for per-word positional claims.

## F147: A-Herbal cth Vocabulary Decline MIXED (cthor 0.24× fastest decline, cthaiin STABLE 1.03×, most words proportional ~0.46×); B-Dialect l-Vocabulary = lchedy(102, 100%B)/lk-forms DOMINANT (1120 B vs 59 A l-tokens); loldaiin is A-EXCLUSIVE (not B-form; exp_139 correction); l is B-Dialect Morphological Parallel to A's cth-Prefix
**Experiment:** exp_140_herbal_cth_vocabulary_shift
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H277 PARTIALLY CONFIRMED: A-herbal cth decline (overall T3/T1=0.598×) is non-uniform. cthor disproportionately declines (T1=6.942‰→T3=1.688‰, T3/T1=0.24, 2.5× faster than overall rate). cthaiin is completely stable (T1=1.633‰→T3=1.688‰, T3/T1=1.03). cthol is relatively stable (T3/T1=0.78). Most other cth-words decline proportionally (~0.46×: cthy/cthey/cthar/cthal). Many "disappearing" words in T1 are hapax legomena — expected sampling behavior in a smaller T3 corpus (1777 vs 2449 words). Pattern: GENERAL cth density reduction (most words ~0.46×) PLUS cthor-specific additional decline. cthaiin stability suggests it is a grammatical/particle form (not a content word) immune to the content shift. H278 CONFIRMED: B-dialect l-vocabulary is massive (1120 B-tokens vs 59 A-tokens, 19× ratio) and structurally distinct. Top B l-words: lchedy(102, 100%B), lchey(39, 100%B), lkaiin(37, 100%B), lkeey(33, 97%B), lkeedy(32, 97%B), lshedy(32, 100%B). B l-paradigm: lch-stem forms (l+ch-class stems with B-suffixes: lchedy, lchey, lshedy) and lk-stem forms (lkaiin, lkain, lkedy, lkar, lky, lkchedy — all essentially 100%B). Suffix paradigm: B l-words = 42.3% B-suffix (vs A l-words = 11.9% B-suffix). 376 of 396 B l-types are B-exclusive (not in any A-folio). Stars has 725 B l-tokens (65% of all B l-tokens). CORRECTION: loldaiin (listed in exp_139 as "clean B-form in late A-herbal") is A-EXCLUSIVE corpus-wide (A=1, B=0) — it ends in -aiin (which is in B_SUFFIXES list) but is NOT a B-dialect word. Revised: genuine B-dialect l-forms in late A-herbal = only lkeedy(1, 97%B) and lkeey(1, 97%B). B l-vocabulary is the morphological parallel to A's cth-prefix system: both are productive prefix morphemes (l- in B; cth- in A) on distinct stem classes with opposite suffix paradigms. lchedy (l+ch+edy) parallels cthol (cth+ol) as the canonical content word form.
**Limitation:** The cthor disproportionate decline (T3/T1=0.24) is based on absolute counts of 12 (T1: 17 tokens) and 3 (T3: 3 tokens) tokens — small numbers susceptible to noise. The cthaiin stability (n=4 T1, n=3 T3) is also small-sample. The B l-vocabulary profile conflates all B sections; within-B section variation in l-vocabulary is substantial (stars=725 vs cosmo=349 vs herbal_B=40 tokens). The "19× B:A l-token ratio" could partly reflect text length differences between A and B sections, not just dialect differences.

## F146: A-Herbal cth Decline is SMOOTH GRADIENT (T1=5.96%→T2=4.82%→T3=3.66%, equal −1.1 pp/tertile); l-Gradient STRONGER (ρ=+0.627) than cth-Gradient (ρ=-0.269) in A-Herbal; A-Herbal l-Onset Words Too Sparse (37 total tokens) to Characterize B-Vocabulary Contamination
**Experiment:** exp_139_herbal_cth_breakpoint_l_gradient
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H275 CONFIRMED (SMOOTH GRADIENT): A-herbal cth decline across folio tertiles is equal-interval: T1(f1-f16)=5.96%, T2(f16-f32)=4.82%, T3(f35-f56)=3.66% — drops of −1.14 pp and −1.15 pp per tertile. This equal-interval pattern rules out a single discrete scribal hand-change at a specific folio. The change-point scan best breakpoint is f54 (diff=0.030), but this is the endpoint of a continuous trend, not a discrete transition. Within-window variance is high (f11-f14: 2.6% vs f15: 10-11%), making single-folio breakpoints unreliable. l-rate in A-herbal: T1=0.39%, T2=0.44%, T3=0.92% — l increases in the final tertile. Spearman (87 folio-sides, recto/verso separate): cth ρ=-0.269, l ρ=+0.627. KEY: l-gradient (ρ=+0.627) is STRONGER than cth-gradient (ρ=-0.269) in A-herbal. The l-increase (toward late A-herbal) is more consistent than the cth-decrease. Possible mechanisms for smooth gradient: (1) content gradient — botanical organization places plants with fewer cth-nominal forms later in the herbal section; (2) continuous scribal drift — same scribe gradually shifted vocabulary; (3) dialect-creep — late A-herbal (f42-f56) approaches A/B boundary and shows progressive B-influence (less cth, more l). H276 NOT CONFIRMED (INSUFFICIENT DATA): A-herbal l-onset word total = 37 tokens (16 early, 21 late), nearly all hapax. Suffix paradigm: early B-suffix=0%, late B-suffix=28.6%. But 4/6 "B-suffix" l-words are transcription artifacts (comma-separated multi-part tokens). Clean B-form l-words in late A-herbal: lkeedy(1), lkeey(1), loldaiin(1) — only 3 tokens. Sample too small for statistical inference on B-vocabulary contamination. Corpus-wide, some late A-herbal l-words (lor=91%B, lo=92%B) are predominantly B-dialect, but each appears only once in late A-herbal.
**Limitation:** The recto/verso split (87 folio-sides vs 44 physical folios) introduces within-folio noise in Spearman ρ calculations; exp_138 aggregate-by-folio gives cleaner ρ=-0.353 for cth. The tertile analysis aggregates word counts, so small folios contribute less to each tertile's rate estimate. The l-word sample (37 tokens) is far too small to characterize dialect origin; many l-tokens contain transcription artifacts (commas, brackets, line-continuation markers) that make onset classification unreliable. "Content gradient" vs "scribal drift" cannot be distinguished without metadata on plant species organization.

## F145: A-Herbal cth Gradient REAL in A-Only (ρ=-0.353; early=5.4% → late=3.7%=0.69×); l-Gradient REAL in A-Herbal (ρ=+0.457); Stars cth ρ=+0.469 = NOISE (19 tokens total, F144 stars-cth claim RETRACTED); f47 = Sampling Artifact (n=134, ch=35.1% by chance)
**Experiment:** exp_138_herbal_gradient_stars_cth
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H272 CONFIRMED PARTIAL: A-herbal-only Spearman ρ=-0.353 (44 folios) — genuine cth decline within A-herbal, not solely a B-insertion artifact. B-insertions contribute (all-herbal ρ=-0.486 → A-only ρ=-0.353), but A-herbal itself has a real gradient. Early A-herbal (f1-f28): cth=5.4%, d=17.2%, l=0.4%; late A-herbal (f29-f57): cth=3.7% (0.69×), d=16.0%, l=0.8% (1.84×). The cth vocabulary is stable across periods (cthy/cthol/cthey dominate both) — fewer cth tokens, not different cth words. l-gradient (ρ=+0.457) in A-herbal is equally notable: later A-herbal has more l-onset words (l=0.8% vs early 0.4%), a B-dialect marker. B-herbal folios: all near-zero cth (confirmed pure B-dialect); single early B-folio f26 has cth=2.0% (slightly elevated, possibly bifolio A-spillover). H273 NOT CONFIRMED (NOISE): Stars cth total = 19 tokens across 7748 words (0.25% rate). The F144 ρ=+0.469 is entirely driven by f113 (7 tokens, 0.77%) and f116 (4 tokens, 0.79%); all other stars folios have 0-3 cth tokens. With 12 folios and 19 total tokens, the Spearman correlation is statistically unreliable — this is sampling noise. Stars cth includes both A-type (cthol=2, cthy=1, cthar=1) and B-cth hybrid forms (cthedy=2, ctheey=1, cthdy=1) — no systematic pattern. F144's "STARS cth ρ=+0.469 (UNEXPECTED)" is RETRACTED. H274 CONFIRMED: f47 (herbal/A, 134 words) is a sampling artifact. ch=35.1% (2.06× A-herbal centroid=17.1%) is driven by chol=11 tokens (3.0× rate), chy=6 (4.6×), chdy=3 (34.9×!) — small-sample over-representation by chance. y=0.0% and qo=0.0% are consistent with n=134 sampling from 6.5% and 2.5% rates (probability of zero y in 134 words ≈ (0.935)^134 = ~0.01; individually possible, collectively a sampling artifact). Cosine similarity: herbal=0.8473 (best match), pharma=0.7031, astro=0.6330, stars=0.5280, cosmo=0.4637. f47 is correctly identified as herbal/A; its cosine deviation (dev=0.2375) is explained entirely by the small-sample ch-concentration. No scribal anomaly.
**Limitation:** The A-herbal cth decline (ρ=-0.353) could reflect: (a) genuine scribe change within A-herbal; (b) content shift (later plants have fewer cth-nominal forms); (c) proximity effect (later A-herbal folios f42-57 adjacent to B-cosmo section). These mechanisms cannot be distinguished from onset/suffix data alone. f47 sampling artifact interpretation assumes 134 words is a random draw from the A-herbal distribution — if f47 has unusual content (a specific plant chapter), the ch-concentration could be content-driven rather than purely stochastic. The B-folio f26 cth=2.0% slight elevation is not tested for significance (n=small).

## F143: -am is WITHIN-PARAGRAPH LINE-FINAL (0 occurrences para-final, 0.00×); Para-Final Lines End with "other" Suffix (97.6%); Universal Core (71 words) = 78.9% MEDIAL (vs section-exclusive 60.2%); l/p/cth ABSENT from Universal Core; Cosmo-Absent Words = 55% A-Dialect Driven (cth=10.90× in cosmo-absent); ol/s/l = Cosmo-Positive Features (0.00× in cosmo-absent)
**Experiment:** exp_136_am_paragraph_universal_core
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H266 NOT CONFIRMED (REVERSED): -am=0 at para-final line-ends (0.00× enrichment) across all 260 paragraphs and all sections. Para-final lines are dominated by "other" suffix (97.6%) — paragraph tail lines (=Pt type in ZL3b) end with short words or transcription markers (`<$>`) not in the 16-suffix taxonomy. -am is additionally suppressed WITHIN para-final lines (0.33× vs corpus baseline 1.79% rate). INTERPRETATION: -am is a WITHIN-PARAGRAPH LINE-FINAL MARKER, not a sentence-final marker. The 7.87×/7.48× line-final enrichments (cosmo/stars, F142) operate at within-paragraph line level only. Para-final boundaries have ZERO -am signal. This confirms and strengthens F086/F094 (B -am suppressed at para-final 2.0% vs 12.6%; A -am suppressed at para-final 1.9% vs 6.4%). H267 CONFIRMED: Universal core (71 types, 6708 tokens) is significantly more medially distributed than section-exclusive words: universal=LF:11.6%, MID:78.9%, LL:9.5% vs exclusive=LF:16.1%, MID:60.2%, LL:23.8%. Universal core contains all positional sub-classes: strong openers (saiin=53.5%LF, dain=29.9%LF), strong closers (dy=41.9%LL, dal=26.9%LL, oty=25.6%LL), and strictly medial words (chey=95.7%MID, cheey=96.3%MID, chol=93.1%MID, aiin=92.8%MID). Onset profile of universal core: l(0%), p(0%), cth(0%) ABSENT — the three most dialect/section-specific onset classes are not in the universal vocabulary. s(9.9%, 2.1× exclusive), ot(8.5%, 1.7×), ok(7%), sh(9.9%) enriched in universal core. After-universal bigram context ≈ after-exclusive context (universal words are positionally flexible, context-neutral). H268 CONFIRMED: Cosmo-absent words (73 high-freq types absent from cosmo) are 55% A-dialect dominated (40/73 with ≥70% A tokens). Onset profile: cth=10.90× enriched in cosmo-absent vs cosmo vocabulary (cthy=96.6%A, cthol=96.1%A); ch=3.43×; k=2.58×; y=1.91×; sh=1.49×. Cosmo-POSITIVE onsets (ol/s/l/r/p) are 0.00× in cosmo-absent set — these are cosmo's unique features not shared with other sections. Mechanism: cosmo is B-dialect → universally suppresses cth (F139 confirmed cth depletion in B) → 10.90× depletion of cth in cosmo-absent vocabulary. The 31 words absent from cosmo but present in all 4 others are: chor(87%A), sho(91%A), cthy(97%A), cthol(96%A) = A-dialect herbal nominals; cheo(48%A) = mixed, stars B-concentrated via e-vowel gradient (F141).
**Limitation:** Paragraph detection uses prefix characters (@/*=para-start, +=continuation, ==tail) from EVA ZL3b locus codes. Paragraphs crossing folio pages are split into two paragraphs (folio boundary = implicit para break), which may inflate paragraph count and misidentify some para-final lines. The "other=97.6%" at para-final line-ends may include legitimate para-closing vocabulary not captured by the 16-suffix taxonomy. The 73 "high-freq cosmo-absent words" threshold (≥10 total freq) is arbitrary; some lower-frequency words may tell a different story. The dialect assignment uses folio-level edy/eedy rate which creates one label per physical folio, not per paragraph or scribe.

Astro's low exclusive fraction (38.7%) is consistent with its heterogeneous composition (F140). 71 word types appear in all 5 sections: daiin(641), ol(318), chol(290), qokeey(276), chey(258) — the d-onset and ol particles dominate the universal core. ## F141: ol-Onset = MEDIAL PARTICLE/MODIFIER (MID=74.6%, LF=7.7%); Cosmo-Concentrated (2.06×); ol Self-Chains (pre-ol=ol 1.68×, post-ol=ol 1.89×); ol = standalone "ol" PARTICLE (n=474) + ol+k-stem B-Cosmo Content Words; ch+eo Has VOWEL-GRADIENT: ch+o=27% Stars → ch+eo=40% → ch+eeo=55% → ch+eeeo=100%; Parallels Suffix Gradient edy→eedy→eeedy (36%→48%→63%); e-Vowel Extension Is Stars-Specific Morphological Marker at ALL Levels
**Experiment:** exp_134_ol_onset_cheo_vocab
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H262 CONFIRMED: ol-onset (1333 tokens, 252 types, 63.9% hapax) is a MEDIAL PARTICLE/MODIFIER class (MID=74.6%, LF=7.7% — almost never a line-opener). Section: cosmo=44.9% (2.06×), stars=27.6% (0.79×). Dialect: B=81.5% (1.23×). Two sub-types: (1) standalone "ol" (n=474, 84.2%MID, cosmo=49.2%, B=78.5%) — the -ol suffix as free morpheme/medial particle; (2) ol+k-stem B-cosmo compound words (olkain=76.5%cosmo, olkedy=80%cosmo, olkeedy=44.4%cosmo — all 100%B). ol-CLOSERS: oly=81.8%LL (n=44, cosmo=63.6%), oldy=66.7%LL, olam/oldam=100%LL. ol self-chains: pre-ol ol=1.68×, post-ol ol=1.89× — strongest onset-class self-clustering in corpus (creates "ol-chains" in cosmo lines). Morphological evidence: most ol-words have exact l-equivalents (olkeedy=36 ↔ lkeedy=36; olkain=34 ↔ lkain=34 — SAME frequency!), consistent with ol = o-prefix + l-stem-word (double-prefixed cosmo forms). Suffix: other=43.0% (standalone ol has no suffix — IS a particle), -y=8.6% (oly), -edy=7.5% (olchedy). Post-ol ch=1.19×, k=1.35×. H263 CONFIRMED (REVISED): ch+eo vocabulary has a vowel-length gradient: ch+o (no e) = 27.1% stars; ch+eo (1e) = 39.9%; ch+eeo (2e) = 54.8%; ch+eeeo (3e) = 100% stars. This is an exact parallel to the suffix gradient from F120 (edy→eedy→eeedy: 36%→48%→63%). The same "e-vowel extension = more stars" mechanism operates at both word-internal level (ch-onset words) and suffix level. ch-onset spectrum: chol/shol (A-herbal, -ol suffix, herbal=61.8%) → ch+eo (A/B mixed, herbal=46.3%, stars=26.1%) → cheeo (stars=54.8%) → chedy/shedy (B-cosmo/stars, cosmo=52.2%). The "stars-exclusive" cheo/cheody from F140 are high-frequency instances of this gradient's upper range (MID=83-96%, not a distinct morphological class). Stars uses e-vowel extension at MULTIPLE STRUCTURAL LEVELS: (1) word-internal (ch+o→ch+eo→ch+eeo), (2) suffix level (edy→eedy→eeedy), (3) standalone suffix-words (F120 triple-vowel forms). THE E-VOWEL EXTENSION IS A STARS-SPECIFIC MORPHOLOGICAL MARKER OPERATING AT ALL LEVELS OF WORD STRUCTURE.
**Limitation:** The ol-onset self-chaining (1.68-1.89×) could reflect a single phenomenon where "ol" standalone particle appears in pairs as a formula (ol...ol within same line). The l-equivalent pairing (olkeedy=36 ↔ lkeedy=36) has perfect frequency match for some pairs but not all (olchedy=34 vs lchedy=113 — NOT equal). The ch+eo gradient (27%→40%→55%→100%) has diminishing n at higher vowel counts (n_tokens: 2692→591→73→1) — the 100% stars for ch+eeeo is based on n=1 token. The ch+eo "no recognized suffix" (other=43% in suffix distribution) conflates several patterns; some "ch+o" words may have recognized suffixes (chol has -ol, chody has -dy) vs the genuinely suffix-less cheo/cho.

## F135: p-Prefix = B-Dialect LINE-OPENER on ch/sh-Stems (Line-Start=71.1%, 5.72×); r-Prefix = B-Dialect LINE-CLOSER on PARTICLE STEMS (raiin/rain/rar/ral, Line-End=28.7%); POSITIONAL PREFIX SYSTEM: y/p=OPENERS, qo/l/o=CONTENT, r=CLOSERS
**Experiment:** exp_128_pr_prefix
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H254 CONFIRMED: p-prefix is a B-dialect line-opener on ch/sh-stems. 523 tokens, 285 types; A/B=0.31 (3.3× B); stars=43.4%, cosmo=16.8%; **line-start=71.1% (5.72× enriched)**. Stem selectivity: ch=45.5%, ol=16.8%, sh=8.6% — DISTINCT from y-/qo-/o-/l- which select k/t-stems. A/B Jaccard=0.095 (near-distinct vocabularies). pchedy=35 tokens (100% B, stars 37%). p-prefix attaches to ch/sh-content stems; top p-words are p+chedy/pol/pchor/pcheol = p+ch-stem forms. Stem recovery=76.9%. H255 CONFIRMED: r-prefix is a B-dialect line-closer on PARTICLE stems. 341 tokens, 117 types; A/B=0.12 (8.3× B); stars=51.6%, cosmo=32.6%; **line-end=28.7%** (line-start=3.2%). Stem selectivity: other-particles=64.5% (aiin/ain/ar/al/or/am); ch=14.7%. r-prefix uniquely attaches to PARTICLE STEMS (not content word stems). Creates "prefixed particle" forms: raiin(61), rain(21), rar(17), ral(15), ror(14), ram(11). Stem recovery=84.8%. A/B Jaccard=0.111. POSITIONAL PREFIX SYSTEM revealed: y-(both dialects, k/t, 39.6% line-start) and p-(B-dialect, ch/sh, 71.1% line-start) = OPENERS; qo-(B-body, k/t), l-(B-stars, ch/sh/k), o-(labels) = CONTENT MODIFIERS; r-(B-stars/cosmo, particles, 28.7% line-end) = CLOSER. p and r form a COMPLEMENTARY LINE-BRACKET pair: p opens B-dialect lines (71.1% line-start) while r closes them (28.7% line-end). r-prefix creates the only prefix class that attaches to particle stems — r-particles (raiin, rain, rar, ral, ror, ram) are B-stars/cosmo forms of the manuscript's fundamental particle vocabulary.

The "particle stems" classification for r-prefix depends on the "other" onset category which may include non-particle words. raiin (n=61) is the most common r-word but the r+aiin analysis doesn't distinguish whether these are really r-prefix on aiin vs independent r-initial words.

## F134: aiin→am=4.62× Is Distributional (Not Fixed Phrase); 4-gram [-ol/-or][aiin][cth][-am/-dy/-al]=4.92× Enriched (3 Observed/0.6 Expected); y-Prefix Splits Into A-y (y+A-paradigm, B%≤25%) and B-y (y+B-paradigm, B%=100%); y-Prefix Selects k/t-Stems (65.4%) = Same as qo-/o-; y Is GRAMMATICAL (Position) Prefix — Line-Continuation Opener (39.6% Line-Start)
**Experiment:** exp_127_line_template_4gram
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H252 CONFIRMED: aiin→am=4.62× is not a fixed [daiin][am] 2-word phrase — 67 aiin→am bigrams span 57 unique pairs; [daiin][dam] appears only n=6 (herbal). Stars=36% of aiin→am bigrams. The enrichment is a distributional artifact: -am is a universal line-closer (A mean=0.799, B=0.925) and -aiin words appear mid-line, so both co-occur in lines at elevated rates without being a lexicalized phrase. H253 CONFIRMED (WEAK): The 4-gram template [-ol/-or][aiin-word][cth-onset][-am/-dy/-al] is enriched 4.92× vs independence baseline (3 observed vs 0.6 expected, P values: P(-ol/-or)=0.229, P(-aiin)=0.111, P(cth)=0.036, P(closer)=0.110). All 3 matches are in A-herbal. The 3-gram (23 matches) is more common — cth-nouns often end lines without an adjacent closer. Canonical A-clause: [chol/chor][daiin][cthy] ± closer. H251 CONFIRMED: y-prefix splits into two sub-types based on dialect and suffix paradigm. A-y (ycheor/ydaiin/ytchy/ykchy): B%≤25%, herbal 60-88%, A-paradigm suffixes (-or/-chy/-aiin), continuation particle function. B-y (yteedy/ykeedy/ykedy/ychedy): B%=100%, B-paradigm -edy/-eedy suffixes, herbal+stars formula openers. Both select k/t-stems (65.4% = same selectivity as qo-/o-). Line-start=39.6% — y-words are predominantly line-initial. y-prefix is a GRAMMATICAL (positional) prefix marking line-continuation, not a register/dialect prefix. Extended k/t-stem prefix paradigm: bare=A-herbal, y=both+line-initial, o=labels, qo=B-body, l=B-stars/cosmo. y- is the grammatical slot marker; qo/o/l are register/dialect markers.
**Limitation:** The 4-gram template has only n=3 matches — too few for robust enrichment calculation. The aiin→am=4.62× from exp_126 was measured across all bigrams; here we find the specific word pairs are diverse (57 unique), making the interpretation ambiguous. The y-prefix line-start=39.6% is computed across all y-words including those that happen to be first in a line for other reasons. The A-y vs B-y split is based on B% thresholds (≤25% vs ≥80%) with a gap in between; some y-words have intermediate B% (e.g., ykeey=57%, ykaiin=73%).

## F133: cth = SEMI-CLOSED Nominal Class (Top5=55.4%, Herbal+Pharma=90%); Within-Line Suffix Grammar: -or(FIRST,0.371) < -ol(0.441) < -aiin(MIDDLE) < -dy/-al(LATE,1.51×) < -am(LAST,0.799/0.925); aiin→am=4.62× (Strongest Suffix Bigram); B-Dialect Less Positionally Structured
**Experiment:** exp_126_cth_vocab_suffix_grammar
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H245 CONFIRMED PARTIAL: cth-onset is a semi-closed nominal class. Top5 word concentration=55.4% (cthy=95, cthol=54, cthey=43, cthor=39, ctho=21 = 252/455 tokens) vs ch=28.1%, sh=36.8%. cth is the most concentrated onset class by top-word coverage — consistent with a small plant-name vocabulary. Herbal+pharma=90% of cth tokens (herbal=71.0%, pharma=18.9%) — the most section-specialized onset class. A-dialect cth has 85 types (71.6% hapax in herbal), B-dialect cth has 20 types (mostly hybrid forms: cthedy/cthdy from F132). A/B cth Jaccard=0.117 (11 shared types of 96 union; distinct vocabularies). cth is NOT a productive morphological prefix — it marks a specialized nominal vocabulary class (herbal plant names, pharma preparations). High hapax rate at the margins (69.1%) indicates many rare cth-nouns beyond the core 5-word vocabulary. H246 CONFIRMED: Within-line suffix grammar exists and is statistically significant in A-dialect. Suffix positional order (mean fraction, 0=first, 1=last): -or(0.371) < -ol(0.441) < -ey(0.451) < -aiin(0.529) < -al(0.584) ≈ -dy(0.586) < -am(0.799). Positional enrichment confirms: -or=1.51× at 0-20% (line-start pre-nominal modifiers); -ol/-ey=1.26× at 20-40% (early-middle); -dy/-al=1.50-1.51× at 80-100% (line-end closers); -aiin=1.22× at 80-100% (late-enriched, consistent with determiner just before noun cluster). Suffix bigrams: ol→ol=1.84×, or→or=1.81× (modifier phrase clustering); edy→edy=2.23×, dy→dy=2.36× (B-paradigm and closer clustering); aiin→am=4.62× (STRONGEST suffix bigram: after determiners, -am line-closers follow at 4.62×). -ol before -aiin=54.6% (876 lines with both; p<0.01, consistent with NP template). -am is universal line-final closer (A=0.799, B=0.925 mean position). B-dialect shows same directional structure but with flatter positional gradients (less positional specialization). Full A-dialect within-line grammar: [-or/-ol modifier phrase] → [-aiin determiner] → [cth-noun] → [-dy/-al/-am closing particles] — the line-level version of the NP template (F128/F129).
**Limitation:** The -or positional enrichment (1.51× at 0-20%) is partially driven by A-dialect where -or is rare in B; B-dialect -or mean=0.451 is less extreme. The -aiin late-enrichment (1.22× at 80-100%) is modest and may reflect -aiin words appearing in various positions. The -ol before -aiin ordering (54.6%) is a weak effect (only 4.6% above 50% null). The suffix bigram aiin→am=4.62× is the strongest pair but is based on relatively small counts. The "semi-closed class" characterization of cth uses top5 concentration as the criterion; the hapax rate of 69.1% is similar to ch/sh, suggesting cth has a long tail of rare words not unlike open classes.
