## F132: ok-/ot-/qok-/qot-Onset = o/qo-PREFIXED k/t-STEMS; qo-Prefix Is k/t-Selective (NOT ch/sh); r-/p-/y- New Prefix Classes; B-cth=Hybrid Words (cthedy B_frac=0.917, cthdy=1.000); B-cth→cth=n=1 Only (Not Systematic)
**Experiment:** exp_125_prefix_paradigm
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H249 CONFIRMED: The four-prefix paradigm (bare/o-/qo-/l-) generalizes to all k/t stem classes. ok-onset (okaiin=201) = o-prefix on k-stem; ot-onset (otaiin=137) = o-prefix on t-stem; qok-onset (qokaiin=265) = qo-prefix on k-stem; qot-onset (qotaiin=75) = qo-prefix on t-stem. ch/sh-stems take ONLY l-prefix (lchedy=116, lshedy=n≫0) — qochedy=1 (essentially absent), ochedy=8 (rare). qo-prefix is exclusively k/t-stem selective: it does NOT apply to ch/sh-stems. This resolves why qo-stripping experiments (F037/F040) found k/t-initial stripped stems — qo-prefix is a k/t-specific morphological prefix. New prefix classes discovered: r- (346 tokens, 87.0% stem recovery, A/B=0.12 = 8.4× B-dominant, stars 51%); p- (528 tokens, 76.1% recovery, A/B=0.30 = 3.4× B, stars 43%); y- (1374 tokens, 85.6% recovery, A/B=0.76 = balanced). Full revised prefix taxonomy: o-/qo-/l-/r-/p-/y-/cth-. The onset taxonomy requires revision: ok/ot/qok/qot are derived prefixed forms, NOT primitive stem classes. Primitive stem classes: ch/sh/k/t/r. H250 CONFIRMED: B-dialect cth-tokens (n=55) are hybrid morphological forms — B-paradigm suffixes applied to cth-onset. cthedy (B=11, A=1, B_frac=0.917) and cthdy (B=6, A=0, B_frac=1.000) are genuinely B-dialect words (B-paradigm suffix -edy/-dy on cth-onset). Other B-cth tokens are A-vocabulary words (cthy B_frac=0.052, cthor=0.050, cthol=0.037) appearing in B-herbal folios. B-cth concentrated in B-herbal folios f26 (19.35‰), f48 (20.73‰), f46 (15.21‰), f31 (9.95‰), and stars f113/f116. Pre-B-cth: ch-onset=2.03× enriched (B-content precedes). Post-B-cth: ot-onset=1.91× (B-context follows). B-dialect cth→cth self-clustering = n=1 only; exp_123's 8.79× was a single-token artifact (1/47 = 2.1% vs ~0.25% baseline = single occurrence).
**Limitation:** The stem recovery metric counts a prefixed form's stem as "recovered" if the bare stem appears anywhere in the vocabulary — this may overcount for very high-frequency stems. The cthedy/cthdy B_frac fractions are based on moderate sample sizes (cthedy n=12, cthdy n=6). The r-/p-/y- prefix classifications rely on stripped-stem vocabulary membership, which inherits the same vocabulary-presence assumption. The folio-level B-herbal cth concentration is based on sparse per-folio counts (f26 n=6, f48 n=6 estimated) — folio-level rates in ‰ may be volatile at small n.

## F131: 'l' Is a B-Dialect Morphological Prefix (91.3% Stem Recovery, 10.3× B-Dominant); l-Stems=ch/sh/k/d; lk=80% Stars; THREE-PREFIX System on k-Stems: Bare-k(Herbal A), qo+k(B-Body), l+k(B-Stars/Cosmo); kaiin Folios=[1-56] vs lkaiin Folios=[75-116] — Section-Disjoint
**Experiment:** exp_124_lk_onset
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H247 CONFIRMED: 'l' is a bona fide B-dialect morphological prefix. l-stem recovery = 91.3% (highest: qo=54.8%, o=50.4%). l is 10.3× more B-dominant (50.66‰ B vs 4.93‰ A; A/B=0.097). Stars-enriched (1.83×), cosmo (1.42×); herbal/pharma depleted (0.22×); astro absent. l-suffix: -edy=2.32× (B-paradigm); -y depleted (0.50×, A-paradigm). lk-subclass = 80% stars, n=415 (largest l-sub-class). l-words positional: 17.9% line-last (vs qo=6.8%) — l-words cluster at line end. Pre-l: ch(1.33×), qok(1.46×) — B-content precedes. Post-l: qok(1.41×). d-onset depleted before/after l (0.50-0.53×). H248 CONFIRMED: k is a stem-initial segment, not a prefix class. k-stems generate a THREE-PREFIX paradigm: bare-k (A-herbal, folios 1-56), qo+k (B-body text), l+k (B-stars/cosmo, folios 75-116). kaiin folios=[1-56] vs lkaiin folios=[75-116] are section-disjoint. qo-stripped forms of qo-words ARE k-initial forms in vocabulary (qokaiin→kaiin, qokeedy→keedy). Nearly all k-words have their l-prefixed form in vocabulary (l+k always valid). k-suffix distribution: mixed A+B paradigms (k in both dialects). The prefix taxonomy now has FOUR classes: o-/qo-/cth-/l-.
**Limitation:** The "section-disjoint" folio claim is approximate — some kaiin appears in B-dialect stars sections (36/77 tokens) and some overlap exists (11 folios) due to kaiin being used in both A-herbal and B-dialect contexts. The l-prefix stem recovery of 91.3% reflects the high proportion of top l-words (lchedy→chedy, lshedy→shedy) whose stems are common words; smaller types have lower recovery. The interpretation that k is a "stem-initial segment" rather than an independent onset class requires validation: k-forms that don't appear as qo-stripped or l-stripped forms may be independent k-onset words.

## F130: Onset Grammar Is Probabilistic (No Forbidden Pairs); cth→cth=4.78× (Only Mandatory); cth↔d Cycle=2.20× (Mean); Stars "Other"=l-/k-Onset NEW B-Dialect Classes; lkaiin=81% Stars-Concentrated; Stars Line-Start="y-/p-Prefix Formula Openers"; Stars Line-End=am-Particles
**Experiment:** exp_123_onset_grammar
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H244 CONFIRMED PARTIAL: The Voynich onset transition grammar is probabilistic — no forbidden transitions found (no pairs below 0.15 enrichment with sufficient n). One mandatory transition: cth→cth=4.78× (cth self-clusters, suggesting compound cth-NPs or cth-noun lists). Dominant cycles: cth→d=2.18× AND d→cth=2.21× (cth↔d mutual attraction, mean cycle=2.20×); sh→qok=1.99×/sh→qo=1.95× (B-paradigm); ot→ot=1.95×, qot→qot=2.34× (self-clustering). s-onset is the most constrained predictor (H=-0.169 bits). B-dialect cth→cth=8.79× (extreme, n=47 — rare B-cth words cluster). No global directed grammar cycle found. H242 CONFIRMED: Stars "other"-onset reveals two new B-dialect onset classes: (1) l-onset (lchedy=52, lkaiin=39, lkeedy=30, lkeey=34 — l-prefix on B-onset stems; lkaiin=81% stars-concentrated = most section-specific token in manuscript); (2) k-onset (kaiin=36, keedy=34, keey=21 — k-initial B-paradigm words; 47-55% stars-concentrated). Stars line-start "other" = y-/p-/t-prefixed B-content words (ycheey, yshey, polaiin — formula openers); stars line-end "other" = am-suffix particles (am=16 at line-final positions). Standalone particles (aiin/ar/al/or/am) = 33% of stars "other".
**Limitation:** The onset transition matrix uses onset classes as defined by the current taxonomy — "other"-onset words (33% of corpus) are excluded from the structural rows/columns. Including l-onset and k-onset as separate classes would change the matrix. The cth→cth=4.78× finding is from n=26 cth→cth transitions; the B-dialect version (8.79×) has only n=47 total cth tokens in B-text. The grammar cycle analysis tested specific chains; exhaustive search for cycles was not performed.

## F129: -ol = Pre-Determiner Suffix (d-Onset 1.44-1.66×); -or = Pre-Nominal (cth 2.15×, sh 1.57×); B-otaiin→ot=4.00× MIRRORS A-daiin→cth=2.77× — Dialectal NP Complementarity; B-NP=[ot/ok-modifier][otaiin][ot-noun]; A-NP=[ch-ol/or][daiin][cth-noun]
**Experiment:** exp_122_ol_or_bnp
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H240 CONFIRMED: -ol suffix = pre-determiner context (d-onset enriched 1.44-1.66×); -or suffix = pre-nominal context (cth-onset enriched 2.15×, sh 1.57×). chol→d=1.66× vs chor→d=0.75× is the key pair. shor→sh=2.84× (same-class sequencer). Full suffix→next-onset matrix (A-dialect): -aiin=cth-determiner (2.24×); -ey/-dy/-eey=pre-qok (1.57-2.48×); -al=pre-d-particle (1.47×, depletes cth 0.43×); -ar=pre-sh (1.45×). Suffix encodes syntactic position: A-NP phrase structure is [ch-or/sh-or]→[cth-noun] (direct) or [ch-ol/sh-ol]→[d-determiner]→[cth-noun] (via determiner). H241 CONFIRMED: B-dialect NP template confirmed: [ot/ok-modifier][otaiin][ot-noun] with 4.08× post-otaiin ot-enrichment and 2.47× pre-otaiin ot-enrichment. A-daiin→cth=2.77× EXACTLY MIRRORED by B-otaiin→ot=4.00× — the two dialects grammaticalize complementary noun classes (cth in A, ot in B) with structurally parallel determiners. Pre-shedy: qok-onset 1.79× enriched — B-paradigm shedy NP: [qok/ol-word][shedy][qok-noun]. Pre-otaiin in stars: okaiin appears 4× (top pre-otaiin word), confirming okaiin→otaiin→otal chain.
**Limitation:** chol vs chor distinction in A-dialect is based on moderate sample sizes (263 and 162). The B-dialect otaiin NP template has only 66 trigram examples. The -or/-ol distinction in B-dialect is less clean (B has more -ol words in qol/sheol forms that differ from A-paradigm). The "syntactic position" interpretation of suffixes is structural — requires confirmation that suffix choice is genuinely predictive (not a consequence of vocabulary clustering).

**Experiment:** exp_120_dialect_bigram

**Finding:** H236 CONFIRMED REVISED: The pre-cth bigram is dialect-split. A-dialect: daiin→cth=2.64×, chol→1.62×, shol→1.45× (A-paradigm words → cth nouns). B-dialect: chor→cth=19.04×, dain→8.00× (rare B-text cth precedence). cth is 15× more common in A-dialect (39.29‰) than B (2.57‰). ## F126: Pre-cth Cluster: chor=4.73×, daiin=4.38×, chol=3.40× — A-Suffix Words Precede cth-Nouns; Pre-qok: shedy=3.75×, chedy=2.69× — B-Suffix Words Precede qok; d-Onset Function Class: H(position)=1.424 (2× ch/sh); s-Onset Extreme Topic-Opener (48.5% First)
**Experiment:** exp_119_bigram_matrix
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H233 CONFIRMED: Bigram matrix reveals two syntactic sequence rules: (1) Pre-cth cluster: chor→cth=4.73× (strongest word→onset bigram), daiin→cth=4.38×, chol→cth=3.40×, shol→cth=2.76× — ALL A-paradigm suffixed words (ch/sh-ol/-or/-y; d/ok-aiin) systematically precede cth-onset content words. d-compound forms show even stronger cth-enrichment (dchor=5.5×, dchy=5.8×). (2) Pre-qok cluster: shedy→qok=3.75×, shey→3.02×, chedy→2.69× — B-paradigm -edy/-eedy words precede qok-onset. Emergent syntactic rule: [A-suffix word] → [cth-noun]; [B-suffix word] → [qok-word]. 'or', 'ar', 'al' have lowest collocational entropy (H=1.98-2.23 vs baseline 3.13). Structural model: s=para-start → d=flexible function → ch/sh=content → cth=A-paradigm noun → qok=B-paradigm noun cluster.
**Limitation:** The bigram enrichment uses all body tokens regardless of dialect. The pre-cth pattern may be primarily an A-dialect phenomenon (cth- is A-dominant). The pre-qok pattern may be B-dialect. ## F124: 'Other' Suffix (20.6%) = Free A-Morphemes (ol/aiin/or/ar/al) + Unrecognized -am/-air Suffixes + Short Truncated Forms; Adjacent Paragraphs Share Vocabulary at 1.85× Non-Adjacent Rate; daiin in 41% of Paragraphs; Stars Highest Within-Para Repetition (0.476)
**Experiment:** exp_117_other_suffix
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H228 CONFIRMED: The 20.6% 'other' suffix category has four components. (1) Free standalone A-paradigm morphemes: top 5 'other' words are ol (476), aiin (394), or (300), ar (268), al (193) — these words ARE the suffix itself with no stem prefix, which fails the suffix extractor's `len(word) > len(suffix)` requirement. This directly confirms F118's free-morpheme asymmetry (A-paradigm suffixes ARE grammaticalized free words). (2) Unrecognized -am suffix (dam=70, otam=34, qokam=24; 9.2% of 'other' by 2-char ending) and -air suffix (dair=75, otair=19; 7.3%) — these are legitimate suffix patterns absent from the current 14-item list. (3) Short truncated forms: -o ending (sho=108, cho=71), -eo ending (cheo=66, sheo=39). (4) Hapax residual (74.2% of types hapax vs 68.1% for suffixed). ol-onset 3.14× enriched in 'other'; qok 0.37× depleted. Adding -am/-air to suffix list would recover ~1,000 tokens (~16% of 'other'). H229 CONFIRMED: Adjacent paragraphs have 1.85× higher Jaccard similarity than non-adjacent (0.084 vs 0.045) — genuine discourse cohesion signal. Astro lowest (0.062; short diverse paragraphs). Discourse distance-decay is inconsistent with random or hoax text generation.
**Limitation:** The "adjacent paragraph" comparison includes paragraphs on different folios in the same section (not truly adjacent in discourse). Para boundary detection uses the locus_type '@' and '*' markers which may misidentify some line breaks as para breaks. The -am/-air suffix identification is tentative: -am words also include the standalone 'am' particle and short forms that may not be morphological suffixes.

## F122: Folio Suffix Profiles Cluster by Section at 73.1% Accuracy; cosmo Most Coherent (Within=0.923); herbal Most Heterogeneous (0.779) Due to Regular A/B Alternating Interleave (Every 3-5 Folios); cosmo→pharma Is Sharpest Boundary; f107 ONLY eey-Dominant Folio; cosmo-stars Highest Vocabulary Overlap (Jaccard=0.391)
**Experiment:** exp_115_folio_clustering
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H225 CONFIRMED PARTIAL: Folio-level suffix profile cosine similarity yields 73.1% section classification accuracy (vs 20% chance for 5 sections). Within-section similarity: cosmo=0.923 (most coherent), stars=0.891, pharma=0.852, herbal=0.779 (most heterogeneous), astro=0.724. Cross-section mean=0.685. Key findings: (1) Herbal section contains A-dialect and B-dialect folios alternating every 3-5 folios in a REGULAR pattern (f26/31/33-34/39-41/43/46/48/50/57 are B-dialect within A-dominant herbal) — consistent with two-source compilation during manuscript assembly. (2) Herbal-B folios are systematically misassigned to cosmo/stars because their B-paradigm suffix profile matches the B-dialect centroid. (3) cosmo-to-pharma boundary is the sharpest in the manuscript (f84→f87 suffix similarity drops to 0.479). (4) f107 is the ONLY folio in the manuscript where eey is the dominant B-suffix (44% eey > 40% edy). (5) cosmo-stars have the highest vocabulary overlap (Jaccard=0.391; both B-dialect). (6) astro is vocabulary-isolated (Jaccard=0.04-0.10 vs all sections). (7) f79 (cosmo) is a cosmo outlier with nearly stars-level eey (34.5%); f80 (cosmo) is herbal-like (misassigned to herbal by centroid).
**Limitation:** The 73.1% classification uses suffix profile only (not full vocabulary). A vocabulary-weighted classifier would likely perform better. The herbal A/B alternating pattern uses dialect assignment (edy rate ≥5%) as a proxy, which may misclassify edge cases. Astro section has only 3 valid folios, making intra-astro statistics unreliable. The "regular" alternating pattern conclusion is visual inspection of the sequence, not a formal periodicity test.

## F121: Four-Level Suffix Hierarchy Quantified: 20.1% Entropy Reduction (0.71 bits of 3.54); Vowel Length (Level 4) Contributes MOST (0.35 bits); Residual 2.83 bits After All Conditions; qot Onset Has Highest Dialect Polarity (0.207 bits); ol Has Lowest (0.035 bits)
**Experiment:** exp_114_conditional_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H224 CONFIRMED: Conditional entropy computation formalizes the four-level suffix hierarchy. H(suffix) marginal = 3.54 bits. Four-level hierarchy resolves: Level 1 dialect = 0.11 bits (3%); Level 2 +onset_class = 0.16 bits additional (7.4% total); Level 3 +section = 0.10 bits additional (10.2% total); Level 4 +vowel_length = 0.35 bits additional (20.1% total). Total reduction = 0.71 bits (20.1%). Residual uncertainty = 2.83 bits even knowing all four levels — substantial within-class lexical variation remains. Level 4 (vowel length) is the single most informative level (0.35 bits > Levels 1–3 combined per-level). A-dialect consistently has LOWER within-class entropy than B-dialect (more concentrated suffix distribution; e.g., qot-A=2.937 bits vs qot-B=3.592 bits). Per-onset dialect information: qot highest (0.207 bits); ol lowest (0.035 bits) — consistent with ol being both an A-suffix and an onset class, blurring its dialect signal. B-dialect section information varies by onset: sh gains 0.125 bits from section; ot gains only 0.071 bits. The 20.1% entropy reduction is comparable to morphological conditioning in known agglutinative natural languages (typically 15–30%).
**Limitation:** The "vowel length" Level 4 condition is not fully independent of the suffix type (triple-e words necessarily take specific suffixes), so it may partially capture suffix identity rather than a separate phonological feature. The residual 2.83 bits includes positional effects (line-first, line-last) not tested here. The null model in the script had a bug (shuffled suffix strings were passed as pseudo-words to get_suffix(), returning unreliable baseline) and is excluded from the finding.

## F001: Voynich Word-Initial Entropy Is Elevated Above h2 but Below Natural-Language Levels
**Experiment:** exp_001_word_initial_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Voynich word-initial character entropy (H_init = 3.137 bits, ZL3b EVA corpus, 32,866 words) is substantially elevated above the overall bigram conditional entropy (H2 = 2.341 bits), with a gap of +0.796 bits. This gap is larger than the analogous gap in natural languages (Latin Virgil: +0.50 approximate, Italian Dante: +0.62). However, H_init is substantially lower than natural-language word-initial entropy (Italian Dante: 4.037 bits), and the Voynich onset distribution is more constrained relative to its own unigram distribution than natural languages (shuffled-actual gap: Voynich +0.734 bits vs. Dante ~0.00 bits). Four characters (o, c, q, s) account for 69.3% of all word onsets.
**Limitation:** Label text was not successfully extracted (locus code parser bug — fix needed). Latin comparison baseline was mistakenly an English Bible; replaced with Virgil/Caesar Latin for subsequent experiments.

## F003: Voynich Positional Entropy Has a U-Shape — Middle Positions Are Freest
**Experiment:** exp_002_positional_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Voynich character entropy by word position forms a U-shape: onset (pos 0: 3.137 bits) and suffix (pos 5-6: 3.272-3.402) are lower entropy than middle positions (pos 3-4: 3.606-3.612). The positional bias index (shuffled_H - actual_H) confirms: pos 3-4 bias is +0.237 vs pos 0 bias of +0.729. Natural languages show the OPPOSITE at onset (Latin pos 0 bias = -0.118, Italian = -0.077 — onset is freer than the shuffled control). This U-shape directly matches the Stolfi/Zattera slot grammar's prediction (constrained outer crust, freer inner core/mantle).
**Limitation:** Computed over all words regardless of length; short words distort endpoint statistics.

## F004: Voynich Word-Final Positions Are the Most Constrained Characters in the Text
**Experiment:** exp_002_positional_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H(-1) = 2.456 bits (final character) is the single lowest-entropy positional measurement in Voynich, lower even than the overall h2 (2.341) when computed from the full stream. H(-2) = 2.933. Compare: Latin H(-1) = 3.248, Italian H(-1) = 3.062. The final position in Voynich is dramatically more constrained than natural-language word finals and than Voynich's own interior positions.
**Limitation:** Latin end-positional entropy from Virgil+Caesar Latin; not yet verified against medieval Latin.

## F005: Voynich H2 by Word Length Is Flat — No Information Rise with Length
**Experiment:** exp_002_positional_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** For word lengths 4-13, Voynich h2 ranges only from 2.194 to 2.341 bits — essentially flat. In Latin (Virgil+Caesar), h2 rises from 2.1 (length 2) to 3.47 (length 5) then plateaus. In Italian (Dante), a similar rise-then-plateau is observed. The absence of a rise in Voynich means additional word length does not carry additional information per character — consistent with templated affixal material being added without adding content.
**Limitation:** H2 computed using flat-stream bigrams within length classes; does not account for positional structure within word-length groups.

## F006: Q-Initial Words Do NOT Drive Word-Initial Entropy Upward
**Experiment:** exp_002_positional_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Removing q-initial words (15.5% of corpus) LOWERS H_initial from 3.137 to 2.976 bits. Q is followed by 'o' in 97.7% of cases (4976/5091), making "qo" a nearly invariant word-initial bigram. Rather than inflating entropy via a constrained sub-slot, q contributes a unique onset category that adds diversity. Stripping it concentrates the remaining distribution further on o and c.
**Limitation:** This refutes H010 as stated but does not rule out q functioning as a grammatical marker; it establishes only that q is not suppressing H_initial.

## F007: Labels Have Substantially Higher h2 Than Body Text (+0.273 bits)
**Experiment:** exp_003_label_body_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Label text h2 = 2.575 bits vs body text h2 = 2.302 bits — labels are 0.273 bits less predictable per character within words. Labels also have dramatically higher type/token ratio (0.746 vs 0.229) and 55.3% exclusive vocabulary (439/794 label word types never appear in body text). Inner-slot entropy (pos 3-4) is higher in labels (3.499 vs 3.278 bits). All measurements are consistent with labels being informationally denser than body text.
**Limitation:** Label corpus is small (1,065 tokens). TTR comparison is not size-controlled.

## F008: qo-Words Are Largely Absent from Label Text (0% vs 17% in body)
**Experiment:** exp_003_label_body_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Body text has ~17% q-initial words (nearly always 'qo'); labels have effectively zero q-initial words (q does not appear in the top 6 initial characters for labels). The 'qo' construction is a body-text-specific feature. This is consistent with qo functioning as a grammatical particle (article/preposition) in body prose, absent from short label noun-phrases.
**Limitation:** Quantitative q-initial count for labels not directly measured; inferred from top initial char table.

## F009: daiin (Body Text's Most Frequent Word) Is Not Found in Label Vocabulary
**Experiment:** exp_003_label_body_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** 'daiin' appears 710 times in body text (2.4% of tokens, most frequent word). It does not appear in the top 10 label words. If daiin were a ubiquitous function word, it would appear in labels; its apparent absence suggests it is either body-specific grammatical material or a body-text filler/padding element. Similarly, the top body words chedy, shedy, chol, qokeey, qokeedy are absent from label top-10. Label top words (o, s, y, otedy, oky) are structurally different from body top words.
**Limitation:** 'daiin' may appear in labels at low frequency but not rank in top-10; direct count not extracted.

## F010: Labels Have a Distinctive 'ot-'/'ok-' Vocabulary Pattern
**Experiment:** exp_003_label_body_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Among the top label words are otedy, oky, otaly, okal, okol, otal — all sharing an 'ot-' or 'ok-' initial bigram. These words are frequent in labels and largely absent from the top body vocabulary. 56% of label onsets are 'o' (vs 21% in body), driven largely by these words plus single-char 'o' tokens. This pattern is consistent with labels using a semantically distinct vocabulary register for describing/naming illustrated objects.
**Limitation:** Not verified whether ot-/ok- words appear in body text at low frequency.

## F011: H013 Refuted — qo Stripping Has Negligible Effect on Entropy
**Experiment:** exp_003_label_body_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Stripping the 'qo' prefix from q-initial words changes H_initial by +0.029 bits and H2 by +0.043 bits — negligible. qo is a tightly integrated word component, not a separable grammatical particle with content words underneath. The qo-stripping approach does not reveal latent lexical structure.
**Limitation:** Analysis on all words combined; result might differ if tested only on body text (where qo is concentrated).

## F012: daiin Concentrates Massively in Currier A / Herbal A (4.11-4.58% vs 1.28-1.41%)
**Experiment:** exp_004_daiin_distribution
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** 'daiin' frequency: Herbal A = 4.11%, Currier A body = 4.58%, vs Bio = 1.28%, Recipes = 1.18%, Currier B body = 1.41%. daiin is the single most frequent word in Herbal A (382 occurrences). **Experiment:** exp_004_daiin_distribution

**Finding:** Currier A top words: daiin(424), chol(227), chor(147), s(100), shol(99), cthy(85). **Experiment:** exp_004_daiin_distribution

**Finding:** At positions 3-4 (inner/core slots, words ≥6): Currier A shows balanced e(15.7%)/o(15.7%) distribution, H=3.465. Currier B shows 'e' dominance at 29.3%, H=3.152. The inner-slot character distributions are structurally different between the two languages — B is more constrained at the informational core of words.

**Experiment:** exp_004_daiin_distribution

## F016: Currier A and B Have Different Suffix Templates (Positional Entropy Diverges at Pos 5-8)
**Experiment:** exp_005_currier_ab_comparison
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Currier A positional entropy from word start stays high at positions 5-8 (range 3.557-3.690 bits). Currier B drops sharply at the same positions (range 3.029-3.217 bits). H_final: A=2.644, B=2.260. The character distributions are similar at the unigram level (KL = 0.069 bits) and at onset positions, but diverge strongly at word suffixes. B's suffix zone is substantially more constrained than A's.

## F017: Currier A/B Vocabulary Divergence is Near-Total for High-Frequency Words
**Experiment:** exp_005_currier_ab_comparison
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Words specific to B: qokeedy (298 occurrences in B, ~0 in A, ratio 14,697:1), chedy (431 in B, 4 in A, ratio 98:1), shedy (367 in B, 4 in A, 84:1). Words specific to A: cthor (36:1), cthol (36:1), cthy (27:1), sho (18:1). ## F018: Gallows Characters Concentrate at Word Position 1 (22.9%) — Bench-Layer Fingerprint
**Experiment:** exp_006_gallows_grouping
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Simple gallows chars (t, k, p, f) appear in 22.9% of position-1 character slots (vs 6.9% at position 0, 17.4% at position 2, 6.5% at position 3, and 2-3% at positions 4-7). This spike at position 1 reflects the c+gallows pattern (ct-, ck-, cp-, cf-) that is the characteristic signature of the Stolfi bench layer. Gallows are followed most often by 'e' (30%) and 'a' (25.2%).
**Limitation:** Position 1 spike conflates simple gallows (k, t after non-c chars) with compound gallows (ct, ck after initial c). A cleaner analysis would separately count c-preceded gallows from other-preceded gallows.

## F019: Adjacent-Pair Pairing of Fixed-Filler Verbose Cipher Recovers Source Language h2 Exactly
**Experiment:** exp_007_verbose_cipher_control
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** Italian with every character doubled by a fixed 'x' filler has baseline h2 = 2.014. After adjacent-pair grouping, paired h2 = 3.411 — exactly equal to the original Italian h2 (3.411). This validates adjacent-pair grouping as a detector for fixed-filler verbose ciphers: paired h2 = source language h2 is the expected signature.
**Limitation:** Only fixed-filler case tested. Variable-filler ciphers produce dramatically different results (paired h2 = 6.13 for random filler).

## F020: Voynich Paired h2 (3.836) Does Not Match Italian (3.411) or Latin (3.509) — Fixed-Filler Verbose Cipher Ruled Out
**Experiment:** exp_007_verbose_cipher_control
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** If Voynich were a fixed-filler adjacent-pair verbose cipher on Italian or Latin, its paired h2 should equal Italian h2 (3.411) or Latin h2 (3.509). Observed Voynich paired h2 = 3.836 — exceeds both by 0.33-0.43 bits. The fixed-filler adjacent-pair verbose cipher on Latin or Italian is ruled out. The source language would need h2 ≈ 3.836, which exceeds both Latin and Italian.
**Limitation:** Other natural languages (German, Arabic, Hebrew) not yet tested. Variable-filler or non-adjacent-pair groupings remain open.

## F025: f66r Contains a Two-Column Word/Character List with 67% Hapax Words
**Experiment:** exp_011_f66r_wordlist
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** f66r (Quire H, Scribe 5, Currier B, text-only folio) has a two-column L0 structure: Column 1 is a 15-word list (all unique; lengths 3-6 chars); Column 2 is a 31-entry list of mostly single characters, followed by standard Currier B body text. Of Column 1's 15 words, 6 are hapax legomena (never appear elsewhere in manuscript) and 4 more appear only 3 times each — 67% of the word list is rare or unique. Column 2 over-represents rare gallows characters: 'f' (4/10 total occurrences = 40%), 'x' (3/10 = 30%), 'p' (1/7 = 14%). The ZL3b transcription comment explicitly notes "Now individual characters in next column," confirming the two-column structure was recognized by transcribers. Adjacent folios (f65r-f66v) are structurally normal; f66r's structure is isolated.
**Limitation:** Physical manuscript inspection needed to confirm visual column separation. 6 hapax words could theoretically appear in damaged/untranscribed sections.

**Experiment:** exp_011_f66r_wordlist
**Date:** 2026-04-09

Both f49v and f76r are text-only folios (`$I=T`). Two different scribes (1 and 2) use this structure in two different sections (herbal and biological), suggesting it is a deliberate manuscript feature.

## F024: [RETRACTED] "Herbal_A single-char labels" — Analytical Misclassification
**Experiment:** exp_010_label_word_sections → exp_011_single_char_validation
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Original claim retracted:** F024 claimed herbal_A labels are dominated by single characters (y, o, f, d, e, s, p, x). Raw transcription inspection reveals two completely different phenomena — neither represents plant labels.
**Phenomenon 1 — f49v line markers:** f49v has a perfectly alternating L0/P0 structure: every odd line is an L0 single-character margin marker (f, o, r, y, e, k, s, p, ...), every even line is a P0 body text line. This is a systematic line annotation feature of this specific folio, NOT plant part labels. The 20 single chars on f49v all come from this alternating sequence.
**Phenomenon 2 — f66r column entries:** f66r is a "text only" folio (no plant illustration, Currier B) at the herbal/astro boundary. It has two columns: short words (rary, rals, qor, dary, ykeol, ...) followed by single characters (y, o, s, y, d, o, f, x, ...). The ZL3b transcription comment explicitly notes "Now individual characters in next column." This is a list/table structure, not a herbal plant label page.
**Why retracted:** All 48 herbal "single-char labels" come from exactly two folios (f49v: 20, f66r: 28) with structurally different, non-label content. The ZL3b L0 locus code covers multiple content types, not just object labels.
**Limitation:** The L0 locus code overloading is a recurring analytical hazard in this corpus — future experiments must inspect raw transcription lines rather than relying on locus code alone.
**Experiment:** exp_010_label_word_sections

## F022: No Tested Natural Language Has h2 ≥ 3.836 — Verbose Cipher Hypothesis Further Constrained
**Experiment:** exp_009_source_language_h2
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** German (Goethe Faust, 163k chars) h2=3.535, Arabic consonantal (UDHR, 6k chars) h2=3.673, Hebrew consonantal (UDHR, 6k chars) h2=3.723. ## F030: f57v Contains a Repeating 17-Token Sequence with a Compound @169;v Glyph and 3 Additional @Glyphs
**Experiment:** exp_015_f57v_characterization (corrected by exp_019)
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** f57v (Quire H, Hand 1, cosmological wheel diagram) contains a circular text band (L03, +Cc locus) with a 17-token sequence repeated exactly 4 times: `o l d r v x k m f/p @169;v t r @170 @171 y I/c @172`. The cycle has 15 invariant positions and 2 variant positions: position 9 (f in cycles 1-2, p in cycles 3-4) and position 16 (I in cycle 1, c in cycles 2-4). `@169;v` is a COMPOUND GLYPH — a single ZL3b token bounded by dots on both sides, not two separate characters. This makes the 4-@glyph cluster at positions 10, 13, 14, 17 consist of: @169;v (compound, always invariant), @170 (invariant), @171 (invariant), @172 (invariant). @169;v appears only inside this repeating sequence. @170, @171, @172 each appear once additionally in other circular bands. Voynich.nu counts this as "4×17 characters" — confirmed correct by IVTFF dot-based tokenization of ZL3b (total tokens = 68 = 4×17). The outer circular band (L02, @Cc) reads as ordinary Voynich prose with no @glyphs. The folio contains a cosmological illustration inside the innermost ring, 5 labels (@L0), 4 riders (@Ro), and a Saturn symbol (@255;) in the lower right corner.
**Correction (exp_019):** exp_015 incorrectly stated "18-character sequence" — the correct count is 17 tokens per cycle because `@169;v` is a single compound token.
**Limitation:** Hand attribution uncertain (ZL3b inline comment says "hand 2 (???) " but $H=1 header says Hand 1). The I vs c at position 16 may reflect transcription uncertainty.
