FULL B LINE STRUCTURE (F095): [y-compound/s-onset LINE-OPENER (LFirst=47%/61%)] → [qo-prefix MID-LINE (LFirst≈background)] → [-am/oly LINE-CLOSER (LLast=74-89%)], with daiin-B as LINE-CONNECTOR (follows o-ending lines, opens next line with ch/sh words, LFirst=33%).
**Limitation:** H151 based on 88 daiin-B non-para-start openings — some noise. H152 preceding-onset analysis: n=94 -am lines and 41 oly/oldy lines — small but consistent with selectional hypothesis. H153 y-compound definition (y+[ch/sh/k/t]): some boundary cases (e.g., yor = y+or — is this y-compound?). The 47.3% LFirst for y-compound may include some y-words that are not morphologically compound.

## F096: Three-Level k/t Stem Positional Paradigm in B (bare<qo<y in LFirst%); B Line Template Not Rigid (Components Independent)
**Experiment:** exp_089_y_qo_paradigm
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H154 STRONGLY SUPPORTED: B dialect has a three-level positional paradigm for k/t stems: bare (LFirst=8.9%) < qo-prefix (LFirst=11.6%) < y-prefix (LFirst=36.2%). y/qo LFirst ratio = 3.12× across 81 shared stems. Individual stem ratios: tal=8.17×, tchedy=6.00×, tar=5.27×, kol=4.30×, kain=3.29×. The y-prefix encodes LINE-INITIAL position; qo-prefix is MID-LINE; bare stems are UNMARKED. This is a PREFIX-ENCODED POSITIONAL PARADIGM — same content stem appears with different prefixes by line position. In A: y/qo ratio=1.28× (weaker — qo has elevated LFirst% of 24.5% in A vs 11.6% in B). H155 NOT SUPPORTED: Full B line template [opener+qo-mid+closer] occurs at 0.7% (chance=0.8%, enrichment=0.95×). Components are independent. Dominant B pattern: qo-mid only (46.5%); none-of-above (23.1%). qo-prefix is the pervasive B line element (65.4%); opener (20.8%) and closer (5.6%) are optional modular additions. B line grammar is probabilistic and modular, not a rigid three-part sequence.
**Limitation:** H154 "bare stem" analysis counts any word not beginning with y- or qo- that matches a known y/qo stem — some of these may be false matches (stem appears in different morphological context). H155 threshold for "y-compound" includes y+ch/sh in addition to y+k/t — broadening opener definition increases opener rate. The section independence (0.95× template enrichment) masks whether specific sections have higher template rates (cosmo=1.1%, pharma=1.9% are highest but still low absolute).

## F097: Grammar Models Not Falsified (she-prefix 45.7% precision, olfchedy 61.5%); A Line Structure Parallel to B (ch mid-line, d-closer)
**Experiment:** exp_090_grammar_falsification
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H146 NOT FALSIFIED: Grammar models have genuine predictive power. she-prefix para-start predictor: precision=45.7% (4.74× base rate); astro A precision=100%. olfchedy/olkey/opchedy B para-start predictor: precision=61.5% (14.72× base rate), recall=7.9%. Daiin para-final predictor is WEAK (precision=13.0%, enrichment=1.35×) — daiin marks general line-endings in A, not specifically para-finals. H156/H157 CONFIRMED: A has parallel line structure to B. A line structure: [opener: y/d/o/sh] → [ch MID-LINE (27.3% at pos1, 23.7% at pos2)] → [d-CLOSER (23.0% at last)]. B structure: [y/s opener] → [qo MID-LINE] → [-am/oly CLOSER]. d-onset splits in A: LINE-OPENERS = {dchor (66.7% LFirst), dchol (72.7%), dchey (66.7%)} — d+ch compounds; LINE-CLOSERS = {dam (63.2% LLast), dy (55.6%), daiiin (55.6%), dal (38.2%)} — d+suffix forms. CROSS-DIALECT STRUCTURAL PARALLELISM: A ch-onset = B qo-prefix (mid-line element); A d-onset closer = B -am/oly (line-closers); A d+ch openers = B y-compound openers. The two dialects implement the same positional grammar template with different morphological vocabulary.
**Limitation:** she-prefix precision (45.7%) but low recall (9.9%) — most para-starts are not predicted. olfchedy/olkey/opchedy recall only 7.9% of B para-starts. The falsification test uses the SAME data used to develop the models — genuine out-of-sample test would require held-out folios. Section-specific precision varies widely (astro A: 100% from only 4 TPs). d-onset LINE-OPENER sub-class (dchor, dchol) has small n (21, 11 tokens).

## F098: A Has Two Line-Initial ch-Prefix Systems (y+ch=85.9%, d+ch=59.6% LFirst); A Line Structure = [y/d+ch Opener] → [bare ch Mid] → [d-Closer]
**Experiment:** exp_091_a_line_structure
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H158 STRONGLY SUPPORTED: A has two line-initial prefix systems for ch-stems: y+ch (LFirst=85.9%, 8.86× vs bare ch at 9.7%) and d+ch (LFirst=59.6%, 6.17× vs bare). Top d+ch forms: dchor=66.7%, dchol=72.7%, dcheey=100.0%. Top y+ch forms: ychor=100.0%, ychol=85.7%. H159 STRONGLY SUPPORTED: A ch-stem three-tier paradigm: bare ch (9.7% LFirst) << d+ch (59.6%, 6.17× contrast) ≤ y+ch (85.9%, 8.86×). Three-stem comparison for 12 stems showing all three forms: cheey has bare=2.8%, d+ch=100%, y+ch=100% (36×/36× contrasts). H160 CONFIRMED: A mid-line is dominated by bare ch-onset words (chol=78, chor=50 at pos1). ch→ch self-continuation at pos2 = 28.4%. A line grammar is modular: [d+ch/y+ch OPENER] → [bare ch MID × N, ch→ch=28.4%] → [d-onset CLOSER (dal/dar/dam/daiin)]. CROSS-DIALECT PARALLEL CONFIRMED (F098): B= [y+k/t opener] → [qo+k/t mid] → [-am/oly closer]; A= [y+ch or d+ch opener] → [bare ch mid] → [d+suffix closer]. Both implement PREFIX-ENCODED POSITIONAL GRAMMAR with same three-slot template. A differs from B in having TWO line-initial prefixes (y and d) vs B's one (y), and in having NO mid-line prefix (B uses qo as explicit mid-line marker).
**Limitation:** d+ch LFirst% (59.6%) based on n=109 shared-stem tokens — moderate sample. y+ch only n=85 tokens total. The "three-tier" A paradigm differs from B in that A has no clear mid-line PREFIX (only bare ch); the "mid-line" designation is based on positional rates, not an explicit morphological marker. H160 template enrichment (1.29×) is modest — A line template is not rigid.

## F099: A y+ch vs d+ch Are Contextually Distinct (0% PS Both); sh-Stem Paradigm Is Universal; p-Onset Dominates A Para-Starts (12.41×)
**Experiment:** exp_092_y_ch_vs_d_ch
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H161 CONFIRMED WITH EXTENSION: y+ch and d+ch are NOT interchangeable. Critical revision to model: BOTH have 0% para-start rate — within-para line openers ONLY (not paragraph starters). Contextually distinct: y+ch follows o-ending lines (23.0%), d+ch follows d-ending lines (35.7%, 2.20× over y+ch). Following-word onset: y+ch→o-onset(24.3%, 8.15× over d+ch); d+ch→qo-onset(16.4%, 6.07× over y+ch), ch-onset(35.8%). Both use same 10 shared ch-stems → prefix encodes syntactic position, not lexical content. d-chain pattern: [d-closer on prev line] → [d+ch opener next line]. H162 STRONGLY SUPPORTED: A 3-tier positional paradigm is UNIVERSAL — sh-stems show bare sh(13.2%) << d+sh(68.8%, 5.21×) ≤ y+sh(85.7%, 6.49×); nearly identical ratios to ch-stems (6.17×/8.86×). Paradigm applies to ALL A consonantal stem classes. H163 NEW FINDING: A para-starts dominated by p-onset words (12.41× enrichment, 28.8% of PS openers!), also k-onset (4.32×) and t-onset (2.72×). y+ch and d+ch are SUPPRESSED at para-starts (0.0%). REVISED A GRAMMAR (F099): (1) PARAGRAPH OPENER: p/k/t-onset words (12.41×/4.32×/2.72×); (2) LINE OPENER (within-para): y+ch(85.9%)/d+ch(59.6%)/y+sh(85.7%)/d+sh(68.8%); (3) MID-LINE: bare ch/sh (~13% LFirst); (4) LINE-CLOSER: d-onset words (33-63% LLast).
**Limitation:** p-onset para-start finding is new and requires dedicated follow-up experiment (exp_093) to identify specific p-onset words and confirm signal. d-chain pattern based on small samples (y+ch n=74, d+ch n=70 inter-line pairs). sh-stem paradigm has small prefixed samples (d+sh n=48, y+sh n=21) — proportions reliable but token counts modest.

## F100: Universal Voynichese Positional Grammar — Gallows-Initial Words (p/k/t) Mark Para-Starts in BOTH Dialects (12.41×/3.71×); y/d/qo Suppressed at Para-Starts in Both
**Experiment:** exp_093_a_para_start_p_onset
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H164 CONFIRMED WITH EXTENSION: A p-onset para-start signal (12.41×) is real. p-onset is OPEN CLASS (43 unique forms, mostly hapaxes). p- PREFIX marks para-initial position; stems vary freely. A's THIRD POSITIONAL PREFIX: p+ch/sh/o-stems = para-starters (alongside y+ch and d+ch as within-para line-openers). H165 CONFIRMED (MODEST): d-closer → d+ch opener = 1.76× enrichment (observed=25, expected=14.2); y+ch simultaneously SUPPRESSED (0.61×) after d-closer. Chains mostly length=1 pairs. o→y+ch chain weaker (1.20×). H166 STRONGLY CONFIRMED — MAJOR FINDING: UNIVERSAL VOYNICHESE PARA-START GRAMMAR: p-onset (A=12.41×, B=3.71×); k-onset (A=4.32×, B=9.91×); t-onset (A=2.72×, B=2.05×) ALL enriched at para-starts in BOTH A and B. y/d/qo/s/sh SUPPRESSED at para-starts in BOTH dialects. GALLOWS-ONSET WORDS (p/k/t) = PARAGRAPH-LEVEL POSITIONAL CLASS across entire manuscript. COMPLETE POSITIONAL GRAMMAR (F100): LEVEL4=Para-Opener (p/k/t gallows-initial); LEVEL3=Line-Opener (y+ch/d+ch in A, y+k/t in B); LEVEL2=Mid-Line (bare ch in A, qo in B); LEVEL1=Line-Closer (d+suffix in A, -am/oly in B). d-chain (H165): real (1.76×) but modest.
**Limitation:** A p-onset forms are mostly hapaxes — individual word-level enrichment is low (small n). The 12.41× overall p-onset enrichment is robust, but the mechanism (specific word classes vs pure p-prefix) needs further study. B p-onset enrichment (3.71×) is lower than A's (12.41×) possibly because B has more diverse para-start vocabulary. k-onset A finding (4.32×) new — not previously characterized. B's k-onset enrichment (9.91×!) is the strongest positional signal found in B for para-starts.

## F101: MASTER FINDING — Voynichese Positional Grammar Is a PREFIX-DEMOTED GALLOWS HIERARCHY; All Four Gallows (p/k/t/f) = Para-Level; Prefix Addition Demotes to Line-Level
**Experiment:** exp_094_gallows_para_start
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H167 CONFIRMED: k-onset is OPEN CLASS para-start marker (like p-onset); all k-onset PS words are hapaxes in both A and B. H168 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: ALL FOUR gallows characters enriched at para-starts: p(A=12.41×,B=3.71×), k(A=4.32×,B=9.91×), t(A=2.72×,B=2.05×), f(A=9.50×,B=7.62×). NON-GALLOWS (ch/sh/qo/y/d) ALL SUPPRESSED at para-starts in both dialects. Gallows glyph class = PARA-LEVEL positional morpheme class. H169 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: Prefix DEMOTES gallows from para to line: bare_k(4-10× PS enriched) → qo+k(0.27-0.32× suppressed); y+gallows = 0% PS in B. H170 CONFIRMED: Same hierarchy in A and B: bare_p strongest para-starter (A=40.2% PS!, B=10.7% PS); bare_t/f intermediate; y+gallows = within-para line-opener (LFirst=30%); qo+gallows = mid-line (LFirst=10%). MASTER FINDING (F101): VOYNICHESE PREFIX-DEMOTED GALLOWS HIERARCHY: BARE gallows = PARAGRAPH-LEVEL; y+gallows = WITHIN-PARA LINE-OPENER; qo+gallows = MID-LINE; NON-GALLOWS (ch/sh) = MID-LINE/CLOSING. Morphological operation: gallows + prefix → positional demotion. The SAME gallows stem (k, t) appears at three positional levels depending on morphological prefix: bare(para), y-prefixed(line-open), qo-prefixed(mid-line). For A: d+ch = A's y+gallows equivalent (within-para line-opener); p+ch = A's para-starter. FOUR-LEVEL POSITIONAL GRAMMAR CONFIRMED UNIVERSAL: bare gallows(para) > y/d-prefix+gallows(line-open) > qo-prefix+gallows(mid-line) > bare non-gallows(line-end/neutral).
**Limitation:** f-onset token counts are small (87 total). bare_k has somewhat mixed positional behavior (5.7-3% PS, 10-18% LFirst) — not as cleanly hierarchical as bare_p. The "demotion by prefix" hypothesis needs checking for whether bare_k and bare_t words have different CONTENT than qo+k and y+k words, or whether the positional difference is purely morphological.

## F102: Complete Prefix × Stem Matrix in A; p+ch=Para-Starter (26.9% PS); Platform Gallows (p,f) > Regular (t,k) for Para-Start; Universal Across ch AND sh Stems
**Experiment:** exp_095_gallows_ch_stem_hierarchy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H172 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: p+ch = A para-starter for ch-stems (26.9% PS!, 61.5% LFirst). f+ch also para-starter (21.4% PS). t+ch = weak (4.1%). k+ch = very weak (3.5%). y/d+ch = line-openers (0% PS, 56-82% LFirst). bare_ch = mid-line (0.3% PS, 7.1% LFirst). H171 SUPPORTED: Platform gallows (p,f) > Regular gallows (t,k) for para-start specialization — consistent ordering across bare gallows (A: 40%/24%/10%/6%) AND gallows+ch (27%/21%/4%/4%). H173 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: p+sh=33.3% PS; t+sh=28.6% PS; y/d+sh=0% PS; bare_sh=1% PS — IDENTICAL hierarchy to ch-stems. Gallows-prefix para-start mechanism UNIVERSAL across all A stem classes. H174 COMPLETE MATRIX: THREE TIERS in A: PARA-LEVEL (PS=20-56%): {p,f,t}+stem or bare_p/bare_f; LINE-OPENER (PS=0%, LFirst=55-86%): {y,d}+stem; MID-LINE (PS≈0%): bare_ch/bare_sh/qo+gallows. REVISED MASTER MODEL (F102): TWO-DIMENSION PREFIX SYSTEM: (1) Positional Level: gallows-prefix=para; y/d-prefix=line; qo/bare non-gallows=mid. (2) Para-Start Strength: Platform gallows (p,f) STRONGEST (56%/24% PS); Regular gallows (t) weaker (10%); k weakest (6%). Platform/regular distinction in EVA maps to discourse-level hierarchy.
**Limitation:** p+ch has n=52 tokens (adequate); t+sh n=28 (small, t+sh=28.6% may be high-variance); f+ch n=14 (very small). The t+sh=28.6% PS rate may be inflated by small sample — needs verification. k vs t hierarchy may not be stable across sections. The d+ch line-opener (0% PS, 56% LFirst) is notably LESS line-initial than y+ch (82%) — their positional roles differ within the LINE-OPENER tier.

## F103: UNIFIED GRAMMAR — PREFIX TYPE Determines Positional Role Cross-Dialectally; p+ch=Para in BOTH A(27%) and B(12%); y/d+ch=Line-Opener in BOTH (0% PS); Positional Morpheme Is the PREFIX
**Experiment:** exp_096_b_gallows_stem_hierarchy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H175 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: p+ch=para-starter in BOTH A(26.9% PS) and B(11.6% PS); y+ch/d+ch=line-openers in BOTH (0% PS, 75-84% LFirst); bare_ch=mid-line in BOTH (0.1-0.3% PS). MORPHOLOGICAL CLASS determines positional role across dialects. Gallows-demotion model is UNIVERSAL. H176 CONFIRMED: B bare_k enrichment (9.91×) is a contrast effect — 92% of bare_k tokens are mid-line; the enrichment arises because k is RARE at within-para line-first (0.78%), giving high ratio despite only 8 PS tokens. H177 STRONGLY CONFIRMED — MASTER UNIFIED GRAMMAR (F103): PREFIX TYPE = POSITIONAL MORPHEME: (1) {p,f}+stem → PARA-LEVEL (A: 21-56% PS; B: 9-15% PS); (2) {y,d}+stem → LINE-OPENER (PS=0%, LFirst=50-96%); (3) {qo}+gallows or bare_ch/sh → MID-LINE (PS≈0%). SAME class has SAME positional role in both dialects. Stem (ch/sh/k/t) = content; prefix (p/f/y/d/qo) = position. Dialect difference: A uses f-prefix more for para-starts; B uses f+ch less and k+sh more. Structurally analogous to positional particles in topic-prominent languages.
**Limitation:** f+ch discrepancy: A=21% PS (para-level) vs B=0% PS (mid-line). May reflect folio-level distribution or small sample (B n=34). k+sh in B=9% PS (para-level) but A k+sh=3% PS — cross-dialect asymmetry for k+sh. Some class PS rates are based on small n (f+sh: B n=3; bare_f: B n=17). The unified model is strong for major classes (p+ch, y+ch, d+ch, bare_ch) but has exceptions for rarer forms.

## F104: Core ch-Stems Appear Across ALL Prefix Classes (Productive Morphology); 87.8% Stem Exclusivity Is Frequency Artifact; Consistent With Natural Language Zipfian Distribution
**Experiment:** exp_097_stem_prefix_independence
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H178 PARTIALLY CONFIRMED: Core stems (chol, chor, chy, cheor, cheey) appear in ALL 4 main prefix classes (p+ch para-starters, y+ch line-openers, d+ch line-openers, bare_ch mid-line). 87.8% of stems appear in only 1 prefix class but these are mostly rare/hapax forms — frequency-limited not semantically constrained. H179 CONFIRMED: f+ch asymmetry is real and section-driven: A f+ch in herbal (21% para-start); B f+ch in stars (0% PS, B-type -edy suffixes). Genuine dialect difference in f-gallows para-start usage. H180 CONFIRMED: 3 stems fully productive (all 7 prefix classes): chol, cheey, cho. ~16 productive stems account for ~47% of all A ch-stem tokens — Zipfian productivity gradient. Consistent with natural language morphology. KEY IMPLICATION (F104): Voynichese stem × prefix combinatorics is consistent with PRODUCTIVE MORPHOLOGICAL SYSTEM (not fixed lexicon). Same stems appear with all prefix types; exclusivity is frequency-driven. Voynichese behaves like natural language: small core vocabulary fully inflected (all positional forms), peripheral vocabulary partially attested.
**Limitation:** The 87.8% exclusivity — even if frequency-driven — could also reflect a PARTIALLY productive system where some stems are semantically restricted to specific positional contexts. The frequency-based interpretation is most parsimonious but cannot rule out semantic constraints on less-frequent stems. f+ch in A (n=14) is very small — the 21% PS rate may be noisy.

**Finding:** H181 CONFIRMED WITH ASYMMETRY: LINE_OPEN tier has near-perfect para-exclusion (B=100% WP, A=98.6% WP — only 1/4 para-starts misclassified). ## F108: o-Onset Is NOT a Para-Start Class; Grammar Strength Correlates With Para Length; Herbal (10-15 line) Paragraphs Have Strictest Grammar (70.7% PARA, 0% LINE_OPEN)
**Experiment:** exp_101_o_onset_para
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H191 CONFIRMED (negative): o-onset overall is SUPPRESSED at para-starts in A (0.52×) and neutral in B (1.28×). Only "op-" sub-class (9.5× A) is para-enriched — because o+p contains p-gallows morphology. Specific olfchedy/olfchey forms (∞ enrichment) are enriched from internal f+ch PARA morphology. The remaining ~17-20% OTHER after v3 classifier represents genuinely diverse, hapax, or section-specific para-start words beyond the positional grammar system. The positional grammar is now essentially complete: PARA = {p,f,k,t}+anything + olf*/olke*/op* (from internal PARA morphology). H192 STRONGLY CONFIRMED: Para-start positional grammar strength is positively correlated with paragraph length. A: 10-15 line paragraphs (herbal) have 70.7% PARA at PS and 0.0% LINE_OPEN — the strictest grammar in the manuscript. Short (2-4 line) paragraphs: 31.4% PARA, 8.6% LINE_OPEN allowed (relaxed). B: monotonically increasing (22%→32%→59%→65% PARA as length increases); LINE_OPEN never violated in B regardless of length. The positional grammar is register-specific: strictest in the canonical herbal text format (12-13 line paragraphs), progressively relaxed in shorter (caption-like) text. Implication: the grammar characterizes a specific linguistic register (main herbal body text), not the entire manuscript uniformly.
**Limitation:** H191 negative result is limited by small sample sizes (only 15 o-onset PS words per dialect, mostly hapax). H192 para-length bins mix sections (short bin includes astro; very-long bin includes cosmo+stars in B) — the length effect may conflate section differences with length effects. The gradient is real but separating section effect from length effect would require within-section length analysis.

## F112: "OTHER" Vocabulary Tier Has Clear Sub-Structure (o-Prefix Words 37%, d-Onset Line-Boundary 19%, Particles 9%); Zipf α=1.050 (Lower NL Range); 44 Universal Words = 21-28% of Each Section's Tokens; Three-Layer Vocabulary Model
**Experiment:** exp_105_other_vocab_zipf
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H200 CONFIRMED: The "OTHER" tier (43.8% of all tokens) is NOT residual. It has clear sub-structure: (1) o-prefix content words (ok/ot/ol+anything = 37% of OTHER) — the body-text object-naming sub-tier related to the label corpus o-prefix system (F043); (2) d-onset line-boundary words (~19%): dal=30% LL, dam=70% LL, dy=46% LL = line-closers; dain=30% LF = line-opener; (3) aiin/ain short particles (~9%); (4) s-onset line-openers (saiin=51% LF, sain=60% LF = 6%). OTHER is skewed SHORT (2-char 2.25×, 7-char 0.57×). qo-onset is 0.08× suppressed in OTHER. The OTHER tier is a coherent second word class with distinct sub-functions: o-prefix=content/objects, d-onset=line-boundaries, short=particles, s-onset=openers. H199 CONFIRMED: Zipf's law α=1.050 overall (lower end of NL range 1.0-1.5). By section: B cosmo=1.105, B stars=0.979, A herbal=0.876, A pharma=0.819. Heaps β≈0.744 predicts α≈1.34, but observed 1.05 — Zipf-Mandelbrot deviation: top words (daiin=707, 2.5%) are LESS dominant than power law predicts. No single "the"-equivalent. Explained by section-specific function words diluting corpus-wide rank (daiin=55.6‰ in A herbal, 12.1‰ in B stars). H201 CONFIRMED: 44 universal words appear in all 5 major sections at ≥3 tokens. Universal tokens = 21-28% of each section's stream (consistent). Universal words: OTHER-tier (57%: daiin, ol, aiin, or, dar, dal, okaiin) and MID-tier (41%: chol, qokeey, chey, shey). No PARA-tier words are universal. 72-79% of each section's vocabulary is section-specific. B_stars has 215 section-exclusive words (most diverse); B_herbal has only 12 (most shared with B sections). A_herbal exclusive: cth-cluster forms (cthor=34, dchor=20, kchy=19). KEY FINDING (F112): Three-layer vocabulary model — (1) Universal core (21-28% tokens): 44 words = function words; (2) Section-specific content (72-79%): thousands of section-restricted words; (3) OTHER tier (43.8% ALL tokens): o-prefix objects + d-boundary + particles. The "OTHER" is NOT noise — it is the complement to ch/sh mid-line words with distinct structural roles.
**Limitation:** The universal word threshold (≥3 tokens in each section) is conservative — some function words may appear at 1-2 tokens in small sections and still be universal. B_pharma (only 398 tokens) was excluded from the analysis. The Zipf α fit uses ranks 10 to 70% to avoid instability at extremes; different fitting ranges would give different α estimates. The "sub-classification" of OTHER words uses heuristic onset-based groupings, not formal morphological analysis.

## F111: "chd" Is NOT a Morphological Unit in B — It Is ch-Onset + B-Type -edy/-dy Suffix; Heaps' Law Confirmed at β=0.661-0.744 (Natural Language Range)
**Experiment:** exp_104_chd_heaps
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H197 CONFIRMED (negative): The B ch+d cluster is NOT a morphological unit. ch+d forms (chedy=424, chedar=25, chdaiin=17, chdal=16, chdy=106) are ch-onset words with B-type -edy/-dy suffixes — the 'd' belongs to the suffix, not a separate morphological element. Positional profiles of chd/ched forms (PS=0.1%, LFirst=1.8%, LLast=11.8%) are identical to all bare_ch in B (PS=0.0%, LFirst=3.7%, LLast=12.1%) — mid-line content word behavior throughout. Suffix enrichment: -edy is 2.97× enriched, -eedy 2.60× enriched; -y suppressed to 0.06×, -ey suppressed to 0.06×. The B-exclusive ch+d pattern from F110 is explained by B's -edy suffix preference applied to ch-stems — not a new morphological category. H198 CONFIRMED: Voynichese obeys Heaps' law (V=K×N^β). Section-level β: B cosmo=0.674, A pharma=0.661, B stars=0.735, A herbal=0.744, B herbal=0.744 (all at upper end of natural language range 0.5-0.7; English prose β≈0.55-0.65). Cosmo B is most repetitive; A herbal and B stars are most diverse. Overall A/B β=0.84-0.85 is an artifact of cross-section vocabulary divergence (different sections use non-overlapping vocabulary), not a property of any single section. KEY FINDING (F111): Voynichese vocabulary growth is consistent with natural language statistics at the section level. Higher-than-English-prose β is consistent with morphologically complex languages. This is strong statistical evidence against pure random/substitution cipher models (which would have anomalous β).
**Limitation:** Heaps' law fit uses log-linear regression on the second half of each section's cumulative word sequence (ordered by occurrence, not randomized), so β estimates may reflect text order rather than pure sampling statistics. A astro (β=0.831) is based on only 437 tokens — less reliable. The β=0.84 artifact at the cross-section level was expected and is not meaningful for per-section analysis.

## F110: ch-Stem Vocabulary Classifies Sections at 73% of Full-Vocabulary Performance; A/B ch-Vocabulary Jaccard=0.181 (Below Independence Expectation); Dialects Have Genuinely Distinct ch-Lexicons
**Experiment:** exp_103_section_classifier
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H195 CONFIRMED: Naive Bayes classifier using only ch-stem words achieves 70.4% accuracy (A, 2.11× baseline) and 53.3% (B, 1.60× baseline). ch-words alone capture 73% of full-vocabulary section-discriminating power (all-word accuracy: A=96.6%, B=73.3%). Most informative ch-words: herbal A = chaiin, char, chol, chy; pharma A = cheom, cheodal, cheos, cheody; stars B = cheeo, chokaiin, cheodaiin; cosmo B = checthy, cheeky, chcthy. The section-distinctive ch-words from F109 are validated as statistically predictive features. H196 CONFIRMED: A and B share only 161/890=18.1% of ch-vocabulary (Jaccard=0.181). Expected under independence: ~260 words shared. Observed: 161 (0.62× expected — LOWER than independence). A and B ch-vocabularies are ANTI-CORRELATED — more distinct than random. Key contrasts: chedy (B=22.74‰, A=0.52‰, 43.9×), chor (A=15.65‰, B=1.39‰, 11.2×). B-exclusive: chedar(25), chdaiin(17), chdal(16), chdar(15) — ch+d cluster pattern. A-exclusive: chom(12), choiin(10), chory(9), chotchy(8) — cho- onset + A-suffix. Cross-dialect divergence is driven by opposite suffix paradigm: A ch-stems take -ol/-or/-y; B ch-stems take -edy/-cthy/-daiin → even shared underlying stems produce different word forms. KEY IMPLICATION: The 18.1% ch-vocabulary overlap (below independence expectation) suggests A and B are not simply two dialects of the same text — they have fundamentally different morphological expression of ch-stem vocabulary, making accidental homography likely for the "shared" 18%.
**Limitation:** Classifier uses sequential 80-20 split (not random), so test set may be biased toward specific sections. The ch-word classification (73% of all-word performance) is robust, but the absolute accuracy numbers depend on the split. Jaccard expectation under independence is an approximation (hypergeometric model). The "ch+d cluster" as B-exclusive pattern needs follow-up to confirm it's morphological (d-element after ch) rather than coincidental hapax forms.

## F113: d-Onset Has VOWEL/CONSONANT Split (d+vowel=OPENER; d+consonant=CLOSER); o-Prefix Body Words (19%) Obey Same A/B Suffix Paradigm Split as ch-Stems — A/B Paradigm Is UNIVERSAL Across All Onset Classes
**Experiment:** exp_106_d_onset_o_prefix
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H203 CONFIRMED: Bare d-onset (8.2% of tokens) is a unified line-boundary class with internal VOWEL/CONSONANT morphological split. d+vowel-onset continuation (daiin=24%LF, dain=30%LF, dair=31%LF, dor=37%LF) = LINE-OPENERs. d+consonant suffix (dal=30%LL, dam=70%LL, dy=46%LL, daly=55%LL) = LINE-CLOSERs. d+gallows (dch=64%LF, dsh=79%LF = LINE_OPEN tier) is strongest line-opener. d-onset suppresses B-type suffixes across BOTH dialects (-edy=0.16×, -ey=0.15×, -eey=0.13×) while enriching -aiin (3.08×). A bare_d is more closing (LLast=31.5%); B bare_d is more opening (LFirst=20.7%). D-chain: after d-ending line, 18% of next lines start with d-onset (10% bare_d + 8% d+gallows); stronger in A (19.6%) than B (14.2%) — weak but real cross-line persistence. H202 CONFIRMED: o-prefix body words = 19.0% of all tokens (5,384 tokens). Low vocabulary overlap with labels (10.8%). Stem overlap with qo-body: 28.3% (all shared stems are k/t-initial, consistent with F043). CRITICAL: o-prefix system follows same A/B suffix paradigm split as ch-stems: A-dominant o-words use -ol/-or/-chor (otchol=44.4× A; okol=5.8× A); B-dominant o-words use -edy/-eedy (otedy=69.3× B; okedy=∞ B; okeedy=49.2× B). Sub-class positional roles: or-onset = strong closer (LL=40.6%); ol-onset = moderate closer (LL=24.2%); ok/ot-onset = mid-line content (LL=14-16%). B has more o-prefix words (20.6%) than A (16.0%). KEY FINDING (F113): The A/B suffix paradigm split is UNIVERSAL — it applies to ch-onset, o-prefix, and qo-prefix vocabulary. In A: ALL onset classes take -ol/-or. In B: ALL take -edy/-eedy. The dialect is a GRAMMATICAL property of the entire text, not a lexical property of specific word stems.
**Limitation:** The VOWEL/CONSONANT split in d-onset is based on word-initial character after 'd', not formal phonological analysis. Some words like 'dal' could be parsed as d + al (consonant-initial suffix) OR as the morpheme 'dal' where 'a' begins the suffix — the structural interpretation is heuristic. The stem-overlap analysis for o-body and qo-body uses string matching (strip prefix, compare) which may produce false matches for words that happen to share suffix strings. The d-chain analysis is subject to false positives when consecutive lines happen to start with d-onset words unrelated to the chain mechanism.

## F114: A/B Suffix Paradigm Is UNIVERSAL Across All 16 Onset Classes; s-Onset Is a B-Paradigm LINE-OPENER (Complementary to d-Onset A-Paradigm); Both Lead to qo-Onset at 2.2-2.5× Enrichment
**Experiment:** exp_107_universal_paradigm
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H205 CONFIRMED: All 16 tested onset classes show the SAME direction of A/B suffix paradigm split (A: -ol/-or/-y; B: -edy/-eedy). Magnitude varies: bare_t=12.6× B-ratio (strongest), d+gallows=9.3×, bare_ch=5.71×, bare_d=5.73×, bare_s=5.17×. d/s-onset in A-dialect: ZERO -edy/-eedy (absolute suppression); in B: 3-11%. The paradigm is a GRAMMATICAL property of the dialect (not the onset class). Notable: o+t-onset has 61.8× B-enrichment for -edy (highest of any class); d+gallows has most polarized split (A: -ol=60.7%; B: -edy=48.2%). H206 CONFIRMED: s-onset (11.8% of tokens) is a LINE-OPENER class (LFirst=18.7%, LLast=9.9% — UNIDIRECTIONAL, unlike d-onset bidirectional LFirst=17.2%/LLast=26.2%). s+vowel = OPENER (saiin=51%LF, sain=60%LF, sor=66%LF, sol=63%LF) — SAME vowel/consonant split as d-onset. But s/d are SUFFIX OPPOSITES: s enriches -edy (1.40×), -ey (1.52×), suppresses -aiin (0.73×); d enriches -aiin (3.08×), suppresses -edy (0.16×). Both s-openers and d-openers are followed by qo at 2.16-2.48× enrichment (same grammatical role). s-onset = B-paradigm aligned (opener); d-onset = A-paradigm aligned (opener+closer). KEY FINDING (F114): TWO LINE-OPENER CLASSES in complementary distribution: (1) s-onset: B-paradigm, unidirectional opener, -edy/-ey rich; (2) d-onset: A-paradigm, bidirectional opener+closer, -aiin rich. Both lead to qo mid-line. Universal paradigm split (H205) confirms a single deep grammatical rule governs all onset classes.
**Limitation:** The "universal paradigm" test uses aggregated A-type (-ol/-or/-y) and B-type (-edy/-eedy/-eey) suffix groups. The -y suffix is included in A-type because it's equally distributed in A, but it appears in B too (y is not strictly A-exclusive like -ol). A stricter test using only -ol/-or (A) vs -edy/-eedy (B) would show an even starker split. The s-onset line-opening function is confirmed but whether s and d are truly "complementary" (not co-occurring) requires a formal complementary distribution test (not done here).

## F120: Voynichese Suffix System Has FOUR-LEVEL Hierarchy: Dialect → Stem Class → Section → Vowel-Length; Stars-B Triple-Vowel Forms (eeedy=63% stars; eeey=59%); A-Herbal=-y Dominant; A-Pharma=-ol Dominant (8.9% diff, 3.5× Weaker Than B)
**Experiment:** exp_113_vowel_ext_asuffix
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H222 CONFIRMED: eee (triple-vowel) words are stars-dominant (17.25‰) and cosmo-suppressed (4.40‰). Vowel-length gradient is MONOTONICALLY stars-concentrated: edy=36%→eedy=48%→eeedy=63% (stars); eey=47%→eeey=59% (stars). Cosmo shows OPPOSITE monotonic decrease with length (45%→40%→25%). eee words are enriched in ok/ol/qo onset classes (1.7-1.9×) and SUPPRESSED in ch/sh (0.37-0.46×) — matching Complex-B flexible-suffix onset classes. Stars-only forms: oteeey(7), lkeeey(7), teeedy(4), lkeeedy(4). Pharma-A has second-highest eee rate (11.61‰) despite being A-dialect. H223 CONFIRMED (partial): A-dialect has mild section variation — herbal-A is -y dominant (ch=29%, qok=37%, ot=31%); pharma-A is -ol dominant (ch=28%, qok=41%, ok=40%, ot=41%); consistent across ALL tested onset classes. Pharma-A also elevates -dy/-ey. Average diff=8.9% (vs B's 31% for -eey). Entropy unchanged (~2.5-2.8 bits — full A-paradigm used everywhere, just different proportions). KEY FINDING (F120): Voynichese suffix system has a FOUR-LEVEL hierarchy: (1) Dialect: A vs B paradigm; (2) Stem class: ch/sh=Simple-B vs qok/ok=Complex-B (B); -y vs -ol by section (A); (3) Section: B=stars→eey/cosmo→eedy/herbal→baseline; A=herbal/astro→-y; pharma→-ol; (4) Vowel length: stars-specific triple-vowel extension (eeedy, eeey) for Complex-B onset classes only. This degree of hierarchical suffix structure is strong evidence for natural language morphology — a substitution cipher would not produce this multi-level grammatical regularity.
**Limitation:** The pharma eee rate (11.61‰) in A-dialect is unexpected and may reflect transcription noise (eee patterns harder to distinguish from ee in some handwriting styles). The A-section suffix variation (8.9% diff) may partly reflect section size differences (pharma-A is smaller, so sampling noise is higher). The -ol dominance in pharma-A may be confounded by the specific pharma vocabulary (many pharmaceutical plant names starting with specific onset classes that favor -ol). The entropy stability across A sections (all ~2.5-2.8 bits) means the variation is in rank ordering of suffixes, not in how many suffixes are used.

## F119: B-Paradigm Suffix Is a THREE-TIER Register System: Tier1=Dialect(B=edy/eedy/eey), Tier2=Stem Class (ch/sh=Simple-B; qok/ok=Complex-B), Tier3=Section (stars→-eey; cosmo→-eedy for qo-prefix; herbal=baseline); Stars Has Triple-Vowel Exclusive Forms
**Experiment:** exp_112_b_suffix_sections
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H220 CONFIRMED (partial): Stars B universally elevates -eey (highest rate across ALL tested onset classes: ch=30%, sh=27%, qok=43%, ok=51%, ot=34%). -eey gradient is MONOTONIC: herbal<cosmo<stars for every class. Cosmo B elevates -eedy specifically for qo-prefix stems (qok=35%, qot=41%, ok=38% eedy) but NOT for ch/sh (which remain edy-dominant at 76-78% everywhere). -edy dominance erodes monotonically from herbal (70-87%) to cosmo (43-76%) to stars (23-61%). Partition is a GRADIENT not categorical switch. Stars and sections share the SAME vocabulary (qokedy/qokeedy/qokeey all present everywhere) but at different proportions. Stars-exclusive: triple-vowel extended forms (oteeey=7, cheeey=6, lkeeey=7) — ONLY in stars B. Per-folio qok data: f103 (stars) = edy=7%, eey=69%; f77 (cosmo) = eedy=47%; f26 (herbal) = edy=82%. KEY FINDING (F119): Voynichese B-dialect has a THREE-TIER suffix register: (1) Dialect tier: B-paradigm (-edy/-eedy/-eey) vs A-paradigm (-ol/-or/-y); (2) Stem-class tier: ch/sh=Simple-B (-edy dominant, H=1.16-1.21 bits); qok/ok=Complex-B (balanced, H=1.57-1.58 bits); (3) Section tier: stars→-eey (universal); cosmo→-eedy (qo-prefix only); herbal→baseline (-edy dominant). **Limitation:** The section-level B-suffix partition may partly reflect SCRIBAL VARIATION rather than dialect/register: different scribes may have worked on different sections and preferred different B-suffixes. The triple-vowel forms (oteeey, cheeey) are rare (6-7 tokens each) and may be transcription artifacts. The -eedy vs -eey distinction is subtle (one fewer 'e') and some ambiguity in transcription conventions may inflate apparent differences.

## F118: olk- Is B-Paradigm Mid-Line Content (Not B-Closer); Secondary B-Suffix Split (ch/sh→-edy; qok/ok→Balanced); A-Paradigm Suffixes Are Grammaticalized Free Words (ol=523, or=356); B-Paradigm Suffixes Are Non-Free (-edy=2 standalone)
**Experiment:** exp_111_olk_suffix_matrix

Linguistic interpretation: A-dialect is morphologically OLDER/CONSERVATIVE; B-dialect is NEWER/INNOVATIVE (added non-free -edy/-eedy/-eey paradigm).
**Limitation:** The suffix extraction uses longest-match suffix stripping from a predefined list; some words may have non-standard suffix boundaries. The olk- analysis treats olk- as a 3-char onset, but olk may be ol+k (compound o-prefix + gallows) rather than a single morpheme — this ambiguity is not resolved here. The standalone free-word comparison (ol=523 standalone vs suffix) conflates cases where ol appears as a genuine free word vs as a typo/error in the transcription. The section-level B-suffix variation (herbal→edy, cosmo→eedy, stars→eey) may reflect scribal variation rather than dialect evolution — cosmo and stars sections are attributed to different scribes.

B-dialect has stronger grammar zone (6.0% PARA at line+1 vs 4.1% in A). LINE_OPEN tier elevated at lines 3+ (2.3-3.3%), not at lines 1-2 (1.2-1.4%). H214 CONFIRMED UNEXPECTED: The B-extreme on the dialect polarity axis is NOT a single onset morpheme like cth-. Top B-dominant clusters (shed=78.8×, ched=45.5×, oked=∞, oted=∞) are -EDY SUFFIX PRODUCTS: they represent sh/ch/ok/ot onset + -edy suffix combinations, where the 3-4 char prefix captures the junction of stem+suffix-onset. No B-exclusive onset MORPHEME parallel to cth- was found. The dialect polarity axis is ASYMMETRIC: A-extreme = ONSET-encoded (cth-=14×, ctho=60.8×, ckho=45.3×); B-extreme = SUFFIX-encoded (-edy applied to any onset class). Closest B-structural class: olk- cluster (olkedy/olkaiin, B/A=9.5×, stars/cosmo dominant). KEY FINDING (F117): The A/B dialect encode their identity through DIFFERENT morphological layers: A uses distinctive ONSET morphemes (cth-/ckh-); B uses distinctive SUFFIX morphemes (-edy). This is consistent with a model where B-dialect added the -edy suffix paradigm onto existing onset classes, while A-dialect retained ancestral onset-extended morphology (cth- gallows extension).
**Limitation:** The onset-cluster analysis uses N-gram prefixes (2/3/4 chars from word start), which can capture onset+suffix junctions for short stems. The apparent "B-extreme onset clusters" (shed/ched/oked) are methodological artifacts of this approach — not genuine onset classes. The -am distribution at paragraph-last lines is based on only 104 paragraphs (4+ lines); shorter paragraphs and labels were excluded. The gram zone (lines 1-2 vs 3+) transition might reflect folio composition (some folios have only 2-line paragraphs which would be entirely in the grammar zone). The dialect comparison (A=60 vs B=44 paragraphs) may conflate section effects with dialect effects.

## F116: -am Class Is Dialect-NEUTRAL Overall but Dialect-SPLIT Within (Onset Controls Identity); 4-gram Cross-Folio Repetition Essentially Absent (0.006%); cth- Is MOST A-Exclusive Onset Class (14× A/B), Gallows-Extended A-Dialect Closer
**Experiment:** exp_109_am_4gram_cth
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H211 CONFIRMED (partial): The -am closed class is dialect-neutral at class level (A/B=1.00×) but dialect-SPLIT within: A-dominant -am words (dam=3.1×, cham=3.5×, sam=11.6×) are A-onset-prefixed; B-dominant -am words (qokam=0.3×, ram=0.2×, okam=0.5×) are qo/o-onset-prefixed. The -am SUFFIX is dialect-neutral; the ONSET determines dialect identity — consistent with F114's universal paradigm. All -am words are LINE-CLOSERS (LL=60-100%). cosmo B strongly suppresses -am class (6.83‰ vs 22-41‰ in other sections). oly/oldy is B-preferred (B/A=2.50×). H212 REFUTED: Only 1/16,210 unique 4-grams repeats across 2 folios (0.006%); 5-grams: 0 cross-folio. Voynichese text generates compositionally unique sequences per folio — no formulaic 4+ word repetition. Consistent with Heaps' β=0.66-0.74 and 72-79% section-specific vocabulary. H213 CONFIRMED: cth- is the most A-exclusive onset class found (14.00× A/B ratio). Positional: LINE-CLOSER (LLast=25.2%), especially in A (26.2%). Suffix: strongly A-paradigm (enriches -y=2.16×, -or=2.24×, -ol=1.96×; suppresses -edy=0.33×, -eedy=0.06×). Section: concentrated in herbal (37.78‰) and pharma (24.31‰), nearly absent in stars/cosmo (~2‰). Low stem overlap with qo- (23.5%) and o- (17.6%) — NOT a parallel prefix system. cth- = GALLOWS-EXTENDED A-DIALECT CLOSER. KEY FINDING (F116): Onset-class dialect polarity axis: cth- (extreme A-pole, 14×) → d-onset (moderate A, line-closer) → ch/sh/qo (paradigm base) → s-onset (B-shifted, opener). The A/B paradigm split (F114) is graded on a single axis from extreme-A (cth-) to B-shifted (s-onset). Onset class encodes BOTH positional role AND dialect polarity simultaneously.
**Limitation:** The -am dialect split analysis uses rate per dialect token, not controlling for section composition (e.g., qokam is B-dominant partly because qo-onset is more common in B). The 4-gram repetition null result may reflect the small corpus size (16K 4-gram tokens) rather than true compositional uniqueness — a larger corpus might reveal rare repeats. The cth- section concentration in herbal/pharma partly explains the A-dominance (herbal/pharma are predominantly A-dialect sections), so the 14× ratio is partly a section effect, not purely an onset-class effect.

## F115: s/d-Onset Are Frequency-Complementary (Not Strictly Complementary); Grammar/Content Split Is at STEM Level (3+ Bit Entropy Gap): Grammar Particles H=0 Bits; Content Stems H=2.9-3.4 Bits
**Experiment:** exp_108_sd_complement_entropy
**Date:** 2026-04-09
**Finding:** H208 CONFIRMED (partial): s/d co-occurrence ratio=0.97× (near independence) — NOT strict complementary distribution. However: s-opener lines suppress d-words (0.67×); B uses s-openers 1.78× more than d-openers; cosmo B strongly prefers s (s/d=2.98×); pharma A slightly prefers d (s/d=0.89×). s/d preference is dialect/section-sensitive, not a categorical alternation. H210 CONFIRMED: Grammar/content distinction is at the STEM level, not onset-class level (all onset classes range only 3.248-3.794 bits H). Grammar particles (cham, otam, dam, okam, ram, ytam = -am closed class from F093) have H=0.0-0.3 bits (fixed forms, no suffix variation). Content stems (ch, sh, qok, ok, ot, k) have H=2.9-3.4 bits (6-8 productive suffixes). The grammar/content entropy gap is 3+ bits — a massive, unambiguous distinction. Medium-frequency words (6-20 tokens) have highest entropy (3.747 bits) — these are the productive paradigm stems. Very-high-frequency words (>100 tokens) have slightly lower entropy (3.636 bits) due to suffix dominance. bare_d is most constrained onset class (H=3.248, driven by -aiin=31.5%). bare_k is most diverse (H=3.794). KEY FINDING (F115): Two-tier vocabulary structure with 3+ bit entropy gap: (1) CLOSED GRAMMAR CLASS (H≈0): -am/-oly words (cham, otam, dam, okam) = invariant grammatical particles; (2) OPEN CONTENT CLASS (H≈3 bits): ch, sh, qok, ok = productive paradigm stems. The grammar/content boundary is SHARP, consistent with natural language morphology.
**Limitation:** The stem-level entropy analysis uses string suffix-stripping (word → stem = word minus suffix), which can produce incorrect stem boundaries for morphologically complex words. Stems with n<10 tokens were excluded, so rare stems (which may be highly constrained) are not counted. The -am closed class stems (cham, otam) are essentially word forms with very specific onset×suffix combinations — the "H=0" finding means they have exactly one form, which may reflect low frequency rather than a grammatical constraint (a productive word form would show entropy increase with more tokens).


## F287: VMS Onset Classes Have Three-Tier Midfix Structure: Sparse Templates (qok/ok/ot/cth), Moderate (ch/sh/d), Rich Body (y/o/l/k)
**Experiment:** exp_288_stolfi_onset_decomp
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Exploratory. VMS onset classes separate into three structural tiers by zero-midfix rate (fraction of words where onset is directly adjacent to suffix, no intervening characters): (1) SPARSE TEMPLATES — B-dialect: qok (ZeroMid=78.4%, MLen=0.52), qot (69.7%, 0.73), ok (68.2%, 0.80), ot (66.7%, 0.82); A-dialect: cth (69.1%, 0.75), d (60.5%, 1.33) — onset+suffix with minimal interior elaboration; (2) MODERATE MIDFIX — ch in both dialects (ZeroMid≈40%, MLen≈1.52), sh (40-51%), s (~57-57%); (3) RICH INTERNAL BODY — y (ZeroMid≈1.3%, MLen≈2.5), o (9-10%, MLen≈2.4), l-B (11.9%, 1.97), k-A (27.1%, 2.05). Suffix entropy also differs across onset classes: A-dialect range=0.678 bits (min=3.02 r-onset, max=3.698 y-onset); B-dialect range=0.789 bits (min=3.131 'other', max=3.920 o-onset). This means knowing an onset class reduces uncertainty about the suffix by ~0.7 bits. B-dialect suffix length is systematically longer than A-dialect (SLen_B > SLen_A for all shared onsets, by 0.27-0.86 chars).
**Limitation:** Exploratory analysis — no pre-specified null hypothesis. Midfix/suffix boundary depends on suffix extraction list coverage (88-93%); ~7-12% of words have no recognized suffix and are counted with full body as midfix, slightly inflating midfix lengths. The three-tier classification is observational; tier boundaries are not formally defined.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** No published per-onset midfix breakdown found in KB. exp_008 reported overall h2 increase of +0.048 bits from crust stripping; the per-onset breakdown is a new measurement. The zero-midfix rate range (1.3% for y-onset to 78.4% for qok-B) is a new quantitative characterization.

## F288: qok Cross-Dialect Midfix Asymmetry: A-qok MLen=1.34 vs B-qok MLen=0.52 — Same Onset Class Deployed Differently in A and B
**Experiment:** exp_288_stolfi_onset_decomp
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Exploratory. The qok onset class has fundamentally different internal structure across dialects. A-qok: MLen=1.34, ZeroMid=44.1% (N=537). B-qok: MLen=0.52, ZeroMid=78.4% (N=2471). This 2.6× midfix mean difference means B-qok words are structurally simpler — predominantly onset[3]+suffix[3-4] directly (e.g., qokaiin, qokedy, qokeedy). A-qok words more often have intermediate characters (e.g., qotchy, qokaiin with midfix in stem). This is a CROSS-DIALECT CHARACTER-LEVEL STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE for the same onset class, distinct from the previously established positional differences (qok-B enriched at different positions than qok-A). Contrast: ch-onset has IDENTICAL midfix length in A and B (MLen=1.52 in both), showing ch is architecturally stable while qok is dialect-variable. Similar pattern: B-dialect ok/ot/qot are sparse templates (ZeroMid 66-70%); A-dialect ok/ot are moderate (ZeroMid 46-47%).
**Limitation:** A-qok token count (537) is 4.6× smaller than B-qok (2471), introducing possible sampling variance. Dialect classification is by edy-rate threshold; border-case folios may be misclassified.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** No prior per-onset cross-dialect midfix comparison found in this project. The 2.6× midfix difference for qok across dialects is the largest cross-dialect character-level structural difference identified to date.

## F289: d-Onset Has Strongest Onset→Suffix Constraint: -aiin Is 22–35% of d-Onset Words in Both Dialects (vs <12% for Same Suffix in Other Onsets)
**Experiment:** exp_288_stolfi_onset_decomp
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Exploratory. The d-onset class selects the -aiin suffix at 34.6% (A-dialect) and 22.5% (B-dialect), which is 3-5× the -aiin rate in other onset classes (ch-A: 6.3%, qok-B: 10.2%). d is the only onset where a single suffix exceeds 20% in both dialects simultaneously. The d-onset suffix distribution is distinctively concentrated: in A, d→-aiin at 34.6%; in B, d→-aiin at 22.5% with -ar as second (14.4%). By contrast, d-onset word midfix length (A: 1.33, B: 1.21) and zero-midfix rate (A: 60.5%, B: 59.8%) are consistent across dialects — d is a sparse-template onset in both. This pairs with F113 (d-onset has vowel/consonant split) and the known d-onset grammatical role (A-paradigm line-closer). The d→-aiin specialization is not fully explained by d being a line-closer: other line-closing onsets (cth, ch-LL) do not show -aiin at this rate.
**Limitation:** Cross-dialect comparison may conflate section effects (d-onset is more common in A-herbal, where -aiin is a common A-paradigm suffix). Suffix coverage for d-onset is ~93% (captures most d words). The mechanism linking d-onset specifically to -aiin is unknown.
**Commitment status:** Not committed. Supports direction of F113 (d-onset grammatical role), does not contradict committed claims.
**Magnitude context:** d-onset -aiin rate (34.6% A) is 5.5× the -aiin rate for ch-onset (6.3% A). This is the largest onset-to-suffix rate ratio identified in the corpus. F115 noted bare_d has H=3.248 bits (most constrained onset class) — consistent with d→-aiin constraint reducing suffix diversity.

## F290: Hapax Words Are a Structurally Distinct Class: WLen+2.7 Chars, MLen 7× Longer, ZeroMid 1% vs 66-71% for Frequent Words; Hapax Onset Distribution KL=0.94-1.62 bits (Z>444)
**Experiment:** exp_289_hapax_structure
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Hapax legomena (69.4% of VMS word types, 15.6% of tokens) are structurally different from frequent words (freq≥20, 3.5% of types): (1) MIDFIX: hapax MLen=3.87-4.15 chars vs frequent MLen=0.55-0.56 chars (7× difference); ZeroMid=0.8-1.0% vs 66.4-70.7% (hapaxes almost never have zero midfix, frequent words almost always do). (2) LENGTH: hapax WLen=7.05-7.18 vs frequent WLen=4.47-5.03 (+2.0-2.7 chars). (3) ONSET: KL(hapax||frequent)=0.94 bits (B) / 1.62 bits (A), Z>444 vs shuffled null (mean 0.006-0.010). Hapaxes are depleted in ch/d/qok (sparse-template onsets) and enriched in o/y/l/other (rich-body onsets). (4) SUFFIX: Hapaxes have 17.8-23.6% unrecognized suffix vs 1.5-5.0% for frequent words; hapaxes have higher suffix entropy (H=3.66-3.92 vs H=3.43-3.70). This reveals a TWO-TIER VMS vocabulary: Tier 1 = template words (short, onset+suffix direct, high-frequency — the grammatical tokens driving positional grammar); Tier 2 = vocabulary-rich words (long midfix, complex interior, appear once — the content carriers).
**Limitation:** Hapax frequency is global (A+B combined); sectional hapaxes counted as non-hapax. Long-word frequency suppression (any language's Zipf law) contributes to the midfix difference, but cannot explain the ZeroMid binary contrast (1% vs 66-71%). The null model KL Z=476 value is in part driven by word-length → onset-class correlation.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** The 7× midfix mean difference (hapax vs frequent) has no published comparator identified. The KL divergence onset gap (Z>444) is the largest statistical separation between vocabulary tiers measured in this project. Consistent with F279 (vocabulary richness gap: simulation over-produces 2.2×) and F287 (sparse-template onset classes).

## F291: Hapax Words Are Position-Stratified: MID Hapax=11-16%, LF/LL Hapax=21-29%; Template Words 79% MID; Hapax MLen STABLE Across Positions (~4 chars); LL Vocabulary-Rich Words 37-44% Hapax
**Experiment:** exp_290_hapax_position
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Mode B's positional split (copy-buffer MID vs cipher LF/LL) is confirmed by the hapax distribution: MID hapax token rate = 11.0% (B) / 16.0% (A), LF/LL hapax rate = 21-29% (2× MID). Frequent words (freq≥20) concentrate at MID: 79.1% of frequent-word tokens are at MID positions. NEW: Hapax midfix length (MLen≈3.94-4.18) is STABLE across LF, MID, and LL positions — hapax words are structurally uniform regardless of line position. Among vocabulary-rich (has-midfix) words, LL has the highest hapax rate: A-LL=44.5% hapax, B-LL=36.9% hapax. Template words (ZeroMid) are almost never hapax (0.1-1.1%) regardless of position. MID has the highest zero-midfix rate (A: 38.6%, B: 47.6%), confirming copy-buffer generates template words.
**Limitation:** Hapax rate differences may partly reflect word-length effects (longer words → rarer). Hapax midfix stability across positions suggests length is not the main driver. Line-position assignment may not exactly correspond to Mode B's paragraph-aware LF/LL/MID categorization.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** 2× hapax rate difference (LF/LL vs MID) is consistent with exp_265 (MID hapax rate 15-24% vs LF/LL 38-48% TYPE-level; this experiment confirms TOKEN-level). The LL vocabulary-rich hapax rate (44.5% A, 36.9% B) is a new measurement not previously reported. Supports and extends F290 (two-tier vocabulary structure).

## F292: VMS Word Zones Have Zone-Specific Character Rules: 'q' Onset-Exclusive, 'n' Suffix-Exclusive, 'e/a/i' Onset-Absent; Midfix Has Highest Character Entropy (3.58 bits) and Bigram Entropy (5.4-5.7 bits); Gallows Compounds (ch, ckh, pch, cth) Appear as Midfixes (Combined ~20% of All Midfixes)
**Experiment:** exp_291_midfix_inventory
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** Exploratory. VMS word zones have distinct character inventories: (1) ONSET zone (onset exclusive): 'q' appears in 11-12% of onset characters but only 0.39% of midfix and 0% of suffix — effectively onset-exclusive; 'h', 'c' appear in onset+midfix but not suffix. (2) MIDFIX zone: no character is exclusively midfix, but zone has highest character entropy (A: 3.592, B: 3.584 bits vs onset A:3.151/B:3.177, suffix A:3.115/B:3.022); top midfix sequences are 'ch' (9.6-10.6%), 'k' (6.7%), 'e' (5.2-7.3%), 'ai' (3.1-5.1%), gallows compounds 'ckh' (2.7%), 'pch' (1-2%), 'cth' (0.9-1.2%). Gallows compounds together represent ~20% of all midfix instances. (3) SUFFIX zone (lowest entropy H=3.02-3.11): 'n' suffix-exclusive (suffix=8-9%, onset=0%), 'y' suffix-dominant (suffix=17-21%); 'e', 'a', 'i' absent from onsets. Midfix bigram entropy (5.4-5.7 bits) is ~2× suffix bigram entropy (3.3-3.4 bits), explaining why midfixes generate most of the hapax lexical diversity. Midfixes are NOT vowel-dominated: 33-39% have >80% consonant-like content.
**Limitation:** Suffix extraction coverage 88-93%; unrecognized suffix cases inflate midfix consonant content. Bigram entropy >4 bits possible from rare bigram distribution; the 5.4-5.7 figure reflects many unique midfix 2-grams.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** Zone character entropy difference (midfix 0.44-0.48 bits above onset) is new measurement. The 'q onset-exclusive' finding confirms published Voynich structural knowledge (q always leads words). The 'ch' compound as top midfix (10% of midfixes) was not previously quantified in this project. Consistent with Stolfi's crust/bench/core model but provides quantitative character-level confirmation.

## F307: 17-Mechanism B-Dialect Architecture 19/19 Stable — am_lf_enr exp_304 Failure Was Seed-Dependent Artifact; R_LF=0.12 Optimal; Architecture Confirmed Across 100 Trials / 10 Seeds
**Experiment:** exp_305_amlf_seed_check
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H507 CONFIRMED. The am_lf_enr=125.3% failure in exp_304 (N=30, SEED=304000, clamp_sparse) was a seed-dependent statistical artifact. Testing 10 independent seeds (100, 200, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, 50000, 287000, 301000, 304000) × N=10 trials each, all 10 seeds give 19/19 PASS. am_lf_enr range: 0.1040-0.1365 (84.9-111.4% of VMS 0.1225); mean=0.1245 (101.6% of VMS). edy_rate stable at 0.185-0.188 (95-97% of VMS 0.194). R_LF sensitivity: R_LF=0.10 fails at am_lf_enr=75.5%; R_LF=0.12 and R_LF=0.08 both pass (19/19). R_LF=0.12 confirmed as optimal. The N=30 sequential run from SEED=304000 in exp_304 sampled trials with unlucky elevated am_lf_enr in the second half of the run. ARCHITECTURE CONFIRMED: 17-mechanism B-dialect simulation (16 prior mechanisms + vocabulary clamping for qok/ok/ot/qot sparse-midfix onsets with full VMS B-dialect type inventory, frequency-weighted) achieves 19/19 PASS stably across 100 trials from 10 independent seeds. Parameters unchanged: p_blind=0.115, p_lf=1.0, cp=0.55, mp=0.90, p_qokch=0.12, p_chqok=0.12, p_stutter=0.006, r_lf=0.12, r_mid=0.20, mu_len=8.4, sigma_len=3.0, p_mf=0.20, p_lf_mf=0.50, p_ll_mf=0.00, gamma=0.30, alpha=0.20, beta=0.30. Performance: Menzerath r≈−0.091 (40% of VMS), MID slope≈−0.041 (71% of VMS), edy_rate≈96% of VMS, CP90 ratios: qok=0.91×, ok=0.81×, ot=0.77×, qot=0.81×.
**Limitation:** "19/19 stable" is scoped to N=10 × 10 seeds = 100 total trials, not N=30 per seed. exp_304 N=30 gave 19/19 at other seeds (baseline was 19/19); the failure was specific to one seed × N=30. R_LF=0.08 also passes but not tested for am_lf_enr stability across seeds. Vocabulary clamping lexicons directly encode VMS type distributions — CP90 reproduction is by construction, not independent prediction.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** 17th mechanism closes the largest residual CP90 gap in project history (qok: 17×→0.91×). am_lf_enr seed variance (84-111%) is consistent with Poisson sampling noise at the token counts in question; the single 125.3% outlier at N=30 was within the tail of that distribution. Architecture stability at 19/19 across 100 trials is the strongest pass count in simulation history.

## F308: beta=0.50 Achieves 19/19 PASS with Menzerath r = −0.109 (48% of VMS); Prior edy_rate Beta Ceiling Fully Removed by Vocabulary Clamping; Architecture Updated beta=0.30→0.50
**Experiment:** exp_306_beta_resweep
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H508 CONFIRMED. Beta sweep (0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50) × N=10 each, all with 17-mechanism clamp_sparse architecture. All beta values give edy_rate 98-101% of VMS — the prior beta ceiling (edy_rate fragility at beta>0.30) is completely removed by vocabulary clamping. Beta=0.50 selected by maximizing |menz_r| subject to ≥18/19 PASS and am_lf_enr ≤120% of VMS. N=30 full run at beta=0.50: 19/19 PASS. Key metrics: Menzerath r = −0.1089 (48.4% of VMS −0.225, up from 40% at beta=0.30); MID slope = −0.0490 (84.5% of VMS −0.058, up from 71%); edy_rate = 0.1902 (98.1%); am_lf_enr = 0.1308 (106.8%); am_mid_enr = 0.2204 (112.8%, highest but still PASS). Sweep shows beta=0.35 and 0.45 also 19/19 with good menz_r (45.1%, 45.9%). beta=0.40 borderline (18/19 at N=10, am_lf_enr=120.6% — likely seed-dependent). ARCHITECTURE: updated to beta=0.50. 17-mechanism B-dialect simulation (16 prior + clamp_sparse qok/ok/ot/qot, full VMS lexicons) with beta=0.50 achieves 19/19 PASS, menz_r=−0.109, MID slope=−0.049.
**Limitation:** Beta sweep covers only {0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50}; beta=0.55+ untested. am_mid_enr at 112.8% is the highest it's been — further beta increase may push it above 120% ceiling. N=10 for sweep values; beta=0.40 failure may be seed-dependent (not retested). Menzerath r at 48% of VMS leaves a substantial gap; structural mechanisms (e.g., repetition distance, section-level variation) likely needed for further recovery.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** Menzerath r gain from beta=0.30→0.50: −0.091→−0.109 (+20% relative improvement in |r|). The first beta introduction (beta=0.00→0.30 in exp_287) gave the largest Menzerath r gain in project history (r from ~−0.04 to −0.10). This second gain adds another 20% on top. Combined, the two beta steps account for the majority of the Menzerath r recovery arc in the B-dialect simulation. Remaining gap (−0.109 vs −0.225) is approximately 52% of the full VMS signal — a structural gap that parameter tuning alone cannot close.

## F309: VMS Menzerath r Is Primarily Within-Section Structure (Weighted Within-Section r=−0.268 > Global −0.225); Herbal/Astro MID Slopes (−0.11 to −0.13) Are 2× Simulation Capability; Bio MID Slope Already Matched
**Experiment:** exp_307_menzerath_section_analysis
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H509 REFUTED (cross-section heterogeneity does NOT explain the Menzerath r gap). VMS B-dialect Menzerath r by section: stars=−0.291 (N=1068, 45% of corpus), bio=−0.208 (N=759, 32%), herbal=−0.329 (N=270), astro=−0.328 (N=50), pharma=−0.338 (N=20), text=−0.129 (N=171). ALL sections individually have stronger Menzerath r than the simulation (−0.109). Weighted within-section r=−0.268 (STRONGER than global r=−0.225). Between-section gradient: Spearman r=−0.60 (moderate cross-section contribution). MID slope by section: stars=−0.063 (sim=−0.049, 78% closure), bio=−0.046 (sim exceeds: 106%), herbal=−0.111 (sim=44%), astro=−0.125 (39%), pharma=−0.110 (45%). INTERPRETATION: (1) Simulation gap is a genuine within-section mechanism deficit, not missing section-level structure. (2) The beta mechanism (position-conditional suffix length penalty) is near-adequate for bio/stars sections but provides only 39-45% of herbal/astro/pharma slope. (3) Bio section's Menzerath r (−0.208) is still 2× simulation (−0.109) despite the MID slope being close (106%) — MID slope alone does not explain the full Menzerath r; LF/LL vs MID word length contrast and line-length variance also contribute. (4) Stars section (45% of corpus) is well-matched: r=−0.291 vs simulation r ≈ −0.109. The corpus weighting toward stars reduces the global target to −0.225.
**Limitation:** Section boundaries are approximated by folio number ranges (following exp_252/297). The "text" section (f117+) may include heterogeneous folio composition. Astro (N=50) and pharma (N=20) have small sample sizes — Menzerath r is noisy at these counts (±0.1 estimated 1σ). Within-section r for "text" (r=−0.129) is a genuine finding but that section has heterogeneous composition.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** The weighted within-section r (−0.268) exceeding the global r (−0.225) is a new insight — VMS sections individually are more Menzerath-compliant than the corpus aggregate. The herbal/astro MID slopes (−0.11 to −0.13) are more than twice the simulation's best (−0.049 at beta=0.50) — this represents a qualitative scale difference, not just a parameter gap. Bio section's MID slope (−0.046) is already reproduced by the simulation, confirming the bio-like word composition is within the current architecture's capability.

## F310: LL Word Length Is Line-Length-Conditional in VMS (r_ll=−0.219); LL Component Is Dominant Driver of Menzerath r; Simulation Missing This Component (r_ll=−0.016, 7.3% of VMS)
**Experiment:** exp_308_menzerath_component_decomp
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H510 CONFIRMED. Decomposing VMS B-dialect Menzerath r=−0.225 into position-class components: r_lf=−0.002 (LF word length vs line length, negligible), r_mid=−0.178 (MID word length vs line length, substantial), r_ll=−0.219 (LL word length vs line length, DOMINANT). VMS LL word length decreases from 5.730 chars (2-4 word lines) to 4.422 chars (11-15 word lines) — a 1.31 char decrease strongly correlated with line length. Simulation LL_wl is nearly flat (5.024→4.926, only 0.098 char decrease, 13× weaker). Simulation r_ll=−0.016 (7.3% of VMS −0.219). Gap analysis: LL component gap = 0.203; MID component gap = 0.070. LL gap is ~3× MID gap — LL is the highest-leverage improvement for Menzerath r. Simulation r_mid=−0.108 (61% of VMS −0.178); simulation r_lf=−0.010 ≈ VMS −0.002. ARCHITECTURAL IMPLICATION: cipher_ll generates LL words independently of line length (line length is not a parameter of cipher_ll). VMS has a structural rule where longer lines terminate with shorter words. A new mechanism conditioning p_blind on line length would address this (H511). Section breakdown: stars r_ll=−0.294 (largest section); bio r_ll=−0.208; herbal r_ll=−0.157 (smaller LL contribution, larger MID contribution); astro r_ll=−0.298.
**Limitation:** Component r's are not simply additive to explain total r — the word lengths at LF/MID/LL positions are correlated with each other and with line length in complex ways. The simulation uses N=10×2411=24110 pooled lines (10 trials × 2411 target lines each) vs VMS 2338 valid lines — different sample sizes affect precision. Astro section r_lf=+0.243 (N=50) is unreliable (small N, high noise). The "13× weaker" LL gradient in simulation is not purely an architectural gap — part of the difference may be that VMS's naturalistic line length variation (driven by content and scribal behavior) is larger than the simulation's Gaussian line length model.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** r_ll=−0.219 for VMS LL words is among the strongest single-position Menzerath effects measured in this project. The 13× simulation deficit in LL word-length gradient (0.098 vs 1.31 chars) is larger than any other measured simulation-VMS ratio discrepancy at a structural level. This finding identifies the primary architectural mechanism missing from the current B-dialect simulation.

## F311: Line-Length-Conditional p_blind (H511) Partially Confirmed: cond_mild Achieves 19/19 PASS with Menzerath r +26% (−0.109→−0.137), but r_ll Only Reaches −0.034 (15% of VMS); Deeper Finding: Non-am LL Word Length ALSO Decreases with Line Length (−1.244 chars, Nearly Equal to Total −1.262)
**Experiment:** exp_309_ll_line_len_conditional
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H511 PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. DIAGNOSTIC: VMS LL word decomposition by line length shows that -am rate increases 6.4%→21.6% (n=2-4 → n=11-15) AND non-am LL_wl decreases 5.671→4.426 (−1.244 chars). The non-am LL_wl drop (−1.244) is nearly as large as the total LL_wl drop (−1.262) — BOTH mechanisms contribute approximately equally. In long VMS lines (n=11-15), non-am LL words (mean 4.426) are nearly as short as -am words (mean 4.408 chars); the LL word class itself becomes uniformly short regardless of -am status. MECHANISM: p_blind scaling alone captures only the -am rate component. SWEEP: conditions tested: baseline (p_blind=0.115, 19/19); cond_mild (p_short=0.060 n≤5, p_long=0.180 n≥10, 19/19); cond_moderate (p_long=0.25, 17/19); cond_strong (p_long=0.35, 15/19); cond_very_strong (p_long=0.50, 15/19). Battery failure above p_long=0.18 is due to am_ll inflation exceeding 120% of VMS. FULL N=30 BATTERY at cond_mild: 19/19 PASS; am_ll=7.001 (106.9%), all 18 other metrics within ±20%. Menzerath r: −0.109→−0.137 (+25.7%, now 61% of VMS −0.225). r_ll: −0.016→−0.034 (+113% relative; 15.5% of VMS −0.219). MID slope: −0.050 (86% of VMS). 18th mechanism adopted: cond_mild p_blind (p_short=0.060 for n≤5, linear interpolation to p_long=0.180 for n≥10; mean p_blind=0.126).
**Limitation:** p_blind conditioning captures only the -am rate component of VMS LL_wl gradient. The non-am LL_wl decrease (−1.244 chars) requires a distinct mechanism (H512: line-length-conditional suffix selection for non-blind LL words). cond_mild is the maximum 19/19-stable p_blind conditioning due to am_ll inflation ceiling. r_ll=−0.034 (15% of VMS) is substantially below target (−0.219) because the non-am word length mechanism is not yet implemented.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** The finding that non-am LL_wl decreases −1.244 chars with line length (nearly matching the total −1.262 drop) is a strong structural constraint on the architecture.

## F312: VMS Non-am LL_wl Gradient Is Driven by "Other"-Suffix (Unrecognized Ending) Words Increasing with Line Length (22.5% → 42.6%); Recognized Suffix Length Stays Flat (2.97–3.12); Beta_ll Suffix Bias Is Mechanistically Wrong for This Target
**Experiment:** exp_310_ll_suffix_bias_cond
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H512 REFUTED as formulated. DIAGNOSTIC: VMS non-am LL word suffix mean length is flat across line lengths (n=2-4: 2.972 chars → n=11-15: 3.124 chars — slight increase); the short/long recognized suffix ratio barely changes (short: 42.6%→38.8%, long: 57.4%→61.2%). The VMS LL_wl gradient (−1.245 chars, n=2-4→n=11-15) is driven by the "other" suffix category increasing from 22.5% (short lines) to 42.6% (long lines, +20pp). "Other" words are systematically shorter than recognized-suffix words, pulling down mean non-am LL_wl in long lines. Suffix-length-bias mechanism (beta_ll) tested: beta_ll_base=0.20 achieves 19/19 battery (metric-level N=30 aggregate) and improves r_ll from 15.7%→36.1% of VMS (−0.034→−0.079), but nonam_delta only reaches −0.213 chars (17% of VMS −1.244). The mechanism depresses LL word length uniformly across line lengths rather than creating a gradient, because beta_ll also applies (weaker) bias to short lines. 19th mechanism NOT adopted. PEARSON r(line_len, nonam_LL_wl) = −0.222 (VMS, N=2071 non-am LL words); r(line_len, all_LL_wl) = −0.217.
**Limitation:** "Other" suffix categorization depends on the current SUFFIX_PATTERNS list. Some words in the "other" category may have suffixes not recognized by the pattern matching (e.g., single 'y', bare 'n'). The mean suffix length computation excludes "other"-category words, so the flat mean_suf_len finding only applies to recognized-suffix words. Different SUFFIX_PATTERNS would give different "other" rates.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** The "other" category increase (+20pp from short to long lines) is the primary VMS LL_wl mechanism.

## F313: Word-Length Filter for LL Non-Blind Path (H513 CONFIRMED): 19th Mechanism — max_ll_len(n)=max(3,round(8−0.3×max(0,n−5))) Achieves 19/19 PASS, Menzerath r −0.163 (73% of VMS), r_ll −0.206 (94% of VMS), Largest Single-Mechanism Menzerath Gain in Project History (+12pp)
**Experiment:** exp_311_ll_word_len_filter
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H513 CONFIRMED. MAJOR RESULT: Line-length-conditional LL word-length filter (19th mechanism) achieves 19/19 PASS (N=30), Menzerath r=−0.163 (72.6% of VMS −0.225, up from 61.2%), r_ll=−0.206 (94.0% of VMS −0.219, up from 15%). This is the largest Menzerath r improvement in project history (+11.4pp). Sweep (N=10 per condition): mild_s30 (max=8→7→6→5 as n increases from 5→8→12→15) is optimal — r_ll=97.6% (essentially VMS), menz_r=75.6%, 19/19; stronger conditions overshoot r_ll (mod_s40: 137.8%; strong_s50: 170.4%); weaker mild_s20: r_ll=55.3%. DIAGNOSTIC: VMS non-am LL words in long lines increasingly use shorter-onset classes: d (15.1%), l (14.3%), other (10.1%) at n≥9 — natural consequence of word-length selection (shorter-onset words pass the cap more easily). Sim n=11-15 nonam_wl=4.410 matches VMS 4.426 at long end; sim n=2-4 nonam_wl=5.114 vs VMS 5.671 at short end (pre-existing deficit). nonam_delta=−0.675 chars (54.3% of VMS −1.244); the short-line deficit compresses the endpoint gradient even though r_ll is 94%. 19th mechanism parameters: base_len=8, slope=0.3, n_ref=5, MAX_RETRY=10. Architecture: Menzerath r progression — 45% (exp_287) → 48% (exp_306) → 61% (exp_309) → 73% (exp_311).
**Limitation:** Same-seed comparison (SEED+7777) used for baseline vs mild_s30, eliminating seed variance. Sweep was N=10 (higher variance); full N=30 confirms mild_s30 19/19. The pre-existing short-line LL word length deficit (sim 5.114 vs VMS 5.671 at n=2-4) is not addressed by this mechanism; a separate mechanism would be needed to raise short-line LL word length. The parameter mild_s30 was chosen as best-calibrated (r_ll≈VMS) but was not verified as strictly optimal across a finer grid.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** r_ll improvement from 15% to 94% of VMS in a single mechanism addition is the most impactful single-mechanism change since the copy-buffer architecture.

## F315: Bidirectional LL Word-Length Filter (H515 REFUTED): Hard Minimum + Longest-Fallback Massively Overshoots r_ll (154-205% of VMS) for All Tested Conditions; Short-Line LL Deficit Requires Softer Mechanism; 20-Mechanism Architecture Confirmed at 87-90% Menzerath r
**Experiment:** exp_313_ll_bidir_filter
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H515 REFUTED in current form. Hard minimum word length (min_ll=6-7 for n≤5) + longest-fallback rejection sampling causes massive r_ll overshoot in all tested conditions: min6_n4 (r_ll=154%), min7_n4 (r_ll=158%), min6_n5 (r_ll=171-185%), min7_n5 (r_ll=200-205%). No condition stays near VMS target (100% r_ll). Root cause: (1) "pick longest" fallback strongly biases toward very long words (mean=6.4 at n=2-4 vs VMS target 5.671); (2) at n=2-4, LL words are a large fraction of total words (50% in 2-word lines) — any length bias has outsized effect on r_ll. Diagnostic: VMS LL word length by bucket n=2-4:5.684, n=5-6:5.334, n=7-8:5.181, n=9-10:4.679, n=11-15:4.422. Sim baseline (20-mech, N=30): n=2-4:5.007, n=11-15:4.277. The short-line deficit (sim 5.007 vs VMS 5.684 at n=2-4, Δ=−0.677 chars) persists. BASELINE CONFIRMATION: 20-mechanism architecture at N=30 (new seed): 19/19 PASS, Menzerath r=−0.197 (87.5%), r_ll=−0.209 (95.4%), r_mid=−0.146 (82.0%). Combined with exp_312's 90.2%, establishes seed-dependent range of 87-90% for 20-mechanism Menzerath r. 21st mechanism NOT adopted.
**Limitation:** min_ll=4-5 (softer minimum below VMS target of 5.684) not tested. A Gaussian preference weighting (no hard minimum, just weight toward longer words) is untested and could enable calibrated short-line boost. The "pick longest" fallback is more aggressive than a neutral fallback — a softer fallback would reduce overshoot but likely not eliminate it at min_ll=6-7 since those values systematically exceed the VMS target. The negative result applies specifically to hard-rejection + longest-fallback with min_ll=6-7.
**Commitment status:** Not committed.
**Magnitude context:** Establishes that the short-line LL deficit cannot be fixed by the most natural "mirror" implementation of the max_ll_len mechanism.

## F323: Body Character Distributions by Onset Class (H521): Four Structural Discoveries — (1) d-onset B0-B3 = a+i+i+n (daiin template character by character); (2) y-onset B0 = 80% Gallows (k+t=79-81%): y-onset is y+Gallows Compound Class; (3) A/B B0 Reversal for ch/sh: B uses 'e'-primary, A uses 'o'-primary; (4) No Exclusive Characters — Distributional Not Categorical Onset Boundary
**Experiment:** exp_321_body_char_distribution
**Date:** 2026-04-11
**Finding:** H521 ANSWERED. Four structural discoveries. (1) d-ONSET BODY = DAIIN TEMPLATE: d-onset B0-B3 traces "d+a+i+i+n" letter by letter. B-dialect: B0='a' 73%, B1='i' 40% (also l=25%, r=21%), B2='i' 42%, B3='n' 49%; A-dialect: B0='a' 70%, B1='i' 53%, B2='i' 55%, B3='n' 64%. A-dialect daiin template even more dominant (64% n at B3 vs 49% in B), consistent with F297 (daiin=32.5% A-d vs 21.7% B-d). Non-daiin forms visible at B1 (l=25%, r=21% for dal/dar). d→-aiin constraint (F289) operates CHARACTER-BY-CHARACTER at B0-B3, not just as suffix selection. (2) y-ONSET = y+GALLOWS COMPOUND: y-onset B0 is 80% gallows characters: B-dialect k=44%, t=36%, p=7%, c=5% (combined gallows=94.2%); A-dialect k=43%, t=38%, p=6%, c=5% (95.1%). y-onset B1: e=44%, a=25% (vowel followers of gallows in EVA). y-onset words are structured as y(onset)+gallows(B0)+vowel(B1). This explains why y-onset is a LF grammar-word class (F293): y+gallows compounds are positional formulas, not content words. No other onset class places gallows at B0 — this is a qualitatively distinct body character set. (3) A/B DIALECT B0 REVERSAL FOR ch/sh: B-dialect ch B0: e=60%, o=13%; sh B0: e=73%, o=10%. A-dialect ch B0: o=48%, e=30%; sh B0: o=45%, e=39%. A-dialect uses 'o' as primary ch/sh body character while B uses 'e'. This is the character-level manifestation of the A/B suffix shift (B: chedy/shedy dominant → A: chol/shor dominant). (4) NO CATEGORICAL CHARACTER BOUNDARY: No EVA characters are exclusive to any single onset class's body at B0-B2. The boundary is DISTRIBUTIONAL (same characters, dramatically different frequencies), not categorical. Cross-onset B0 matrix: d uses 'a' 73× more than 'e'; sh uses 'e' 41× more than 'a'. THREE B0 GROUPS: {d,s}='a'-primary; {qok,ch,sh,ok}='e'-primary (B) or 'o'-primary (A for ch/sh); {y}=gallows-primary.
**Limitation:** MID words only; y-onset 'c' at B0 may represent 'ch' compound (not bare 'c'); the daiin-body tracing is inferential from character frequency (word-type confirmation would require type inventory); small N for s-onset (A: 97 words).
